articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The United States Capitol Police (USCP) on Tuesday arrested a California man after officers spotted a guillotine in the back of a pickup truck in broad daylight, just steps from the U.S. Capitol.

USCP officers said Philan-Tam-Duy Le, 35, of Julian, had driven across the country before officials spotted the guillotine near Capitol Hill, close to the Supreme Court building.

According to officials, the pickup truck was illegally parked, while the device stood upright in the truck bed.

PIRRO SAYS US HAS ‘CROSSED THE RUBICON’ AS PEOPLE TRAVEL TO DC FOR POLITICAL VIOLENCE

USCP officers arrested Philan-Tam-Duy Le, 35, of Julian, California, on Tuesday after finding a guillotine propped in the back of his pickup truck. (United States Capitol Police)

Le was arrested and charged with carrying a dangerous weapon in connection with his possession of the guillotine.

Investigators are now examining what motivated Le to travel from California and what prompted him to bring the massive guillotine with him.

"USCP investigators are going through the suspect’s background to learn more about why he came to Washington, DC," officials said.

The guillotine discovery is the latest in a series of unusual weapons found in and around the Capitol complex, one of the most heavily secured areas in the country.

8 INDICTED IN PLANNED SNIPER ATTACK AT WHITE HOUSE UFC 250 EVENT, DOJ SAYS

Capitol Police arrested a California man after finding a guillotine in his pickup near the U.S. Capitol. (United States Capitol Police)

More than a week ago, officials found a homemade sword and brass knuckles at a Senate office building, Fox 5 DC reported. The items were reportedly discovered inside a man's bag during a security screening.

Last year, a man was arrested after a machete and knives were discovered at a screening checkpoint in the Capitol Visitor Center (CVC), according to USCP. The 44-year-old man was arrested on multiple counts of carrying a dangerous weapon, officials said.

A massive guillotine was found in an illegally parked pickup truck near the US Capitol on Tuesday. (Ken CEDENO / AFP via Getty Images)

In 2021, a California man was arrested after officers discovered an unmarked truck displaying White supremacist symbols near the Democratic National Committee headquarters after midnight, according to USCP. A bayonet and machete were found inside the vehicle, officials said.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

articles.title: Infantino has no future at FIFA, says European Leagues chief
articles.excerpt: Gianni Infantino ⁠cannot have a future at FIFA, European Leagues president Claudius Schaefer has said, stressing the importance of reforming world football’s governing body and the responsibilities of...
articles.body_text:
Gianni Infantino ⁠cannot have a future at FIFA, European Leagues president Claudius Schaefer has said, stressing the importance of reforming world football’s governing body and the responsibilities of its boss.

In ⁠an interview with The Athletic published on Wednesday, Schaefer said European Leagues, which represents 53 professional men’s and women’s football leagues, was deeply concerned about Infantino’s leadership.

“We question his suitability to continue as ⁠president. Here in Switzerland, we’ve had a close view of FIFA, and it seems that the influence of the president has grown from year to year,” he added.

“Major decisions are taken without meaningful consultation with stakeholders who will be affected.”

Schaefer’s comments come amid a bitter conflict among governing bodies, prompted by FIFA’s now-abandoned ‌proposal to sell off a slice of the World Cup’s commercial rights.

Infantino is under pressure from three confederations to resign, including Europe’s UEFA, Asia’s AFC and CONCACAF, which represents North and Central America and the Caribbean. The sport’s regional bodies have also discussed a potential vote of no confidence against the FIFA chief.

Concerns have been raised over the inaugural FIFA peace prize awarded to United States President Donald Trump in December and the ⁠overturning of a ban for USA forward Folarin Balogun during this year’s World ⁠Cup following a call from the Republican leader.

“FIFA is an association under Swiss law and in this association you have rules. The president and the board members have to perform their duties with care. This is a legal matter,” Schaefer said.

“If you take ⁠such a decision [as the peace prize] without even informing the council, that, in my view, is a breach of law. And then, during the World ⁠Cup, we all know about the red card issue.

“It was a ⁠real scandal. I can’t ever recall a political intervention of this kind relating to a sporting matter. Such acts call the integrity of the game into question. That’s why there is no future at FIFA for Infantino. There can’t be.”

Infantino will be seeking ‌re-election for a fourth term next year and will likely face stiff opposition, but Schaefer said it was more important to redefine the role of FIFA president than it was to get someone else ‌into ‌office.

“For us, getting these reforms is the most important task, and they can only happen with another president,” he added.

articles.title: Bill Gates calls for ‘human reserved’ jobs in face of AI takeover
articles.excerpt:
Microsoft co-founder also expresses concern governments not prepared for technology’s impact in 6,000-word essay

Bill Gates has called for “human reserved” jobs in certain sectors to prevent AI repla...
articles.body_text:
Microsoft co-founder also expresses concern governments not prepared for technology’s impact in 6,000-word essay

Bill Gates has called for “human reserved” jobs in certain sectors to prevent AI replacing them, and expressed concern that governments are not prepared for the impact the technology will have.

In a 6,000 word essay titled The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make are critical, the billionaire Microsoft co-founder likened the need to spare roles from digital encroachment to how nature reserves operate to protect the environment.

“Many jobs will disappear forever,” he said, in his first lengthy piece on AI in three years. “I believe that as AI and robots improve, we’ll set aside certain things for only people to do.

“I’ve started calling this domain human reserved. I like the phrase human reserved because it makes me think of nature reserves - places where we could put buildings and roads, but we choose not to because the loss would be too great.”

He cited examples including the health professionals who cared for his father, who died of Alzheimer’s disease six years ago.

“Something in the care they gave my dad was irreplaceably human, no robot could or should have done it,” he said. “Imagine a robot giving you the awful news that you have an incurable disease. There’s no technical reason why it couldn’t. Yet it shouldn’t.”

Wednesday’s essay is one of Gates’s first major public interventions since he became embroiled in the Jeffrey Epstein scandal. An external review commissioned by the Gates Foundation found last month that there had been about 30 meetings between Epstein and foundation leaders and staff – including Gates – between 2011 and 2014.

Gates, who has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s crimes, remains chair of his $89bn (£65bn) charitable foundation and previously said he regretted “every minute” he spent with the sex offender.

Gates warns in his essay that governments are not prepared for the scale of the impact of AI.

“The highest priority is a monumental task: creating a domestic and international framework for dealing with AI,” he wrote. “After the attacks of 9/11 the US government went through its biggest reorganisation since World War II for the purpose of improving just one function, national security.

“AI will require much, much more. It will affect national security as well as employment, education, taxation, energy, elections, air and water, public health, the financial system, law enforcement, transportation, public lands and IT systems.

“It is fair to wonder whether the world’s institutions are up to the task of designing and implementing this new architecture.”

Gates also said that as part of a global effort “some co-operation between the US and China will be required”.

His staff are working to set up a meeting with China’s president, Xi Jinping, in November to discuss global efforts to mitigate the growing risks posed by AI.

Gates last met with Xi three years ago, when he became the first foreign entrepreneur the Chinese president had hosted since the global Covid pandemic.

The tech billionaire also expressed concern in his essay about the impact of AI on education.

“Ironically, the same tool that will allow people to learn more than ever could also lead to many people learning less,” he wrote. “One preliminary survey suggested that heavier AI use was associated with less critical thinking. The effect was stronger for young people.”

articles.title: Darline Graham wins South Carolina GOP nomination to replace her late brother in US Senate – US politics live

South Carolina chooses Darline Graham as Republican nominee for...
articles.body_text:
Sister of late Lindsey Graham, who has been backed by Trump, overcomes concern about lack of experience to win place on November ballot

South Carolina chooses Darline Graham as Republican nominee for US Senate

One of the oldest abortion rights groups in the US is endorsing Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee in Maine’s critical US Senate race, according to details first shared with the Guardian.

Reproductive Freedom for All is supporting Jackson, the former state senate president, in challenging Susan Collins – the five‑term Republican incumbent who has been dogged on the campaign trail for her role in overturning abortion access in the US.

Collins voted in 2018 to confirm conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh to the supreme court. In 2022, Kavanaugh joined the majority opinion overturning Roe v Wade, a landmark abortion rights protection. In the aftermath, more than a dozen states enacted near‑total abortion bans. This year’s midterm elections mark the first time Collins is on the ballot since the decision.

“Flipping the Maine Senate race is a critical path to winning a Senate majority, and we do not restore a federal right to abortion without flipping the Senate majority,” said Mini Timmaraju, the group’s president.

Timmaraju will join Jackson on Wednesday in Brunswick for the launch of the campaign’s Women for Troy coalition.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Senator Darline Graham has won the Republican nomination to replace her late brother, Lindsey, on South Carolina’s general election ballot.

Her success marks another win for president Donald Trump after he threw his support behind the political novice.

Graham defeated US representative Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s special Republican primary runoff, two weeks after they were the top two finishers in a 10-way primary.

With nearly all of the ballots counted, Graham had received 52.4% of the vote, according to the Associated Press, ahead of Norman’s 47.6%.

Lindsey Graham, a US senator for more than two decades, won the party’s primary in June, but died the next month. Days later, Darline Graham, was appointed to serve out the remainder of her brother’s Senate term.

“The critics say I shouldn’t run for the Senate,” she told a rally audience Friday. “They say I’m not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged.”

Graham will face the Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a Charleston-area pediatrician, in November. Andrews faces steep historical odds; the last Democrat to win a statewide race in South Carolina was state superintendent Jim Rex in 2006.

Trump recommended the appointment of Darline Graham, a career civil servant who was head of South Carolina’s Commission for the Blind, then encouraged her to run for a full term – upending a Republican scramble to select a new Senate nominee.

“What I really want you to do is pretend – please – that I’m on the ballot,” Trump said at a rally in Myrtle Beach on Friday. “Just come and vote.” Trump’s Maga Inc Super Pac spent more than $800,000 in support of Graham during the campaign.

The US supreme court lifted one of two injunctions that block the Trump administration from pressing ahead with a sweeping effort to restrict mail voting

The court’s decision “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections”, justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote in a blistering dissent.

The NAACP, which sued in April to block the order to restrict mail-in voting, said that Republicans are trying to make it harder to vote in November because they “know full well that they are unpopular and will lose in a free and fair election”.

The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for asylum status in the United States, according to US state department documents obtained by the Associated Press.

Donald Trump responded to criticism of his new tariffs on Canadian imports from the premier of Ontario, Doug Ford, by comparing him unfavorably to his late brother, Rob Ford, a former mayor of Toronto best known for smoking crack.

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced that the US has begun an “unprecedented” sanctions campaign against Iran “and its enablers”.

articles.body_text:
Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair royal correspondent and co-host of "The Royals Uncensored," says Prince George passed Eton's admissions process like other applicants before accepting his place at the prestigious school.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are expected to steer clear of releasing photos, making comments or generating other news that could overshadow Prince George’s highly anticipated first day at Eton College, according to a royal expert.

"The Sussexes have assured the King that they will not hijack or derail major royal events, notably the first day of school term for Prince George at Eton," royal broadcaster Neil Sean told Fox News Digital. "By that, no pictures or comment from either one on that day in September."

A representative for Archewell told Fox News Digital: "This is not something we would comment on." Kensington Palace did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The reported understanding comes as the Prince and Princess of Wales prepare for a major family milestone. Kensington Palace confirmed in June that George, 13, will attend Eton beginning this September, following in the footsteps of both his father, Prince William, and his uncle, Harry.

PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON WRESTLED WITH MAJOR DECISION OVER PRINCE GEORGE'S FUTURE: EXPERT

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle won’t "hijack" Prince George’s start at Eton, according to a royal expert. (Getty Images)

Royal commentator Amanda Matta told Fox News Digital that George’s arrival at the prestigious boarding school carries significance beyond a typical first day.

"Prince George’s start at Eton isn’t just a personal milestone; it’s the beginning of his public-facing path as heir to the throne," Matta said. "The Palace is incredibly protective of that narrative, and any competing headline — especially one involving Harry and Meghan — threatens to distract from the ‘steady, future-focused’ brand the Prince and Princess of Wales have worked so hard to build."

PRINCE WILLIAM ‘BLINDSIDED’ BY HARRY, MEGHAN RETURN AS KATE FEARS NEW TURMOIL FROM ROYAL FEUD: EXPERTS

She added that, while the matter may not weigh heavily on Prince William and Kate Middleton personally, it could be important to palace staff working to keep the focus on the future king.

Prince George of Wales is said to be excited that he'll be attending Eton College in the fall. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"It would certainly be a shame for his first days at Eton to see him embroiled in a ‘feud’ narrative with his uncle and aunt," Matta said.

In a statement shared with The New York Times last week, a spokesperson for the Sussexes said, "On the heels of a wonderful trip with family and friends this summer, Harry and Meghan have decided to spend an extended period in the U.K. this autumn. They are excited to have their children spend more time in the country that’s such an important part of their family’s story."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

The spokesperson confirmed that the couple’s businesses will remain unchanged and based in the U.S. Meghan and Harry will also keep their home in California.

Matta said the reported agreement may reflect an informal attempt to avoid competing headlines during significant occasions, though the couple's public profile makes a complete break from the royal news cycle unlikely.

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex will be returning to the UK this fall.  (Chris Jackson - Pool/Getty Images)

"The Sussexes generate headlines simply by existing in public space," she said. "That’s been true since 2018 and hasn’t changed with their location or job titles."

PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE'S UK RETURN SIGNALS ‘SPECTACULAR DEFEAT’ AS ROYAL EXPERTS WARN OF WILLIAM SHOWDOWN

"If they also want to avoid collisions, it would require a level of coordination with the Palace that seems very unlikely given the current climate," she said. "Harry and Meghan have not conferred with the Palace about their personal or professional plans for several years now."

The more realistic outcome, Matta said, may be "an informal understanding of when to lay low, and when an overlap could be workable."

While palace aides may be concerned about maintaining the royals' carefully planned media strategy, Matta cautioned that not every competing headline is the Sussexes’ doing.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Prince Harry and Markle have been residing in Montecito, Calif. with their two children.  (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Palace aides know better than anyone how quickly a delicate PR plan and media cycle can be dominated by a competing story," she said. "It’s not necessarily even about the Sussexes’ actions, but it’s completely up to the editors running headlines."

MEGHAN MARKLE RETURNS TO BRITAIN WITH PRINCE ARCHIE AND PRINCESS LILIBET FOR FIRST TIME IN YEARS

She added, "Meghan stepping outside will generate headlines even if it’s just to buy groceries or ice cream with the kids."

British broadcaster Hilary Fordwich echoed that concern, telling Fox News Digital that even the absence of a Sussex appearance can fuel coverage and public speculation.

"Just their mere presence or lack thereof will now be making headlines and, indeed, likely to clash with royal priorities and media focus on causes," she said.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle stepped away from royal duties in 2020.  (Matt Dunham - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

Fordwich said George’s first term at Eton should remain "private" and serve as "a life transition for both him and the family," who live nearby in Windsor.

Matta said the reported restraint could represent a tentative attempt at a "headline truce," but she questioned whether the pressure to plan their lives around the royal calendar should fall entirely on Harry and Meghan.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"The U.K. tabloid press will manufacture that narrative regardless of what the Sussexes do," she said. "What they can control is their own family and their own goals."

The couple tied the knot in 2018.  (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)

Sean noted that the alleged agreement will face its first major test when George begins school next month.

"We can only assume that they will stick to their word," he said. "But this will be an interesting development."

Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.

articles.title: Missouri grandma ordered to stop serving free breakfasts refuses to back down, 'They are my family'
articles.excerpt:
Kathy Kite says she's "just a grandma cooking a meal" for her small community as health officials say she needs a permit.

A Missouri grandmother says she was frightened she could end up in legal trou...
articles.body_text:
Kathy Kite says she's "just a grandma cooking a meal" for her small community as health officials say she needs a permit.

A Missouri grandmother says she was frightened she could end up in legal trouble after county health officials told her to stop serving free homemade breakfasts without a permit, but she told Fox News Digital she has no intention of giving up the morning tradition that brings her tiny community together.

"I'm not gonna stop providing for my community," Kathy Kite of Harrisburg, Missouri, told Fox News Digital in an interview Tuesday. "I wouldn't stop feeding my children, I wouldn't stop feeding my family. I'm not gonna stop feeding my community cause they are my family….This is bigger than that. It's about love and appreciation because they appreciate what I do."

Kite has been cooking a free breakfasts for her neighbors and friends since May. In July, she received a letter from the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department that said she needed to obtain a food permit or face possible legal action.

YOU SHOULDN’T NEED A PERMIT TO PRAY IN YOUR OWN HOME — THE SUPREME COURT SHOULD AGREE

Missouri grandmother Kathy Kite prepares breakfast for her friends and neighbors. (Kathy Kite)

"I got the letter in July, it upset me, because I didn't understand what I was doing wrong," Kite said. "It hurt my feelings, and it upset me because I knew at that point I was afraid I was gonna go to jail because the letter stated that if I didn't stop making breakfast for my community, that I was facing fines and jail, and so I posted it on Facebook and people responded."

The Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department denied that their letter threatened jail time, in comments to Fox News Digital.

Kite said that after the local gas station where she works stopped serving breakfast following COVID, regular customers kept asking for it, so she invited them to her home and began cooking breakfast for them, herself.

Kite said that what began as an early-morning breakfast for a few regulars quickly spread across the town of fewer than 300 people. More residents began stopping by for coffee and breakfast, staying to talk about farming, the weather and childhood memories. The growing sense of community motivated her to wake up even earlier to cook, and soon local mothers were bringing their children by for breakfast before school.

ORTHODOX JEW ASKS SUPREME COURT TO HEAR CASE AFTER CITY ALLEGEDLY TARGETED HIS HOME PRAYER GROUP

Kathy Kite stands by a slow cooker of breakfast food she has prepared for her friends and family. (Kathy Kite)

Kite said the letter from the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department says that she must install a commercial kitchen in her home.

"In order for me to comply with what they're asking, I would have to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars to have a commercial kitchen in my home," Kite said. "I live in a 115-year-old home. It's a beautiful home. I'm not gonna jeopardize the integrity of my home to put a commercial kitchen in to make some free burritos."

She said she would welcome city officials into her home so they could see firsthand what she is doing.

"Come have a burrito. I'm [not] doing anything wrong. I don't, I just, I can't understand. Come to my home, see my home, and see that my home is not dirty," Kite said. "I don't have cats. I'm not making people sick. I am just a grandma cooking a meal for my friends and family and enjoying life."

The Goldwater Institute sent a letter Thursday to the Boone County health department demanding they answer questions by Friday about their legal reasoning. The group said that no lawsuit has been filed to date, but it is on the table.

GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS

Kathy Kite assembles a breakfast sandwich at her home. (Kathy Kite)

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Dave Roland, Goldwater Institute's director of allied litigation, said, "Kathy’s story is a textbook example of bureaucracy run amok. Citizens should not be required to get the government’s permission before offering passers-by some coffee and a bite to eat while they socialize. The government exists to protect this sort of neighborly kindness, not to punish it."

The Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department told Fox News Digital that food permits are not required when providing food for family and friends, but a permit is required when providing food to the public, citing the Missouri food code.

"At the time the complaint was received, Ms. Kite’s home had an open sign, tip jar, advertised food on social media and a sign in her yard — all things that are typically associated with a food establishment," the spokesperson said.

"No citations or cease-and-desist orders were issued," the statement continued. "We also did not threaten jail time. We sent a letter to Ms. Kite following a complaint we received that food served in her establishment made someone ill. Our role in public health is to work with food establishments to promote safe food practices and prevent food-borne illnesses. There are safe, allowable ways to provide homemade food to the community with and without a food permit. We regularly work together with individuals and businesses who want to provide free food to the community."

Rachel del Guidice is a culture reporter for Fox News covering the intersection of politics, faith, family, and American culture.

articles.title: New data shows record number of arrests and deportations of immigrants in the US
articles.excerpt:
Trump administration has moved away from high-profile, militarized raids as its deportation spree has ramped up

The Trump administration arrested and deported a record number of immigrants in July, a...
articles.body_text:
Trump administration has moved away from high-profile, militarized raids as its deportation spree has ramped up

The Trump administration arrested and deported a record number of immigrants in July, according to newly released government data – apprehending an average of 1,500 people and removing 1,100 people daily.

This latest data confirms what attorneys and immigrant advocates have been seeing across the US – although the administration has moved away from the high-profile, militarized raids that came to define its immigration enforcement approach last year, it is quietly ramping up its operations.

“The way that people are being detained is far less flashy, but we are still continuing to see arrests,” said Melissa Shepard, director of legal services at the southern California-based immigrant services group ImmDef. “It’s just on a quieter scale instead of, you know, 10, 12 officers making one arrest, you have a handful of officers pulling someone over.”

Overall, 49,571 people were arrested last month, according to government data obtained by the Deportation Data Project – the highest number since October 2022, and a 15% increase from the previous record set in June of this year.

Despite the administration’s insistence that it is targeting criminals, a record number of people caught in the surge of arrests in July had no prior criminal history. July was the first month during the second Trump administration that the majority of people – 51% of arrestees — had no criminal convictions or charges, according to the Guardian’s analysis.

Removals were also at a record high in July. Nearly 34,000 people were removed from the US last month, the most since the start of the second Trump administration.

Boosted by a $70bn funding surge, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) – the agency that oversees ICE and the border patrol – has been working to ramp up to the White House goal of 2,000 arrests every day. Immigrants are being arrested when they report to mandated appointments at ICE offices, at traffic stops, outside their homes and, increasingly, at US airports.

“I think it’s just they’re looking for any way to be able to continue to detain people,” said Shepard. “They are being creative.” In recent weeks, she said, ImmDef has advised even clients with pending or valid immigration statuses, who are legally cleared for travel, to avoid flying due to the uptick of enforcement.

Attorneys are also advising clients with temporary protective status (TPS) to make sure they apply for different forms of immigration relief after the supreme court cleared the way for the administration to strip the designation from 50,000 Haitians and 6,100 Syrians.

In the past month, the administration has been particularly focused on enforcement in the Springfield, Ohio, area, where a large group of Haitians with TPS had settled in recent years. Advocacy groups in Springfield said that Haitians were being called in to ICE offices and fitted with ankle monitors.

The first deportation flight to Haiti since the supreme court decision landed last week. TPS for Salvadorans is set to expire in September – ending protections for 170,000 people.

“I am anticipating and a little afraid for what it’s going to look like with the end of TPS,” said Shepard. “I think we are at the precipice.”

ICE’s enforcement powers have also been boosted by the rapidly expanding 287(g) program – which deputizes local law enforcement agencies to carry out immigration enforcement. Markwayne Mullin, the DHS secretary, called the program “the greatest partnership we can have” – and said it was a key part of his goal to conduct enforcement in a “more quiet way”.

Attorneys and advocates told the Guardian that these sorts of immigration arrests can go unnoticed in many communities, because it can be difficult for passersby to discern whether a local police officer is making a routine traffic stop or an immigration apprehension. Volunteer groups that, amid the militarized raids last winter, had trained to document ICE arrests and take down details to help locate those in detention later are now recalibrating how to track enforcement in their cities and provide assistance.

articles.title: Wiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with Canada
articles.excerpt:
Paper products among hardest-hit sectors after trade negotiations broke down, with 25-50% tariffs estimated

Are you a Canadian boycotting US products? We’d like to hear from you

Using the bathroom o...
articles.body_text:
Paper products among hardest-hit sectors after trade negotiations broke down, with 25-50% tariffs estimated

Are you a Canadian boycotting US products? We’d like to hear from you

Using the bathroom or having a cry is about to become more expensive for North Americans as the US and Canada enter a full-fledged trade war that threatens to flush away decades of peaceful trading between the two nations.

After trade negotiations broke down between the two countries last weekend, Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, vowed to match US tariffs “dollar for dollar” and unveiled a list of nearly 900 American goods that will face 25% to 50% tariffs starting on 8 September.

Paper products are among the hardest-hit sectors, with Canada threatening to put tariffs of between 25% and 50% on “toilet paper or face tissue stock” from 8 September in retaliation for a 50% hike from Washington DC.

Though American toilet paper and tissues are often made domestically, they heavily rely on lumber-rich Canada for raw materials. Procter & Gamble, the owner of Charmin toilet paper, said last year that it would have to increase prices amid tariffs that were in place at the time.

The US imported $328m worth of toilet paper from Canada in 2024, according to the World Bank, making it by far the largest exporter of the product to the US. Retailers including Costco source much of their paper products from the country.

The US accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption despite having only 4% of the world’s population. The average American uses 141 rolls of toilet paper per year, making them No 1 for No 2s globally, just ahead of Germans, each using an average of 134 rolls annually.

It’s not just paper products that could rise in price. The trade war highlights the deep economic ties shared between the two countries as consumers continue to worry about inflation on both sides of the border.

US tariffs are specifically affecting Canadian liquor, including popular whiskey brands Crown Royal and Canadian Club, which are currently under a 50% tariff.

While Canada has not introduced a tariff on American liquor, most Canadian provinces have introduced their own bans on American alcohol, in retaliation for earlier tariffs on Canadian products. Donald Trump used these province-wide bans on American alcohol as part of his legal justification for his new tariffs against Canada.

Carney has asked province leaders to consider putting American liquor back on the shelves, though as the Nova Scotia premier Tim Houston told CBC News: “Whether Nova Scotians or Canadians will actually buy it when it’s back on the shelves, that’s a whole other discussion.”

Trump also said that his new tariffs are in retaliation for Canadian levies against the American dairy industry. He introduced a 50% tariff on nearly all Canadian dairy products, with the exception of Canadian cheese.

In response, Canada has a 50% tariff on American dairy products, along with a 25% tariff on American cheese.

Canada also took a swing at the US fishing industry, with a 25% tariff on American fish and seafood, including frozen lobster. The move prompted Republican senator Susan Collins, facing a tough re-election battle in lobster-capital Maine, to call Trump’s latest move “a mistake”.

A 25% tariff on Canadian cars and auto parts is set to affect the American auto industry, which relies heavily on Canadian parts for manufacturing. Trump has threatened to double the tariff to 50% if a deal isn’t made by 1 January 2027.

With negotiations down the drain, it’s unclear if or when the tariffs will be lifted. But the Trump administration is adamant that “there’s no possible way” the trade dispute with Canada will affect US consumers, according to Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative.

“The fundamentals are good,” he said. “I don’t think this is going to affect anything.”

articles.title: Sonya Massey’s family says death of sheriff’s deputy who killed her ‘doesn’t feel like justice’
articles.excerpt:
A cousin says death of Sean Grayson in prison ‘doesn’t give Sonya back her life or return her’ to her children

The death in prison of the former Illinois sheriff’s deputy convicted of murder after fa...
articles.body_text:
A cousin says death of Sean Grayson in prison ‘doesn’t give Sonya back her life or return her’ to her children

The death in prison of the former Illinois sheriff’s deputy convicted of murder after fatally shooting Sonya Massey in her home “doesn’t feel like justice to me”, a cousin of the woman has said in an emotional statement.

“It doesn’t give Sonya back her life or return her back to her [two] children”, who were aged 15 and 17 at the time of the killing, Sontae Massey wrote in the statement on Monday. Referring to Sonya Massey’s mother, the statement continued: “It doesn’t give my aunt back her daughter. And it doesn’t give our family the accountability were still waiting for …

“Sonya should still be here. That is the loss we are still living with.”

Sontae Massey’s statement provided a notable reaction to the death of the former Sangamon county deputy Sean Grayson, which was announced on Sunday by his attorney, Daniel Fultz.

Grayson, 32, was diagnosed with stage three colon cancer in 2023. The cancer had spread to his liver and lungs, according to his legal team, by the time of his sentencing in January, when he was given 20 years’ imprisonment for a second-degree murder conviction in connection with Massey’s killing.

The Illinois prison review board in late July had denied Grayson a medical release that he requested. At that proceeding, Sontae Massey spoke in opposition to the former deputy’s request, saying: “I’m not sure that I can write, speak or articulate anything that can encompass the devastation that Sean Grayson has created for our family.”

Grayson, who was white, shot Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman, to death amid a 6 July 2024 encounter that was captured on body-worn camera video.

The footage showed Grayson and another deputy enter Massey’s home in Springfield, Illinois, to investigate reports of a prowler that she had called in herself.

At one point, Massey picked up a pot of boiling water from her stove, prompting Grayson to back away, according to court testimony.

Grayson later testified that he feared Massey would throw the boiling water on him after she twice said, “I rebuke you in the name of Jesus.” He said he interpreted the remark to be a threat.

The body camera video showed Grayson then pointing his gun at Massey and threatening to shoot her. On the video, she apologized and dropped to the floor – but he fired three times, striking her in the face and killing her.

Jurors presiding over Grayson’s trial heard, among other things, that he declined to offer her first aid.

The case prompted anti-racism protests and a federal justice department review.

And the Illinois governor, JB Pritzker, signed the Sonya Massey Act, a law requiring stricter background checks for policing hires. Sangamon county officials also agreed in early 2025 to a $10m settlement for Massey’s family.

In his statement after Grayson’s death, Sontae Massey wrote that his family had “been asked to carry more than most people can imagine today”, particularly Sonya’s mother, Donna.

And Grayson’s death just six months into his sentence meant that “Aunt Donna … [is] being asked to absorb something else connected to the loss of her daughter”, Sontae Massey’s statement said.

“I’ll be clear about this for myself, too,” he added. “I’m angry.”

articles.title: College baseball player fatally shot after trying to enter wrong house, mom says
articles.excerpt: From his dream of teaching history to his love of baseball, a heartbroken mother shares the story of her son’s life—and the tragic mistake that cut it short. Erin Pysher's son, Glen "Bubba" Pysher, wa...
articles.body_text:
From his dream of teaching history to his love of baseball, a heartbroken mother shares the story of her son’s life—and the tragic mistake that cut it short. Erin Pysher's son, Glen "Bubba" Pysher, was fatally shot on Aug. 23, 2026.

A college baseball player was fatally shot by police in Pennsylvania after he accidentally tried to enter the wrong home after a night out, his family said.

The Office of Montgomery County District Attorney Kevin R. Steele confirmed to Fox News Digital that Glenwood "Bubba" Pysher IV, 22, was killed on Sunday, Aug. 23

Investigators say a 911 call came in early Sunday, just after midnight. The Upper Pottsgrove Township Police Department responded to a call about a possible break-in at a home on Snyder Road.

WATCH: TERRIFYING MOMENT SPEAR-WIELDING MAN LUNGES AT CALIFORNIA COPS BEFORE SHOTS RING OUT

Pysher was allegedly coming back from a bar after a night out with friends before he was shot and killed. (Erin Pysher)

The DA's office confirmed police arrived on scene "to find a male in the rear of the residence," he said.

They said police shot and killed him after an "encounter."

ARIZONA POLICE SHOOTING SUSPECT ARRESTED, ANOTHER REMAINS AT LARGE AFTER KILLING 1, WOUNDING FIANCEE

Pysher was a college baseball player who had made stops at Francis Marion University, Northampton Community College and Holy Family University, and was preparing for his senior year at St. Elizabeth College in New Jersey, according to his obituary.

His mother, Erin Pysher, told Fox News Digital her son was not armed when he was allegedly "shot twice" by an officer.

"He's never been in trouble—he was a good kid. I don't know what prompted the cop to think that the shooting was necessary," she said.

Before he was fatally shot, he was "bar-hopping with friends" and walked up to a home on the street he had mistaken for a friend's and tried to get in, his mother said.

Glenwood "Bubba" Pysher, center, is pictured with his parents, Glen and Erin, at Pottsgrove High School in 2022. (Pottsgrove School District)

"I dropped him off with his friends at a bar to celebrate his friend's 21st birthday," she said. After the bar, the men were headed to a friend's house to continue their evening.

The friends eventually split up, Pysher said. She told Fox News Digital her son opted to walk to the house.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"He took a wrong turn and ended up at the wrong house," she said.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

"After a few drinks, he didn't realize it—he was at their back door knocking, thinking it was his friend's house, saying, 'Hey, let me in,'" Erin Pysher said. "The homeowners, not knowing, called the cops saying it was an attempted burglary."

"He was the biggest sweetheart—carefree and loving. He loved life, loved hanging out with his friends, and fishing. Baseball was his life; he played it in college and was getting ready to leave Sunday afternoon to start his senior year. He wanted to become a history teacher and coach baseball," she said.

The Upper Pottsgrove Police Department in Pennsylvania. (Google Maps)

The police department confirmed the officer involved was placed on administrative leave following the incident.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

The DA's office told Fox News Digital, "The fatal shooting is an active investigation. When the investigation is complete, we will provide media with the findings."

"He was a great kid; I couldn't ask for a better son. A little jokester—we had our inside jokes, and he loved teasing his three younger sisters. There's a huge hole in our life without him. He was the best kid ever; I don't know how else to describe him," Erin Pysher said.

articles.title: One US dollar now costs 2 million rials in Iran, and here’s what it can buy
articles.excerpt: The Iranian rial has fallen to a new all-time low against the US dollar, dropping past 2 million rials to $1 on the free market after Washington launched its toughest sanctions yet in efforts to stran...
articles.body_text:
The Iranian rial has fallen to a new all-time low against the US dollar, dropping past 2 million rials to $1 on the free market after Washington launched its toughest sanctions yet in efforts to strangle Tehran’s economy.

Iran’s economy has been crippled by decades of US and international sanctions, especially over its nuclear programme – the Iranian rial has crashed and inflation woes are piling up misery for people. The US-Israel war on Iran, launched on February 28, worsened the economic woes for the country of some 92 million people.

To understand how much everyday items now cost, Al Jazeera tracked the prices of food, clothing and medicines on the streets of Tehran, comparing them with what the same goods cost in the days before the war.

Before the war, 2 million rials could buy about 4kg of tomatoes, half a kilo of chicken and a little less than a litre of cooking oil.

Today, the same amount buys about half as much, with the average price of tomatoes increasing by 71 percent, chicken by 74 percent and cooking oil by 177 percent.

The price of insulin, the baseline survival for diabetics, has shot up by 642 percent, while essential medicine like paracetamol has become dearer by 93 percent, and baby formula, largely subsidised by the government, has become costlier by 95 percent.

The graphic below breaks down the average costs of food, clothing and medicine before the war and on Wednesday. Prices remain highly volatile, and the figures reflect average values.

For Iranian families, this has meant changing not only how much they buy, but also what they eat.

Afsaneh*, a 35-year-old mother of a one-year-old who lives with her husband in Tehran, says her family’s weekly grocery bill has increased by 20 to 30 percent.

“Before the war, we could think about what we wanted to do three or six months down the road, but now our only concern is making it to the end of the month with the income we have,” Afsaneh told Al Jazeera.

“My husband and I both work, and we have a one-year-old child. The daily cost of childcare at daycare centres has now reached around 500,000 tomans [5 million rials or $2.5], which is difficult for us to afford.”

Toman is the term Iranians use for the rial as an unofficial unit equal to 10 Iranian rials, widely used because it makes the country’s large currency figures easier to manage.

The government subsidy on baby formula helps families like Afsaneh’s, but their monthly wellness checkups and nutritional supplements are not covered by insurance, making it difficult to afford quality care for their infant.

For Afsaneh, their small family is limited to survival and covering food and other necessities. “Many purchases, such as new clothes or upgrading our car, have been cut from our plans. And I don’t think things are going to get better anytime soon,” she said.

War damage has disrupted production, while a US naval blockade of Iranian ports has complicated imports and exports.

While the falling rial has pushed up the cost of goods, sanctions have restricted Iran’s access to international markets. At the same time, wages have failed to keep pace.

The government-approved minimum wage for the current Iranian calendar year ending in March 2027 is 166 million rials ($82). With government assistance and benefits, the figure comes to less than 220 million rials ($108).

Zamir*, a 35-year-old man from Tehran who works in men’s retail fashion, told Al Jazeera that sales have dropped by 40 percent compared with last year, and he is struggling to keep his business running.

“I can say that it is completely predictable that many of the people working in this market will go bankrupt before the end of winter and will have no choice but to shut down their businesses,” he says.

“Everything has become more expensive,” Zamir explains. “Workers’ wages, the cost of raw materials, and just about anything else you can think of have gone up.”

He says many retailers are selling their summer stock below cost, and in the autumn this new wave of price increases will be reflected in retail stores.

“From the moment you leave your house until you get back home, you spend at least 2 million tomans [$10] on things like coffee, cigarettes, water, and transport. Even if you are extremely careful with your spending, you still have to spend at least 700,000 to 800,000 tomans [$3.5-4] a day, and that doesn’t include regular groceries and household necessities,” Zamir said.

For those living on salaries, inflation creates another problem: the value of today’s pay can fall before the next payday.

Salama*, 28, is a mother of one who works as a fisher in Hormozgan, Iran’s southern coastal province, overseeing the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.

For her, the rising cost of groceries has had a big impact.

“We used to do our weekly grocery shopping for around 500,000 tomans [$2.5], but now we have to spend at least 5 million tomans [$25] for the same groceries, and we’ve had to cut back on things like meat and chicken or eliminate them altogether.”

Salama* says her income, instead of increasing, has actually decreased, forcing her to limit expenses severely.

“Even a simple cold medicine for children or seasonal allergy medication, including Iranian brands, now costs around 300,000 tomans [$1.5], and even a simple visit to a general practitioner costs no less than 1 million tomans [$5],” she says.

The war did not create Iran’s economic problems, but it has magnified them. War damage, disrupted production and the blockade have added new pressures, while unemployment and stagnant purchasing power have reduced families’ ability to absorb them.

For millions of Iranians, the question is no longer how much prices have risen, but how much of a month’s food, housing and necessities a month’s salary can still buy.

*Names have been changed to protect identities.

articles.title: Extreme heat linked to deaths of over 40,000 people in England between 1988 and 2025
articles.excerpt:
ONS data shows rising toll of climate crisis, with officials warning this summer on track to set further records

Over 40,000 more people died on the hottest days in England between 1988 and 2025 than...
articles.body_text:
ONS data shows rising toll of climate crisis, with officials warning this summer on track to set further records

Over 40,000 more people died on the hottest days in England between 1988 and 2025 than would be expected, according to data published by the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday.

The figures do not include this summer, when England has sweltered under a succession of heatwaves and is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths. The UK Health Security Agency announced on 30 July that an estimated 2,877 people had died in the May and June heatwaves alone. The total is almost double the figure for the whole summer in 2025.

The number of people dying prematurely due to high temperatures is expected to rise further as the climate crisis caused by the burning of fossil fuels continues to push up temperatures and the population ages. Elderly people, as well as children and the unwell, are particularly vulnerable to heat. The heat in 2027 will be further exacerbated by the super El Niño weather system now building in the Pacific Ocean.

Emergency departments in England’s hospitals have experienced their busiest period ever this summer, with almost 2.5 million patients attending A&E each month in May, June and July and the heat cited as a main reason. Nurses were collapsing during shifts amid “inhumane and impossible” conditions caused by extreme heat, their union warned earlier in August.

London had the highest number of deaths attributable to the hottest temperatures, the ONS said. The London ambulance service has dealt with 25,000 more calls this summer than last, surpassing the record number seen during the peak of the Covid-19 pandemic.

Historically, more deaths in England were associated with the coldest temperatures than the hottest. There were 139,000 deaths associated with the coldest days between 1988 and 2025, according to the ONS data. However, the agency said: “The proportion of deaths associated with the hottest days has increased in recent years, and the gap between heat- and cold-related deaths is narrowing.”

In continental Europe, at least 35,000 more people died during the baking-hot summer than would normally be expected, according to figures available so far from barely half the continent.

The heatwave that scorched western Europe in late June was the most severe and widespread ever recorded and was only possible due to the climate crisis driven by fossil fuel burning, scientists found. The World Health Organization said in May that heat-related mortality in its European region had increased by more than 30% over the past 20 years.

Rising global heat kills one person a minute around the world, according to a major report published by the Lancet in October.

articles.title: At least eight killed as Nepal flash flood damages roads, energy facilities
articles.excerpt:
Nepal sent helicopters to the rescue after a huge flash ⁠flood swept away villages, killing at least eight people and damaging roads, bridges and power projects in areas near Tibet, authorities said.
...
articles.body_text:
Nepal sent helicopters to the rescue after a huge flash ⁠flood swept away villages, killing at least eight people and damaging roads, bridges and power projects in areas near Tibet, authorities said.

The waters were too high for helicopters to land in Nepal’s affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in the mountainous district of Rasuwa, with a population of about 50,000, officials said on Wednesday.

“There could be heavy casualties or loss of property,” district administrator Narendra ‌Pariyar told the Reuters news agency. “But I cannot say for sure now.”

Pariyar urged those living on the banks of the Bhote Koshi River in the area to seek higher ground, pointing to reports that nearby villages and infrastructure project sites were washed away.

Across the border, Tibet reported “major casualties” with people missing in the neighbouring county of Gyirong after a mudslide ⁠hit a land crossing between China and Nepal, the Xinhua official news agency said.

The mudslide hit China’s Gyirong port, cutting off roads, communications and power in the Shigatse region, Xinhua added, without giving details.

President Xi Jinping urged “all-out” efforts to search ⁠for the missing, and ⁠called for strengthening monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary disasters.

As the flood swept through Nepal’s northern Rasuwa district, videos shared by Nepal Police and others on social media showed torrents of muddy water crashing through mountain valleys.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah convened an emergency meeting of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority to take stock of the situation.

“Work has started to take necessary steps in coordination with the medical team, scouts, and Red Cross,” Shah said in a social media post.

The Nepal Army said it had deployed helicopters and disaster response personnel to the affected area.

“The work of collecting details of the damage is under way,” it said in a statement.

The Nepal Electricity Authority said about 430 megawatts of production capacity, including from hydropower and solar facilities, have been damaged.

“The disaster has damaged the production, transmission and distribution facilities of the Authority … resulting in disruption of electricity supply,” it said.

Several highways were also closed, authorities said.

The ⁠Bhote Koshi River originates in Tibet ⁠and empties into Nepal’s Trishuli River that eventually flows into India as the Gandak River.

A flood last year in the Bhote Koshi River killed nine people, ‌with 24 missing, and washed away the “Friendship Bridge” linking Nepal and China, disrupting transport and trade for several months.

That flood ‌was ‌triggered by the draining of a supraglacial lake in Tibet, a regional climate monitor said.

Monsoon rains from June to September regularly trigger deadly floods and landslides across South Asia.

Scientists say climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events in the region.

articles.title: Ukrainian drone attacks kill 3 as fire destroys Wildberries warehouse
articles.excerpt: Separate Ukrainian drone strikes across Russia have killed at least three people, while another attack triggered a massive blaze at a warehouse belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries in the...
articles.body_text:
Separate Ukrainian drone strikes across Russia have killed at least three people, while another attack triggered a massive blaze at a warehouse belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries in the Tambov region.

Tambov Governor Yevgeny Pervyshov said on Wednesday that the ‌logistics centre was “completely destroyed by fire”. He said earlier that about 100,000 square metres (1.1 million square feet) of the facility were set ablaze, the equivalent of 14 football pitches.

One person was injured in the strike, he wrote on the Telegram messaging app. He did not say if the fire had been extinguished.

The overnight strike targeted the Wildberries logistics centre in Kotovsk, about 500 kilometres (310 miles) southeast of Moscow.

Another industrial facility in the Nizhny Novgorod region was also damaged in a drone attack, according to the regional governor.

In the Lipetsk region, a man and a 14-year-old were killed in a fire lit by a falling drone, while a woman was killed in a drone attack in the Belgorod region bordering Ukraine, the Reuters news agency quoted local authorities as saying on Telegram.

Ukraine has been hitting Wildberries facilities since mid-July, and it has also targeted the retailer’s main rival, Ozon, in recent days.

The two companies dominate one of the fastest-growing segments of the Russian economy, which is otherwise close to stagnation after four and a half years of Russia’s war on Ukraine.

Ukraine has accused Wildberries of having a role in Russia’s military supply chain. Moscow and the company say its facilities are used for civilian purposes.

Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed 426 Ukrainian drones during the night, including over Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.

Both Moscow and Kyiv have repeatedly denied targeting civilians since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. But strikes on both sides of the front have intensified in recent months, causing a growing number of civilian casualties.

articles.title: Abortion rights group endorses Democrat Troy Jackson in critical Maine Senate race
articles.excerpt:
Reproductive Freedom for All – one of the country’s oldest pro-choice groups – backs Jackson in his fight against Republican Susan Collins

One of the oldest abortion rights groups in the US is endors...
articles.body_text:
Reproductive Freedom for All – one of the country’s oldest pro-choice groups – backs Jackson in his fight against Republican Susan Collins

One of the oldest abortion rights groups in the US is endorsing Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee in Maine’s critical US Senate race, according to details first shared with the Guardian.

Reproductive Freedom for All is supporting Jackson, the former state senate president, in challenging Susan Collins – the five‑term Republican incumbent who has been dogged on the campaign trail for her role in overturning abortion access in the US.

Collins voted in 2018 to confirm conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh to the supreme court. In 2022, Kavanaugh joined the majority opinion overturning Roe v Wade, a landmark abortion rights protection. In the aftermath, more than a dozen states enacted near‑total abortion bans. This year’s midterm elections mark the first time Collins is on the ballot since the decision.

“Flipping the Maine Senate race is a critical path to winning a Senate majority, and we do not restore a federal right to abortion without flipping the Senate majority,” said Mini Timmaraju, the group’s president.

Timmaraju will join Jackson on Wednesday in Brunswick for the launch of the campaign’s Women for Troy coalition.

Jackson, a former logger who began his political career as a Republican, once cast votes restricting abortion access before reversing course years later. He has expressed regret for his record and his earlier belief that abortion should “never be legal”.

In a July interview with MS Now, Jackson said he recognized he had been “wrong”.

“Early on, I wasn’t real clear on reproductive rights. But I had a lot of conversations over time. A lot of conversations with women, doctors, community members, just people that I came to trust,” he said. “And it became more and more clear to me that abortion access was healthcare.”

Since 2017, Jackson has held a 100% rating from Planned Parenthood and has become one of Maine’s most consistently pro‑choice Democrats. In 2023, the year after the supreme court overturned Roe v Wade, he co‑sponsored legislation expanding abortion access to include medically necessary procedures after fetal viability.

His evolution has extended beyond reproductive rights: Jackson has also shifted his positions on marriage equality and other social and economic issues, emerging as one of the Pine Tree State’s leading progressives during his time in the legislature.

“[Jackson] in many ways reflects the reality of a majority of independents and Republicans in this country who now support abortion rights, but might personally have felt conflicted in the past,” Timmaraju told the Guardian. “Having someone like Troy in the Senate who can talk to his Republican colleagues and talk to some of those moderate Democratic colleagues who don’t have the same courage that he has is actually going to be a huge value add for our movement.”

In June, Collins – who has long cast herself as a moderate Republican supportive of abortion access – said she did “not regret that vote” for Kavanaugh. Jackson’s campaign has seized on the remark to tie her to the Trump administration’s anti‑abortion agenda. “She can defend that vote all she wants. I’m running for Senate to restore and expand the federal right to abortion and make damn sure politicians never again get to take this freedom away from Mainers,” Jackson said in a statement.

Planned Parenthood’s Super Pac announced this month it would spend more than $600,000 on ads criticizing Collins’s record on abortion in Maine.

But strategists in both parties note that Collins’s seniority in Congress – and the millions of federal dollars she has steered back to Maine over the years – has historically proven difficult to beat. In a midterm shaped by record inflation, affordability concerns, and the military conflict with Iran, they argue her vote to confirm Kavanaugh may not be top of mind for many Mainers weighing their choices at the ballot box.

Jackson – who mounted an unsuccessful bid for governor earlier this year – secured the Democratic nomination in July at a snap convention. He replaced Graham Platner, the oyster farmer who exited the race after facing allegations of sexual assault, which he denies.

The turmoil around the race “gave us pause”, Timmaraju said, explaining the group’s decision to wait before endorsing Jackson. “We needed a little bit of time to regroup. We needed to follow the lead of people on the ground in Maine.”

articles.title: The Bulgarian village that fears becoming an Iranian target
articles.excerpt:
Bezmer, Bulgaria – The news landed on Saturday, bringing relief to nearby villagers: two United States Air Force (USAF) refuelling aircraft had left Bulgaria’s Bezmer airbase.

“The USAF air tankers t...
articles.body_text:
Bezmer, Bulgaria – The news landed on Saturday, bringing relief to nearby villagers: two United States Air Force (USAF) refuelling aircraft had left Bulgaria’s Bezmer airbase.

“The USAF air tankers took off yesterday and left Bulgaria,” the country’s defence minister, Dimitar Stoyanov, announced, as President Iliana Yotova declared: “For now, this mission is over.”

The US Air Force said the Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers, intended to aid Washington’s war on Iran, had left to support “other operational requirements”.

The village had spent weeks worrying that the aircraft could make their area in southeastern Bulgaria a target for Iranian attacks.

Tehran had urged Bulgaria against allowing its territory to be used for the US and Israel’s military operation against Iran. Later, citing unnamed Iranian sources, the Financial Times reported that in the event of Washington’s escalation in Iran, Iranian forces had “assessed striking US assets in southeastern European countries such as Bulgaria” after Sofia had approved the use of its Bezmer airbase for US refuelling aircraft.

“I pray to God that our village won’t be attacked,” a woman working at a local grocery shop, who requested anonymity, told Al Jazeera days before the tankers left. “We are scared, but nothing depends on us.”

Although the planes are gone, geopolitical tensions – as well as fears in Bezmer of being drawn into the US-Israel war on Iran once again – persist.

This week, Stoyanov told reporters that Iran had carried out an effective hybrid operation, aided by Bulgarian politicians in the opposition.

“Unfortunately, this hybrid operation will continue,” he predicted in comments understood to have been directed at the opposition. Stoyanov did not elaborate further.

In Bezmer, a village of about 1,000 people that sits beside the base, Bulgarian military aircraft have long been part of the landscape. Many residents work at the base, according to Rosen Rusev, the mayor, and the sound of aircraft overhead is routine.

But in late July, the Bulgarian government proposed – and Parliament approved – the deployment of as many as eight US Air Force Stratotankers and up to 250 personnel.

Within two days, residents of Bezmer and nearby villages had collected more than 3,000 signatures against the deployment and held peaceful protests.

They did not want their village to become part of the war on Iran.

Rusev said a buzzy atmosphere took hold of Bezmer on Friday, when residents realised the tankers had left.

“Now they feel their voice is finally heard,” he told Al Jazeera. “It happened just as they wanted.”

The government had moved to reassure residents. Stoyanov said military intelligence had identified no threat to national security, the US aircraft or other facilities in Bulgaria. A United Kingdom assessment requested by the government had reportedly judged the risk as extremely low.

But reassurances did little to calm everyone.

With temperatures soaring to about 30 degrees Celsius (86F), two friends, Dinka Todorova, 67, and Ganka Vlaeva, 78, sat in plastic chairs in the shade.

Both have children who work at the airbase.

“We shiver day after day and pray that the war doesn’t come here,” Vlaeva said. “We are the first target, and many people will die.”

“And children, too,” Todorova added quietly. “For the ambitions of the greedy.”

Vlaeva said she was disappointed with the government and lawmakers, accusing them of ignoring the villagers’ petition.

“They don’t want to hear the voice of the people who elected them,” she said.

Not everyone in Bezmer shared that concern.

Ivan, a 33-year-old who sat beside the village church with his electric bicycle nearby, said that “groundless panic” was spread “recklessly”.

“There’s no danger for the village,” he concluded.

He is more worried about the possibility of interceptor missiles, or “something coming from Russia across the Black Sea”.

As residents protested, Antoniya Ivanova, whose father is a serviceman at the base, hung a white sheet over an aerial photograph of Bezmer. Animated films were projected onto it for children “to wind down the accumulated stress”, she explained.

“We’re the most innocent in this whole situation,” she said. “We didn’t want those aeroplanes near our homes.”

Children filled the playground as the afternoon cooled.

“Maybe there is a chance of attacks, but I think the media exaggerates,” said Tsonka Moskova, a mother in the village. “Whatever is meant to happen will happen. Those above us decide – the government. They are to blame.”

A low-flying AS532 Cougar helicopter passed overhead. Nobody looked up. The residents are accustomed to Bulgarian military aircraft.

Rusev, the fourth-term independent mayor, spent days trying to navigate between the villagers’ fears and officials. The protests were not an attempt to bring down the government, he said.

“We just wanted adequate information about the potential threats if the planes remained stationed here and what the guarantees for our safety were,” he said.

Social media made the situation harder, he added.

In Facebook groups, officials and experts struggled to compete with thousands of comments, many speculative and panic-inducing.

Military police also patrolled the village and the area around the airbase, adding to a sense of fear for some, and a sense of safety for others.

While Bulgaria is in the range of some Iranian missiles, some analysts argue that Iran is unlikely to have the capacity – or genuine will – for successful missile attacks against Bulgaria or elsewhere in continental Europe.

On Monday, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said that the tankers had not made a single flight “south from the airport”, but had travelled to fellow NATO member nations for training and exercises.

But also on Monday, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Tehran reserved the right to counter “any action regarded as supporting US and Israeli military aggression” against it.

“We have no issue with the Bulgarian people,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said. “It was previously announced – and reports have also confirmed – that several refuelling aircraft have left Bulgarian territory.

“As many Bulgarian citizens and politicians themselves have acknowledged, this action is contrary to international law and amounts to support for the military aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran.”

Back in the village, a woman said she was not afraid of Iran’s threats.

She did not want to be named or photographed for this article.

“I am definitely not scared. God is keeping us safe,” she told Al Jazeera. “I lie down and sleep in peace, for you alone, Lord, make me live in safety,” she said, reciting a line from the Bible.

articles.title: Now you seafood, now you don’t: $350k worth of oysters vanish without a trace in NSW
articles.excerpt:
About 400,000 juvenile Sydney rock oysters were taken from an oyster farm on state’s mid-north coast earlier this year, police say

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Police ...
articles.body_text:
About 400,000 juvenile Sydney rock oysters were taken from an oyster farm on state’s mid-north coast earlier this year, police say

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Police are on the hunt for a seafood swindler after 400,000 oysters were allegedly stolen from a farm at a river on the New South Wales mid-north coast.

About 320 bags of juvenile oysters, worth an estimated $350,000, were taken from an oyster farm in Scotts Creek, Oxley Island, earlier this year, according to NSW police.

Officers received a report of the theft on Tuesday morning and are urging members of the public with CCTV or dashcam footage to come forward.

Latitude 31 Oyster Co, which runs a Sydney rock oyster farm on Manning River adjacent to Scotts Creek, on Tuesday revealed it had been the target of a “massive” oyster theft that had been reported to police.

“Oyster theft impacts far more than just the individual farmer. It affects our businesses, our families and the reputation of the entire NSW oyster industry,” the business wrote in a social media post.

“There are a lot of good people in this industry, and we know farmers look out for each other.”

The business urged the community to look out for anyone who is trying to move, or has suddenly come into possession of, a large quantity of cocktail or bistro-sized oysters.

Latitude 31 Oyster Co said the stolen oysters were not ready for immediate sale and would need to be grown for another four to six months.

Guardian Australia has contacted Latitude 31 Oyster Co to confirm the thefts are the same.

Oyster farmer Gary Rodley, who owns Tathra Oysters on the NSW south coast, said fully grown oysters could be worth significantly more, estimating they could fetch about $1.50 to $2 a piece.

The age of the stolen molluscs and the amount taken suggests the culprit could be a fellow producer, he said.

“That’s not a theft where someone’s getting a feed of oysters,” he said.

“That’s disturbing to think that it might be a one of our peers in the industry.

“It’s a very high-risk activity that person’s carrying out, and I would fancy that they would come unstuck very quickly doing that sort of thing.”

A Manning River oyster farmer, who wished to remain anonymous, said there had been a recent shortage of the coveted Sydney rock oyster.

Major flooding in 2021 and 2025 wiped oyster stocks in the region, and because Sydney rock oysters are farmed on a three-year cycle, it could take another two years before farmers’ incomes stabilise.

“The worst case scenario is it could be someone within the industry that has had a shortfall, who has gone past that area of the river and knows it only gets used certain times of year, and they’ve gone ‘they’ll never know until they get back’,” he said.

Theft is not uncommon in the Manning River area, but when he has been targeted, his oysters were taken by locals who had all year to scope out the area.

The farmer took the issue into his own hands and bought an artificial oyster with a tracker from France that cost more than $2,000.

It allowed him to take a thief to court in 2022, where the culprit was fined $500.

Many oyster farmers, including Rodley, have bought surveillance equipment to act as a deterrent as demand for Sydney rock oysters has grown.

“They’re a rare oyster that only grow up and down the New South Wales coastline, so they’re a very, very small percentage of the world’s oyster crop,” he said.

“It’s regarded as probably the best flavoured oyster in the world by a lot of people – they’re a very flavoursome oyster and highly regarded as a table oyster that’s eaten natural.

“That’s a particular set of circumstances that a lot of people value highly.”

A crime scene has been established and police investigations are ongoing.

articles.title: Brighton & Hove Albion sign Algerian left-back Jaouen Hadjam
articles.excerpt:
Algerian defender Jaouen Hadjam has joined Brighton & Hove Albion from Swiss champions Young Boys for an undisclosed fee on a contract until 2031, the Premier League club has confirmed.

Brighton anno...
articles.body_text:
Algerian defender Jaouen Hadjam has joined Brighton & Hove Albion from Swiss champions Young Boys for an undisclosed fee on a contract until 2031, the Premier League club has confirmed.

Brighton announced the signing on Tuesday with a video showing the left-back sipping mint tea in a cafe.

Hadjam joins Manchester City’s Rayan Ait-Nouri and Hull City’s Mohamed El Bachir Belloumi as Algerian internationals playing in the Premier League.

Former Leicester City and Manchester City winger Riyad Mahrez is arguably the most famous and successful Algerian to have played in the league.

The Paris-born player represented France at youth level before switching allegiance to Algeria in 2023. He has earned 21 caps for his country.

Hadjam, 23, made 98 appearances for Young Boys in all competitions after joining the Swiss side from Ligue 1 club Nantes in 2024. He played in Paris Saint-Germain’s youth academy.

He was part of Algeria’s squad at the FIFA World Cup 2026, where he played in three of the team’s four matches.

Brighton started their league campaign by beating Europa League holders Aston Villa 4-0 on Sunday.

articles.title: Dog treat founder eats her own products, even packs them in her kids' lunches
articles.excerpt: Sarah Goldberger, New York-based founder and CEO of Lord Jameson, tells Fox News Digital how ingredients like blueberries create colorful canine snacks and demonstrates the quality of the products by ...
articles.body_text:
Sarah Goldberger, New York-based founder and CEO of Lord Jameson, tells Fox News Digital how ingredients like blueberries create colorful canine snacks and demonstrates the quality of the products by eating one herself.

It's National Dog Day, and one dog treat creator thinks dogs should be included in the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) initiative, which emphasizes whole, nutrient-dense foods.

"We have never used anything artificial," Sarah Goldberger, New York-based founder and CEO of organic dog treat company Lord Jameson, told Fox News Digital.

"We've never used fake food coloring. We've never used fake flavoring. All of our bright, beautiful colors come from real fruits and vegetables."

CHEAP, HEALTHY FOOD IS REJECTED BY MOST AMERICANS EVEN AS MAHA MOVEMENT PUSHES IT

Since becoming an official federal initiative in February 2025, the MAHA Commission has promoted a greater focus on whole, nutrient-dense foods while calling for reductions in refined carbohydrates, added sugars and certain artificial additives.

Goldberger believes those nutritional priorities will "translate into the pet space."

Lord Jameson founder Sarah Goldberger says her company avoids artificial colors, flavors and preservatives in its dog treats. (Lord Jameson)

"My hope is that as a brand, we can inspire other pet brands to make better choices to really impact the lives and the health and wellness of dogs," she said.

Goldberger started Lord Jameson in 2019, inspired by her late dog, Jameson, after noticing what she described as a void in the market for healthier dog treats.

HERE'S WHY DOGS DON'T NEED 'HUMAN FOOD,' SAYS VIRGINIA VETERINARIAN: 'NO REASON FOR IT'

"Jameson had gone through a pretty serious medical issue, and the medication he was being given actually created toxicity in his body," Goldberger said.

Goldberger said she wanted to offer treats made with "completely clean ingredients, organic, gluten-free, no preservatives, no toxins, no artificial colors or flavors."

"So we started working with a homeopathic vet, and we were reminded of the power of plant-based medicine. A lot of the formulas, especially in our wellness products, are meant to serve dogs during a time of needed healing with plant-based products, more herbs and botanicals."

When she set out to create the brand, Goldberger said she surveyed more than 1,000 pet parents and found that many reported their dogs had allergies or sensitivities to various animal proteins, preservatives and food colorings.

Lord Jameson makes organic, plant-based dog treats using fruits, vegetables, herbs and grains. (Lord Jameson)

Goldberger said she wanted to offer treats made with "completely clean ingredients, organic, gluten-free, no preservatives, no toxins, no artificial colors or flavors."

Despite not using preservatives, the treats have an 18-month shelf life, which Goldberger said is "very difficult to achieve in production" and is "another key selling point for us."

Lord Jameson, Goldberger said, has "truly reimagined what dog treats can be and should be."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

She said she eats the treats herself and even puts them in her children's lunchboxes.

They've been a hit with pet owners for a variety of reasons, including what Goldberger described as their effect on dogs' digestive systems.

"As a dog mom myself, I know the frustration when you go to the store, you buy food or a treat, you bring it home and all of a sudden they have diarrhea," she said.

"Because we're using whole-food ingredients and no preservatives, you're going to get a nice firm poop after they eat. It sounds funny to say, but this is something you'll see in a lot of our reviews."

National Dog Day puts the spotlight on canine health, wellness and the choices owners make for their pets. (Lord Jameson)

Goldberger also said the treats can be suitable for some dogs with colitis, diabetes or other specialized dietary needs.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Lord Jameson has since launched a line of "protein-inspired" flavors as part of its Love Puffs line, made with organic sorghum, a whole grain that contains protein and fiber.

Another feature that sets Lord Jameson apart, Goldberger said, is that the brand is "completely vertically integrated," with its manufacturing operations, including its kitchen, warehouse and fulfillment center, based in Boulder, Colorado.
