articles.body_text:
In Indonesia’s Kalimantan, fires have ravaged tens of thousands of acres, with suffocating smoke reaching Malaysia and putting Singapore on alert

Suwadi can barely see five metres in front of him when he steps outside his home in Indonesian Borneo.

Each breath, he says, feels “like smoking a cigarette”.

It has been like this for weeks in Kalimantan, the Indonesian side of Borneo island, where fires have raged across tens of thousands of acres of land, including ancient rainforest, triggering a trans-boundary haze now threatening Malaysia and Singapore.

In West Kalimantan there has been a spike in emergency room visits, with about 5,000 people arriving with respiratory symptoms each week since July, compared with 500 per week in the first half of the year, health ministry data shows.

Children continue to go to school and adults to work, but many are suffering from the unhealthy effects of breathing in thick smoke, constantly. “What about babies, the elderly, and pregnant women who are exposed to this?” asks Suwadi.

Some classes have been suspended, with parents urging schools to switch to online learning.

Fires each year in Kalimantan are often blamed on “slash and burn” techniques used to clear land for plantations that produce palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer.

Authorities say this year’s “super” El Niño may be intensifying the blazes, with the weather phenomenon expected to peak in September.

Experts have warned the worst could be yet to come as the dry season continues into October, and the rains that could extinguish the fires look unlikely before November.

The haze is fast becoming a regional issue, with Malaysia and Brunei agreeing to raise it at Asean as thick smoke from forest and peatland fires drifts across the border.

On Tuesday, the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur, was the most polluted city on earth, followed by Jakarta, according to air quality monitoring company IQAir. Almost 600 schools in the Malaysian state of Sarawak on Borneo island closed due to hot and dry conditions. Singapore went on alert.

On social media, Indonesians have tried to draw attention to the issue – highlighting the huge blazes in Kalimantan, and also in Sumatra, West Papua, and in Lombok where a fire destroyed a traditional Sade village over the weekend.

Forestry ministry data shows that nearly 94,000 hectares (232,000 acres) have burned nationwide this July alone.

On Monday, the Indonesian president, Prabowo Subianto, ordered authorities to revoke the business permits of corporations suspected of directing the land clearing, state news agency Antara reported. Indonesian police arrested 72 people suspected of starting fires in Borneo and Sumatra, with most accused of deliberately burning land to clear areas for plantations.

The response comes as regional experts fear this could be another devastating fire year, with many of Indonesia’s most severe blazes occurring during El Niño cycles. In 2015, another El Niño year, more than 6m acres were burned, with trans-boundary haze again plaguing neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore.

During a recent visit to the region, Prabowo promised government resources to contain the fires, including helicopters and water pumps.

But some Indonesians have expressed frustration at what they see as government inaction against the companies allegedly involved.

Indonesia’s unique rainforests are home to peatland ecosystems, which should be naturally resilient to fire when water tables remain high.

However, drainage networks built to clear land for pulp and oil palm plantations have robbed the soil of its natural capacity to retain water, experts say.

Fires on degraded peatlands are more difficult to control because they burn deep underground, says Justin Sentian, a professor in climate change at Universiti Malaysia Sabahand. And they produce thick, acrid smoke.

“If authorities only act after hotspots appear, they will forever be playing catch-up,” says Sentian. “True prevention must address the soil itself by halting the conversion of peatlands and actively restoring degraded areas.”

On Monday another fire broke out near the factory where Suwadi works in Kalimantan. With houses burning and smoke everywhere, Suwadi says he is afraid for the future of the region.

“The fire is getting dangerously close to homes,” he says, “People are [in] panic now.”

With Agence France-Presse and Associated Press

articles.title: Sydney shark attack survivor describes moment she came to face-to-face with ‘monster’
articles.excerpt:
In her first media interview since the June incident, Leah Stewart, 34, says her thoughts while being bitten were of her one-year-old daughter

An Australian woman who lost an arm after a shark attack...
articles.body_text:
In her first media interview since the June incident, Leah Stewart, 34, says her thoughts while being bitten were of her one-year-old daughter

An Australian woman who lost an arm after a shark attack at a beach in Sydney’s eastern suburbs has recalled the moment she came face-to-face with the “monster”.

Leah Stewart, a 34-year-old teacher and mother of a one-year-old daughter, was attacked by a large shark while on a morning swim at Coogee beach on 13 June.

She remained in a critical condition for more than two weeks while receiving treatment for life-threatening injuries that required the amputation of her arm.

In a snippet from her first media interview since the attack, Stewart recalled that her first thoughts during the attack were of her daughter.

“It was holding onto my leg, then I just thought of August. I thought, ‘She’s not going to have a mum. She’s going to grow up without a mum,’” she told Nine Entertainment.

“I couldn’t handle that. I didn’t want her to not have a mum.”

Through tears, Stewart said the shark’s “face was horrific” and that she would “never forget its face … it was a monster.”

In an update to a fundraiser set up to cover Stewart’s medical procedures and support her family, she said on Sunday that she had been “focused on my healing” and thanked donors.

“After what has been an incredibly difficult few months, I’m so happy that I’ve progressed enough to build some independence, and I can finally see some light after all of this,” she wrote.

“I’ve been actively trying to do everything in my power to get back to some sort of normal life. I still have a long way to go, but my recovery has been remarkable, and a huge part of that is because of the absolute army of love, support, prayers and encouragement surrounding my family and me from all over the world.”

The GoFundMe page has raised more than $558,925 since the June attack. Donations have now been turned off.

“I want to say the biggest thank you for looking after me, for caring for my family, and for being generous enough to help my family through this,” Stewart wrote.

“What you’ve offered has given us enough to recover, to stay in our home, and to give us options for further medical treatment down the road.”

Stewart ended the note by saying she felt as though she had been “given a second chance at life”.

“I’m not going to waste it. As I get better, I know I’ll make something of this second chance and aim to give back even more in generosity, care and love.”

articles.title: Freddie Mercury’s ‘splendid things’ to go on display at V&A
articles.excerpt:
Eight costumes spanning Queen frontman’s career will feature in a free trail developed with his former fiancee

Eight famous costumes worn by Freddie Mercury, including the outfit featured on the cove...
articles.body_text:
Eight costumes spanning Queen frontman’s career will feature in a free trail developed with his former fiancee

Eight famous costumes worn by Freddie Mercury, including the outfit featured on the cover of Queen’s debut album and the catsuit from the video for Bohemian Rhapsody, are to go on display at the V&A in London this autumn to mark what would have been the singer’s 80th birthday.

Freddie Mercury | Splendid Things, a free trail developed with Mercury’s former fiancee and close friend Mary Austin, will run from 24 October 2026 to 17 January 2027. Austin is lending seven of the looks, which span Mercury’s career from the 1970s to his final years.

Among them is a monochrome ensemble worn for an early Queen gig at Imperial College and pictured on the cover of the band’s eponymous debut album. Also on display will be the “Mercury Wing” catsuit, designed by Wendy de Smet and worn during the A Night at the Opera tour in 1975-76, as well as in the groundbreaking Bohemian Rhapsody video.

Mercury’s crown and cloak, designed by Diana Moseley and worn during Queen’s 1986 Magic Tour, will also feature. He wore the outfit for the band’s final live performance at Knebworth that year. The display will also include a costume from the Made in Heaven music video, as well as accessories and items from his personal wardrobe.

The trail takes its name from a remark Mercury made in 1978: “I like to be surrounded by splendid things. I want to lead a Victorian life surrounded by exquisite clutter.”

Austin first met Mercury when she was 19 and he was 24, while they were both working around Kensington’s Biba fashion scene. Mercury, born as Farrokh Bulsara on 5 September 1946 in Zanzibar, was selling his artwork and vintage clothes from a stall in Kensington Market. They became engaged on Christmas Day 1973, the year Queen released their debut album.

Their relationship ended in the mid-1970s, but they remained close for the rest of Mercury’s life. When he died in 1991, he left Austin his Kensington home, Garden Lodge, and his possessions.

Austin has described Mercury’s clothes as central to the image he created as a performer. “The clothes were part of that exploration,” she said in A Life in Lyrics, due to be published in September. “Freddie understood early on that he wasn’t just wearing clothes; he was providing an image to match the scale of the space and the vastness of the crowd.”

Austin said the clothes and costumes to be displayed at the V&A “tell a hugely important part” of Mercury’s story both on and off the stage: “Never mere accoutrements, his costumes and clothes were essential to his performances, creative vision, and wider self-expression, carefully designed to create a lasting visual and emotional impact that has reached across the generations and still reverberates today.”

The installations have been designed by Tom Piper, whose work includes productions for the Royal Shakespeare Company, the Tower of London poppies and the V&A’s Alice: Curiouser and Curiouser and Taylor Swift | Songbook Trail.

Each of the trail’s six stops will be staged differently, using sets, sound and lighting to evoke moments from Mercury’s career.

Kate Bailey, the V&A’s senior curator of theatre and performance, said the display would explore Mercury’s “love of ‘splendid things’” and his interest in art, design and fashion.

articles.title: Europe’s heatwaves threaten insurers’ earnings, rating agency S&P says
articles.excerpt:
Rise in claims linked to heat-related deaths and illness, especially among older people, could drive up premiums

Europe’s intense heatwaves could hit insurers’ earnings as companies face a rise in cl...
articles.body_text:
Rise in claims linked to heat-related deaths and illness, especially among older people, could drive up premiums

Europe’s intense heatwaves could hit insurers’ earnings as companies face a rise in claims linked to heat-related deaths and worsening health conditions, the rating agency S&P has said.

While a long summer of extreme heat will have increased drought and wildfire-related claims, the rating agency said there would also be fallout for life and health insurers, and for the reinsurers who provide financial protection to insurance companies.

That could ultimately translate to higher premiums for customers, as insurers try to cover increased payouts to policyholders.

Europe’s heatwaves, paired with its ageing population, have created a perfect storm, with the health impacts of high temperatures falling disproportionately on older people. That fact has resulted in a wave of life insurance claims over heat-related deaths, and increased demand for private medical services, at a time when rising temperatures have not yet been fully reflected in original contracts.

Between 2004 and 2024, the share of people aged 65 and over in the EU rose from 16.4% to 21.6%, while the proportion of those aged 80 and over rose from 3.8% to 6.1%. “The increasing share of elderly people – who are particularly vulnerable to heat stress – suggests that heat-related mortality in Europe is likely to rise,” the S&P report said .

About 9,000 of the 10,650 excess deaths recorded during the 22-28 June heatwave were among those 65 and over, as rising heat exacerbated underlying conditions such as heart disease and dehydration.

“Beyond heat-related deaths, it’s also deteriorating health conditions and the resulting increase in treatment and hospitalisations that might weigh on re/insurers’ financials and, subsequently, increase premiums,” the report said.

A study in The Lancet Planetary Health recently found that people aged 60 and over face dangers from exposure to heat at much lower temperatures than previously thought. Older adults sweat less, their hearts work harder in the heat, and their blood vessels are less able to widen, limiting their capacity to stay cool.

In the UK alone, the four-day heatwave in May and eight-day heatwave in June together caused 2,877 excess deaths, compared with the 1,504 seen during the summer of 2025.

There has been little reprieve, with the mercury rising beyond 40 degrees Celsius across Europe earlier this month, breaking records in countries including Slovakia, Austria and Hungary earlier this month. And given heatwaves can affect large regions and last for weeks, they could end up compounding financial risks for insurers.

While the heat had not yet hurt company ratings – which indicate how safe or risky their shares or bonds are for investors – that could change over the medium term to long term “as extreme summer temperatures become more frequent and intense, and Europe’s population continues to age”, S&P said.

“We will continue to monitor their impact on the performance of rated re/insurers,” it added.

articles.title: NHS England to offer women ‘gamechanging’ free home testing kits for cervical cancer
articles.excerpt:
NHS has target of eliminating the cancer by 2040, but up to 4 million eligible women are not up to date with screening

Millions of women in England who have missed cervical screening appointments wil...
articles.body_text:
NHS has target of eliminating the cancer by 2040, but up to 4 million eligible women are not up to date with screening

Millions of women in England who have missed cervical screening appointments will be offered free home testing kits on the NHS.

The move comes amid concerns that only two-thirds of women attend in-person cervical screening appointments when asked to do so, leaving as many as 4 million women not up to date.

The rollout is being described as a “gamechanger”, offering a “discreet and convenient option” to encourage more women to get screened.

The kits contain a swab to collect a sample from the vagina. This is then posted back to the NHS free, where it is tested in labs for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV).

If high-risk HPV is detected, patients will then be asked to attend a cervical screening appointment with a clinician.

HPV is a group of viruses that can be passed on through sexual contact and cause no symptoms. About 13 high-risk types of the virus are known to cause 99.7% of cervical cancers.

Starting on Tuesday, eligible women between 30 and 65 who have not attended screening appointments will be sent invitations via the NHS app, text message, email or letter.

They will then be able to order a kit through the app or website. The scheme is part of the NHS’s target of eliminating cervical cancer by 2040.

Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women’s health at NHS England, said: “Screening saves thousands of lives each year by preventing cancers and catching them earlier, but only around two-thirds of women are attending cervical screening appointments when invited by the NHS.

“Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a gamechanger – making it easier than ever for them to get tested for HPV.”

Women aged between 24 and 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years, or more often if HPV is detected.

The latest figures from NHS England show 68.8% of eligible women are up to date with cervical screening, below the 80% target. It means about 4 million women are not up to date, according to NHS estimates.

“There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening – embarrassment, lack of time, or worries about discomfort – and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test,” said Mann.

“So, if you’re invited to take part, please order a test – it’s a simple swab you can do at home in minutes.”

Athena Lamnisos, chief executive of the Eve Appeal, welcomed the move, saying that self-testing at home would be a “step-change” for many women.

Michelle Mitchell, chief executive of Cancer Research UK, said: “Cervical screening is a powerful tool that saves lives – it can prevent cervical cancer or spot it at an earlier stage when treatment is more likely to be successful.

“While it’s best for cervical screening to be done by a nurse or doctor, there are barriers that make it challenging for some people to attend. At-home HPV self-testing kits will help more people take part in a way that works for them.”

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said the aim was to make it as easy and convenient as possible for women to keep up with their screening. She said: “This is the future NHS we are building – there for all of us when we need it, and acting as early as possible to stop preventable deaths.”

articles.title: At least 35,000 excess deaths recorded in Europe’s back-to-back heatwaves
articles.excerpt:
True figure likely to be much higher as it only covers about half of continent and does not include August totals

At least 35,000 more people died during Europe’s four record-breaking, back-to-back h...
articles.body_text:
True figure likely to be much higher as it only covers about half of continent and does not include August totals

At least 35,000 more people died during Europe’s four record-breaking, back-to-back heatwaves this summer than would normally be expected, according to incomplete figures from barely half the continent.

Excess mortality in three of the EU’s larger countries – Germany, France and Spain – alone has already exceeded 25,000, according to the provisional national figures, and experts say the toll will rise significantly once August totals are consolidated.

The consecutive heatwaves across western Europe since May shattered all-time historical temperature records across hundreds of weather stations, and France recorded its hottest national average day on record.

Records fell for three straight days in Germany in late June, when 46 stations topped 40C (104F), while Spain endured persistent highs above 42C. Scientists say human-made global heating is making such extreme events more frequent and intense.

The death toll is highest in Germany, which late last week reported an estimated 14,000 heat-related deaths from 6 April to 9 August. The Robert Koch Institute (RKI) public health agency said 9,600 people had died in the week of 22-28 June alone.

Systematically compiled EU-wide excess mortality figures, available since 2008, show the only other summer week in which a higher rate of additional deaths has been recorded was in July 2022, when Covid-19 was still active.

This summer has been by far the worst for heat-related deaths in Germany since records began. The previous high in the EU’s most populous country was 8,900 in 2018. Heat-related deaths during normal summers are often below 2,000, RKI said.

Figures from the Carlos III health institute’s mortality monitoring system suggest 4,947 deaths in Spain can be attributed to heat between May and this week, making 2026 Spain’s worst year on record for heat-related deaths, exceeding the 4,520 recorded in 2022.

Different countries calculate and present their data in different ways. Spain and Germany model estimated heat-related deaths in real time, comparing daily temperatures and mortality rates to calculate deaths attributable to heat.

Such estimations are necessary because heat is rarely stated as a direct cause of death. In most cases, heat aggravates a pre-existing health conditions such as respiratory or cardiovascular disease, and victims die of a heart attack, stroke or kidney failure.

Final attribution can take weeks or even months, and many countries have yet to release figures even for early August. Karl Lauterbach, a former German health minister, said last week that figures released so far would probably prove to be underestimates.

France, where more than 500 weather stations recorded temperatures higher than 40C and at one stage 98% of the country was under heat alerts, reports an initial “all causes” excess death figure and definitive attribution later.

Its national health agency said last week that “all cause” excess deaths between late May and 22 July stood at 7,300. August figures were not yet available and initial data was based on electronic death certificates, which account for only 80% of total mortality, it said.

Italy, whose national heat surveillance system uses local municipal data, meaning it is often subject to significant delays, has so far only reported incomplete real-time indicators rather than a consolidated national death toll.

Modelling suggests 2,700 more people died than usual between 22 and 28 June alone and epidemiologists have said the country’s total heat-attributable death toll would probably be between 5,000 and 8,000 by the time it is formally recorded.

Other European countries to have already reported excess death tolls include the UK, where the health security agency said in July that its modelling suggested the May and June heatwaves had resulted in 2,877 heat-associated fatalities in England.

Belgium has said its preliminary data shows it recorded a 39% increase in mortality between 18 and 29 June, equating to 1,222 additional deaths, and the Netherlands has said at least 900 more people than usual died between 22 June and 5 July.

A rapid modelling study cited by the European Commission estimates that 1,070 more people than usual died in Poland during the late-June heatwave, and Swiss public health authority data suggests excess heat-related deaths of 220 in the same week.

Early figures from Luxembourg, Greece, Romania, Bulgaria and Denmark indicate about 40 excess deaths in each of those countries. Agence France-Presse has calculated that areas inhabited by more than 80 million Europeans experienced temperatures above 40C this summer.

The World Health Organization said in May that heat-related mortality in its European region had increased by more than 30% over the past 20 years and was on course to climb significantly as a result of the climate crisis and population ageing.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy trial: Postpartum is real, but child killing demands accountability, veteran prosecutor says
articles.excerpt: Jonathan Hatami, who rose to national prominence after prosecuting the murder of Gabriel Fernandez by his mother and her boyfriend in Los Angeles, says anyone who hurts a child, whatever the reason, s...
articles.body_text:
Jonathan Hatami, who rose to national prominence after prosecuting the murder of Gabriel Fernandez by his mother and her boyfriend in Los Angeles, says anyone who hurts a child, whatever the reason, should not be considered a victim themself.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

While failures by people, medical professionals and systems around Lindsay Clancy deserve scrutiny, nothing should erase a parent’s responsibility for killing a child, according to a veteran prosecutor who said he's concerned that public support for the Massachusetts mom is overshadowing the killing of her three young children.

Clancy is accused of killing her three young children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — and trying to end her own life by dropping from a second-floor window after sending her husband to pick up takeout and something from a pharmacy, according to the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office.

But as the case has drawn national attention, Clancy has also attracted supporters both online and in-person at the courthouse, and experts have warned that that support has taken attention away from the victims.

LINDSAY CLANCY'S THREE CHILD VICTIMS FORGOTTEN AMID CROWDS OF SUPPORT: MOTHER OF SIX

Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

"Nobody who murders children is a victim no matter what they’re suffering through," said Jonathan Hatami, a veteran child abuse prosecutor. "You're never a victim if you murder people because victims don't do something. Something happens to them."

(L) Lindsay and Patrick Clancy with two of their three children in this undated photo. (R) Lindsay Clancy listens to testimony from her former mother-in-law at her murder trial in Plymouth Mass., Tuesday Aug. 18, 2026 in Plymouth, Mass. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/ Facebook and Jonathan Wiggs/Pool The Boston Globe via AP)

The defense does not dispute that Clancy caused the deaths — but she has pleaded not guilty and is contesting criminal responsibility.

Hatami has spearheaded a number of high-profile cases against child abusers in Los Angeles, California, including the murder of 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez, who was tortured and killed by his mother and her boyfriend. Gabriel's killing exposed a series of missed red flags by the county's Department of Children and Family Services and inspired a Netflix docuseries.

LINDSAY CLANCY DEFENSE SCORES ‘EXTREMELY HELPFUL’ PSYCHOSIS CONCESSION AS EXPERT FLAGS NEXT HURDLE

Exterior view of the home of Patrick and Lindsay Clancy in Duxbury, MA on Wednesday, Feb. 15, 2023. Lindsay Clancy allegedly killed their three children here before attempting to take her own life on Jan. 24, 2023. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

"Gabriel Fernandez was tortured and murdered by his mom and her boyfriend — however, there were a lot of other people...that were responsible," Hatami told Fox News Digital. "There were a lot of people that missed signs through the eight or nine months of Gabriel's torture. There were a lot of people in government, in law enforcement, social workers, who missed all these different signs that really could have saved Gabriel — and they didn't do it. However, Pearl Fernandez and Isauro Aguirre were ultimately responsible for the torture and murder of Gabriel and were prosecuted for that and they were convicted of that."

LINDSAY CLANCY MURDER TRIAL BECOMES SOCIAL MEDIA OBSESSION AS TIKTOKERS, SLEUTHS DEBATE CONTROVERSIAL CASE

Lindsay Clancy reacts as doctors testify about efforts to save her children Friday, July 31, 2026. Prosecutors allege that after she strangled them with workout bands, she jumped out of a second-story window, causing injuries that left her paralyzed. (Josh Reynolds for Daily Mail /Pool)

In Clancy’s case, he argued, many of the people and systems around her deserve scrutiny — but that should not turn her into the central victim of the story. In his view, she's been too much of the focus.

"Instead of about the three victims who were innocent kids," he said.

Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside of Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 20, 2026. (John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

While failures of government and the child welfare system were investigated after Gabriel's murder, that didn't take responsibility away from the killers, he said. And in the Clancy case, he said he sees a risk that the focus on her mental health could eclipse the three children who were killed in their own home.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"I didn't see people out in the streets cheering on Pearl Fernandez because there were other people that were somewhat responsible for what happened to Gabriel," he said. "And the same thing plays in this case. Lindsay admitted to strangling her three children to death. She admitted to strangling them to death with exercise cords."

Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside of Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 20, 2026. (John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

LINDSAY CLANCY DESCRIBED A MALE VOICE ORDERING HER TO ‘KILL HER CHILDREN AND KILL HERSELF’: TESTIMONY

Clancy's defense has said she sought help repeatedly as she struggled with depression, sleeplessness, suicidal thoughts and voices urging her to harm herself and the children.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has argued that Clancy was under the effects of postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors allege she acted deliberately and understood what she was doing was wrong.

"If you murder your children, you need to be held accountable and responsible for that," Hatami said. "No matter what the whys are, no matter what reasons are."

Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside of Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 20, 2026. (John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

SUSAN SMITH ELIGIBLE FOR PAROLE AGAIN AFTER BEING DENIED RELEASE FOR DROWNING HER 2 SONS IN 1994

If convicted of any of the three counts of first-degree murder she faces, Clancy would see a sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"Your children should be your life. And if you take their life, you should, as a person, want to be punished for that," Hatami said.

Fox News' Sarah Rumpf-Whitten and Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

articles.title: NZ religious sect leader jailed over death of Chinese follower
articles.excerpt:
New Zealand police released a picture of Shulai Wang

A New Zealand court has jailed a religious sect leader over the death of an elderly follower who had travelled from China to live with his family....
articles.body_text:
New Zealand police released a picture of Shulai Wang

A New Zealand court has jailed a religious sect leader over the death of an elderly follower who had travelled from China to live with his family.

Kaixiao Liu was found guilty of manslaughter and kidnapping, and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison.

The body of 70-year-old Shulai Wang had been found wrapped in rice bags near Auckland's Gulf Harbour in March 2024, sparking a major homicide investigation which eventually led to Liu.

Liu, a musician who previously appeared in a talent show in China, had denied the charges. He also denied he is a cult leader and said he only attracted followers through his music.

During the trial the court heard that Wang had travelled from Hainan island in China to New Zealand in August 2023.

She moved in with Liu and his family at their house, which Liu had called "the Ark",  along with several other female followers.

Prosecutors said that the women acted in "servitude" to Liu and his family, and their lives were tightly controlled by Liu, where they referred to him as "Lord" or "Master".

Wang reportedly spent her days taking care of Liu's children, studying scripture, and planting vegetables.

The court heard that Wang had struggled to comply with the strict rules, possibly due to her old age, and was frequently disciplined.

In March 2024, Wang tried to escape but was caught and restrained. She died later that day, the court heard.

The court heard that Liu, his family, and his followers dumped Wang's body near a marina at Gulf Harbour. Liu had taken his children along for the trip "as camouflage".

The body was found by a fisherman days later. Police eventually traced the rice bags used to wrap Wang's body to Liu, who had made unusually large purchases of that brand of rice.

Besides Liu, his wife, Lanyue Xiao, was sentenced to nearly eight years in jail for kidnapping and manslaughter, amongst other charges. His mother, Xiuyun Li and father, Jingui Liu, had earlier been convicted of kidnapping and misconduct to human remains and are due to be sentenced later this year.

On Tuesday's sentencing, Liu's lawyer asked for leniency arguing that his client feels remorse and "is not a cult leader, nor requires people to follow his cult", according to Radio New Zealand.

Shulai Wang's body was found near the marina at Gulf Harbour in Auckland

New Zealand media outlets reported that Liu had attended a military-based university in China.

In 2011, he was a contestant for China's Got Talent - clips posted online showed him singing onstage blindfolded.

Sometime in 2017, he moved to New Zealand along with Xiao, and the couple became permanent residents.

Liu attracted followers on Chinese social media where he posted religious discussions, video diaries, and clips of himself singing. He also set up a project called Universal Choir that produced cosmic-themed orchestral music.

During the trial a police officer who interviewed one of Liu's female followers gave testimony. He said in court that the woman told him she "met the people over the internet through a song website, and she referred to the occupants of the house as friends".

During the sentencing, Justice Mathew Downs said Liu had shown "callous indifference" towards Wang.

"Because of you, Ms Wang died a lonely, frightening death. You display no remorse whatsoever. You should feel shame."

articles.title: Massachusetts woman suspected of killing police officer husband found dead
articles.excerpt:
Karen Solomon had been missing for six days after her husband Kurt Solomon was found dead at their home

A mental health advocate suspected of killing her police officer husband was found dead on Mond...
articles.body_text:
Karen Solomon had been missing for six days after her husband Kurt Solomon was found dead at their home

A mental health advocate suspected of killing her police officer husband was found dead on Monday, six days after she disappeared from her Massachusetts home, authorities said.

Karen Solomon, an advocate who called for improvements and greater awareness of police mental health issues, had disappeared after Worcester police officer Kurt Solomon was found dead at their home just before 5.30am on 18 August. Officials had named Karen Solomon a suspect and said she was believed to be armed.

“We believe this case is a tragic murder-suicide that occurred,” the Worcester police chief, Paul Saucier, said at a news conference Monday.

Two people who worked at Fairlawn Rehabilitation Hospital reported finding human remains nearby, and officers recovered a woman’s corpse, Saucier said. A final ID was still pending, but authorities said they were confident it was Karen Solomon.

A handgun found near her body was not a Worcester police service weapon, and investigators were working to determine who owned it.

On 19 August, authorities released doorbell camera footage of Karen Solomon walking down a street in a T-shirt, shorts and flip-flops, just minutes after officers responded to the couple’s home and found her husband’s body.

Kurt Solomon, who had served 31 years with the police department, was mortally injured with a sharp object, authorities have said.

Worcester county district attorney Joseph Early Jr said Karen Solomon had been at the house on the morning of her husband’s death, and investigators were looking to question her. An arrest warrant issued over the weekend charged her with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon.

Police handed out flyers with her photo to drivers in the area. An intensive law enforcement search that included local, state and federal agencies centered on the area near the couple’s Worcester home and a reservoir about a mile (1.6km) away. Authorities had deployed drones, boats and tracking dogs.

Karen Solomon, 58, co-founded the group First Help, which advocates for the mental health of police officers. She also wrote two books – Hearts Beneath the Badge and The Price They Pay – about the physical and psychological experiences of first responders.

In a 2020 interview on the Dr Phil show with Phil McGraw, she said police departments often offered little help to the families of officers who took their own lives.

In a statement read by Saucier during Monday’s news conference, the Solomon family thanked law enforcement for helping them find some answers.

“The nightmare of the past week has left our family heartbroken and rudderless,” the family said. “The compassion, dedication and empathy of all agencies involved have given us light in face of darkness.”

A wake for Kurt Solomon was scheduled for Tuesday, and his funeral for Wednesday, the police chief said. The local police union president, Thomas Duffy, described him as “a tremendous human being” who was like family.

articles.title: Caste divides make scorching summers harder in a parched corner of India
articles.excerpt:
Mamta, from the Dalit (formerly untouchable) community, says access to water in her village becomes harder in the summers

A couple of months ago, just after sunrise, 40-year-old Mamta began the first...
articles.body_text:
Mamta, from the Dalit (formerly untouchable) community, says access to water in her village becomes harder in the summers

A couple of months ago, just after sunrise, 40-year-old Mamta began the first of as many as 10 journeys she would make that day.

Carrying three empty plastic buckets, she walked a few hundred metres to the nearest handpump in her village in Jalaun district, in the drought-prone Bundelkhand region of northern India. Temperatures in parts of the region were soaring above 40C.

The taps installed under a government drinking water scheme had been dry for two years, she said, leaving most of the village's 1,000 residents dependent on a handful of handpumps.

Mamta said collecting enough water for her 11-member family and their livestock took hours. But the heat was not her only obstacle.

Mamta belongs to the Valmiki community, part of the Dalits - groups once regarded as "untouchable" under India's centuries-old caste hierarchy and which continue to face widespread discrimination.

She said she waited until members of the village's dominant castes finished using the handpump before approaching it.

"If they are standing there, we cannot fill water. We have to wait until they leave," she said.

Afterwards, she said, some upper-caste residents poured water over the pump to "cleanse" it.

Bundelkhand, a semi-arid region that spans several districts in the states of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, is notoriously drought-prone. It faced several major droughts between 2002 and 2016, making it almost a symbol for water scarcity in a country where several regions face similar hardships.

The rocky terrain of the Bundelkhand plateau means it can store little groundwater. Erratic rainfall and hotter temperatures have also made access to water unpredictable despite several government and community-led conservation efforts.

A study of more than a century of weather records found temperatures had risen across almost the entire region, and in recent summers, parts of Bundelkhand have neared 48C.

Bundelkhand is a dusty and rocky region where temperatures often climb above 40 degrees

Residents and researchers say worsening heat and water stress are putting new pressure on an old divide.

As more families compete for scarce shared water, Dalits who have long faced barriers in accessing it are encountering those inequalities more often.

"Conflict over water is not new," said Mitashi Singh of the Centre for Science and Environment.

"What is changing is the role hotter summers are playing in making water scarcer and intensifying tensions that already existed."

Local officials reject claims that the region faces water shortages or caste discrimination at public water sources.

Dominant-caste residents interviewed by the BBC also denied discriminating against others, although they acknowledged growing pressure on water supplies.

Ram Gopal Singh, who is in his 50s, pointed to several abandoned village wells.

"These wells have been dry for almost 20 years," he said. Other sources had dried up or become polluted, while unreliable tap connections had pushed more families towards handpumps.

Everyone tried to collect water in the cooler morning hours, he said, leading to arguments over turns and how much each family could take.

"But there is no caste-based dispute at these handpumps," he insisted.

There are just a handful of handpumps in Mamta's village

Dalit residents interviewed by the BBC described something different.

There is no formal queue at the pumps, they said. Instead, families try to collect water at different times to avoid confrontations.

Mamta said she usually went very early in the morning or late in the afternoon.

"The fear of being targeted stays with me throughout," she said.

About 50km away in Shahjahanpur, Shiv described a similar experience.

He said members of his community would not approach the handpump while dominant-caste families were using it.

"No matter how hot it is, even if we have to wait for hours for one bucket of drinking water, we wait because we do not have a choice," he said.

In summer, when his family needed more water, those waiting periods became more frequent.

"Even if my parents are thirsty, we sometimes wait for hours before we can drink."

Mamta says she either goes early in the morning or late in the afternoon to fill her buckets

Three years ago, Shiv's mother Parmi Devi said she was assaulted after an argument with a member of a dominant caste at a village handpump.

"I was thrashed and beaten up and thrown on the ground three times," she alleged.

"It was not just about water. It was because of our caste."

Devi filed a police complaint alleging assault. No arrests have been made yet.

Such disputes have surfaced repeatedly in complaints documented by the Dalit Dignity and Justice Centre (DDJC), a non-profit organisation in Uttar Pradesh.

The group said police registered 113 cases under India's law against caste-based atrocities in the area in 2025.

Kuldeep Singh Baudh of DDJC told BBC Hindi a majority of the complaints it tracked during the hottest months of May and June involved water, though the organisation has not published a detailed breakdown.

"To truly understand [the heat's] impact, you have to see it from the perspective of the communities that are the most excluded," he said.

The office of District Magistrate Rajesh Kumar Pandey rejected the allegations.

"There is not even one instance wherein caste-based discrimination is being practised when it comes to access to water in the region," it said in a statement.

Shiv's mother Parmi Devi was allegedly assaulted for using a handpump

The statement also disputed claims of water shortages, pointing to the federal government's Jal Jeevan Mission, which aims to provide piped drinking water to every rural household, and other local efforts to restore ponds and recharge groundwater.

There have also been wider efforts to tackle Bundelkhand's water crisis. Traditional water bodies, including ponds and check dams, have been revived across the region, while women-led groups known as Jal Sahelis work in villages to monitor supplies and promote water conservation.

Mukul Sharma, a researcher on caste and environmental politics, said increasing water supplies was only part of the solution.

Climate change is "not the origin of these injustices, but a threat multiplier", he added.

More water alone will not solve the problem if caste still shapes who gets to use it, Sharma said.

That morning in May, Mamta waited beside the handpump as other families filled their buckets, three empty plastic containers at her feet.

In cooler months, she said, she made the journey only a few times a day. In summer, it could be eight or 10, each trip determined partly by who was already at the pump.

When her turn came, she filled her buckets and carried them home. Later that day, she would return.

articles.title: Woolworths’ Ooshies craze causes Coles sales slump with parents shopping at rival supermarket to collect toys
articles.excerpt:
Coles full-year results show that despite gaining market share over past 12 months, sales fell over four weeks of ‘competitor’s collectables campaign’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest u...
articles.body_text:
Coles full-year results show that despite gaining market share over past 12 months, sales fell over four weeks of ‘competitor’s collectables campaign’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Woolworths’ latest Disney “Ooshie” collectables have not only captivated Australian children, they have led to a short-term slump in competitor Coles’ sales.

The latest rubber figurine promotion was scheduled to end on Tuesday, but strong customer interest meant Woolworths prematurely ran out of Ooshies a week ago.

Coles on Tuesday released its full-year results, showing it had grown supermarket sales and gained market share against Woolworths in the 12 months to June.

Growth continued into July but then slumped amid a “competitor’s collectables campaign”, Coles announced.

That was a reference to Woolworths’ recent Ooshies promotion of Disney, Marvel and Star Wars characters that could be collected after a customer spent $30.

The Coles chief executive, Leah Weckert, said the moderation in sales was a “temporary impact” lasting nearly four weeks. It mostly affected bricks-and-mortar shops rather than online shopping.

RBC Capital Markets analyst Michael Toner said the impact of the Woolworths campaign could scare Coles investors.

Ooshies, designed to fit onto the top of pens or pencils, come in generic packaging. It’s not clear what figure you’ve recieved until the pack is ripped open, mostly by keen children who then trade the Ooshies at home or school in an attempt to collect all 40 characters.

Schoolchildren also stage Ooshie battles where they flick the characters to try and knock down competitors’ figures.

Woolworths has hosted dedicated swap meets across the country in recent weeks to help customers complete their collections.

Adult customers have turned to online marketplaces to trade Ooshies. A dedicated Facebook Ooshie swap group added almost 2,500 members in the past week and now has more than 45,000 members.

The 2019 Ooshies craze culminated in two farmers destroying a rare lion Ooshie live on TV in a protest against online bullying.

Prof Gary Mortimer, a consumer behaviour expert at the Queensland University of Tehcnology, said Ooshies could help children build social skills – similar to when youngsters traded marbles last century.

“Those games taught us the art of competing, fair-play, learning to deal with disappointment and celebrating wins,” Mortimer wrote on LinkedIn.

“Swaps taught us ‘friendly’ negotiation skills, compromise and the principles of value exchanges.”
 But some schools have moved to shut down trading.

A Queensland independent school, Bellevue Park state school, posted on Facebook that it had banned Ooshies due to “distractions, conflict and unfair trading”.

“We need your support to make sure these items remain safe at home and are not bought to school where they can become lost, damaged or stolen,” it wrote in a Facebook post.

One Sydney after-school care centre said it was no longer allowing the toys because there had been “disputes around trading and ownership, and situations where children have become upset or distressed”.

The bans are a badge of honour for Alan Ngov, the chief commercial officer at Headstart International, the company that developed Ooshies.

“You know it was a good one when you get banned from the school yard! What an amazing campaign from the Woolworths, Disney and Headstart teams!” he wrote on LinkedIn.

Nearly two-thirds of parents surveyed by polling company YouGov said they changed their shopping behaviour due to the Ooshies promotion, including shopping at Woolworths more often.

One in five adult Ooshies collectors planned to sell the products online, YouGov’s survey released this week found. Millennials were most keen on collecting them, while baby Boomers were interested in passing them on to loved ones.

Fumin Rianto, a research director at YouGov Australia, said the products had struck a chord and developed a genuine online resale economy.

But “there’s a real conversation to be had about where all these tiny plastic collectables end up once the craze fades,” Rianto said.

Environmental groups are concerned about the volume of plastic that will eventually end up in landfill.

Kirsten Junor, the chief executive of not-for-profit Reverse Garbage, said the carbon emissions used to make and transport Ooshies outweighed any benefit.

“It’s just future landfill,” she said in a video posted on social media earlier this month.

“Kids don’t need them. We don’t need them. The planet doesn’t need them. Stop making them. You don’t need to get a reward every time you go shopping for what you need.”

Woolworths has said the Ooshie figures are made from “97% recycled thermoplastic rubber”. The company has offered dedicated collection bins in some stores to recycle the figures.

Weckert, the Coles boss, said on Tuesday the supermarket planned to continue its own promotional collectable campaigns in the future.

Coles reported its net profit rose 1% to $1.09bn in the year to June. Its supermarkets increased their profit margin on earnings from 5.3% to 5.7%.

articles.title: Woodside scraps long-term emissions and clean energy targets despite windfall oil profits caused by Iran war
articles.excerpt:
Australia’s biggest oil and gas company recorded a 27% increase in sales profit to $1.67bn in the six-month reporting period

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking n...
articles.body_text:
Australia’s biggest oil and gas company recorded a 27% increase in sales profit to $1.67bn in the six-month reporting period

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Woodside Energy has scrapped its long-term emissions and clean energy targets, even after enjoying a period of windfall oil profits caused by the Iran conflict.

Australia’s biggest oil and gas company recorded a 27% increase in sales profit to $1.67bn ($A2.33bn) in the six-month reporting period, according to financials lodged on Tuesday, after the price of crude surged amid disruptions to global supplies.

It expects more trading gains by redirecting barrels to markets paying premium prices for barrels of oil.

At the same time, the Perth-headquartered company said it would drop its commitment to invest $US5bn ($A7bn) in new energy products, such as hydrogen, by 2030.

It has placed its new ammonia business in the US under strategic review; an asset previously described as one of Woodside’s highest potential options for decarbonising power sources.

Under the new chief executive, Liz Westcott, Woodside is doubling down on fossil fuels while shifting the company further away from clean energy and decarbonisation targets.

Westcott told analysts on Tuesday the company would “retire” its so-called scope 3 investment and abatement targets, which refer to emissions produced by its customers, because the targets “were established in a different market context”.

“The reality is that markets for emerging lower carbon opportunities, including hydrogen, ammonia, and carbon capture and storage, have developed more slowly than anticipated,” Westcott said.

The company said that its new energy business would be guided by “customer demand and commercial markets”.

Woodside is one of a growing list of large oil companies amassing profits because of the Iran conflict at the same time as emissions-fuelled climate change affects communities around the world.

A recent run of deadly heatwaves in the northern hemisphere, made more likely and more severe by burning fossil fuels, has reignited calls for those same fossil fuel companies to shoulder the growing environmental costs of rising temperatures.

Brett Morgan, investor campaigns manager at climate activists Market Forces, said big polluters must be held accountable for environmental damage.

“Woodside has ditched its already feeble scope 3 emissions reduction and new energy investment targets, despite years of investor pressure demanding stronger climate action,” Morgan said.

He said major Woodside investors, including Australian super funds, must respond by demanding an end to the company’s plan to expand fossil fuel operations.

Woodside declared an interim dividend of US57c per share, up from US53c last year.

articles.title: Scots College students charged with sexual assault of teen girl appear in court
articles.excerpt:
Three boys, two aged 14 and one aged 13, on bail and yet to enter a plea after alleged assault in Sydney’s east

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, fr...
articles.body_text:
Three boys, two aged 14 and one aged 13, on bail and yet to enter a plea after alleged assault in Sydney’s east

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Three teenage boys from a prestigious Sydney private school who allegedly raped a 14-year-old girl in an alleyway in Sydney’s eastern suburbs have faced court for the first time.

On Tuesday the three boys, two aged 14 and one 13, all pupils at Sydney’s Scots College, had their matter heard in Surry Hills children’s court but remained outside the courtroom.

The court heard the trio, who are on bail, had been issued an AVO which states that they cannot go within 200 metres of the girl they allegedly assaulted.

The boys, who cannot be named for legal reasons, were charged after an alleged incident on Wednesday, 22 July.

One of the 14-year-olds and the 13-year-old are charged with aggravated sexual assault in the company of others and two counts of aggravated sexual touching.

The other 14-year-old was charged with aggravated sexual assault in the company of others and one count of aggravated sexual touching.

Court documents which provide brief detail of the allegations against them allege that the incident occurred over 55 minutes.

Judge Sue Duncombe also warned media in court about the need to protect the identities of the teenagers after the court heard some of their names had been revealed in online comment sections.

“This matter has obviously attracted a lot of media attention so far,” Duncombe said. “There have already been some repercussions on some of the young people from being identified.”

The matter was adjourned for eight weeks until 20 October.

On Monday, defamation lawyer Rebekah Giles, who is representing two of the boys, sent a letter to media outlets reminding them of their obligations under the Children Criminal Proceedings Act, which prohibits the identification of any children involved in criminal proceedings.

The accused trio are on bail and are yet to enter a plea.

The Scots College, where the trio are students, is one of Sydney’s oldest and most expensive boys’ schools, charging fees of up to $47,000 a year.

The school has said it is cooperating with police regarding the alleged rape.

“Scots College is aware three students are under investigation by NSW Police in relation to an alleged incident that occurred outside school hours,” the school said in a statement on 13 August.

articles.title: Israel’s Netanyahu claims Iran tried to kill one of his sons
articles.excerpt:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed that Iran tried to kill one of his sons, but gave no details on when or where the alleged plot took place or which of his sons was targeted.

Neta...
articles.body_text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed that Iran tried to kill one of his sons, but gave no details on when or where the alleged plot took place or which of his sons was targeted.

Netanyahu’s allegation on Monday came as his coalition trailed in opinion polls ahead of the general election in October, in the wake of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.

The war began with a joint US-Israeli strike on Tehran that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and four members of his family, including his daughter, Boshra, and his 14-month-old granddaughter, Zahra.

According to The Jerusalem Post, Netanyahu made the claim about the alleged Iranian plot against his son during a phone interview with Channel 14, a conservative Israeli outlet known for favourable coverage of the government.

“This is an unbelievable case. Iran targeted one of my sons. Iran tried to murder him, tried to murder one of my sons,” Netanyahu said.

He was responding to reports that one of Israel’s security agencies had declined to provide a security detail for Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is running neck and neck with Netanyahu for the next prime minister ahead of elections.

Netanyahu voiced support for around-the-clock protection for Eisenkot, saying it was “not a luxury”.

“Without that, [the Iranians] will succeed,” he said.

Netanyahu has two sons and a daughter. Both of his sons and his wife were granted extended personal protection by Israeli authorities in July, according to The Jerusalem Post.

His elder son, Yair, 35, has spent extended periods in the US city of Miami since early 2024, drawing controversy in Israel over the cost to taxpayers of protecting him.

Iran, meanwhile, has promised revenge for the killings of Khamenei and his family.

Khamenei’s son, Mojtaba, was named the new supreme leader a week after Ali Khamenei’s death.

Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen in public since his appointment, but in a message published on the occasion of funeral ceremonies for his father, he pledged to “avenge the blood” of the former supreme leader.
