articles.title: Trump administration touts ‘hard reset’ for American schools, vows to put parents ‘back in charge’
articles.excerpt: Education Secretary Linda McMahon outlines plans to shift education control from the federal government back to local states and parents. McMahon and President Donald Trump joined families Monday in t...
articles.body_text:
Education Secretary Linda McMahon outlines plans to shift education control from the federal government back to local states and parents. McMahon and President Donald Trump joined families Monday in the Rose Garden during the event.

President Donald Trump on Monday marked the back-to-school season by promoting his administration’s school choice agenda and pledging to put parents "back in charge" of where and how their children are educated.

Speaking at a White House event alongside Education Secretary Linda McMahon, students, parents and educators, Trump said his administration is working to expand school choice while removing what he called "far left extremism" from classrooms.

"We're putting the parents back in charge," Trump said. "They're the ones that love our children. They're the ones that should be in charge."

Trump argued that despite how much the U.S. spends on education, student outcomes should be stronger and families need more schooling options.

NEW YORK JOINS FEDERAL SCHOOL CHOICE INITIATIVE DESPITE TRADITIONAL DEMOCRAT OPPOSITION

President Donald Trump speaks during an event Monday in the Rose Garden of the White House in Washington, D.C.  (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"We want every parent to have the power to send their child to a high-quality school that shares their values. It's so important," Trump said.

The president highlighted the Education Freedom Tax Credit, which beginning in 2027, will offer taxpayers a credit of up to $1,700 for eligible donations to scholarship-granting organizations.

Those organizations can provide scholarships for education-related expenses, including private school tuition, tutoring, school fees and classroom supplies. The funds can also benefit students attending public schools.

The White House said nearly 52 million students could be eligible for the Education Freedom Tax Credit.

DEMOCRATS AIM TO KILL SCHOOL CHOICE FROM WISCONSIN TO THE REST OF THE US

Trump addresses young students in the Rose Garden of the White House on Monday, where he said student outcomes should be stronger and families should have more options when choosing where to send their children to school. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Trump also highlighted changes to 529 education savings plans that allow families to withdraw up to $20,000 annually for K-12 expenses, doubling the previous limit.

Several parents joined Trump at the event to describe how expanded school choice could help their families.

Caleb Griffith, a North Carolina father of five who said his family includes two children with special needs, said the Education Freedom Tax Credit will give his children "access to the services they need to be successful in the most formative years of their lives."

"I want to tell you, we only get one chance to educate our children, and our children are the future of America," Griffith said.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TARGETS HEAD START BUREAUCRACY IN MOVE ADVOCATES SAY PUTS PARENTS IN THE DRIVER'S SEAT

McMahon said the administration is seeking what she described as a "hard reset" in American education, with a goal of returning "to common sense."

"This school year, American parents and students have so much to be excited about because the Trump administration is steering education back to its rightful focus, serving students so that they are prepared for successful futures," McMahon said.

Sophia Compton is a Writer at Fox News Digital. Sophia was previously a business reporter covering finance, energy and tourism and has experience as a TV news producer. She graduated with a journalism degree in 2021 from the University of Hawaii at Manoa. Story tips can be sent to sophia.compton@fox.com.

articles.title: Ceasefire monitoring mission arrives in Democratic Republic of Congo
articles.excerpt:
A monitoring mission has been deployed in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to verify the formal ceasefire between the DRC’s army and M23 rebels said to be backed by Rwanda.

The United N...
articles.body_text:
A monitoring mission has been deployed in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to verify the formal ceasefire between the DRC’s army and M23 rebels said to be backed by Rwanda.

The United Nations and government sources said on Monday that the monitoring team had arrived to track the progress of the Qatari-mediated truce. Despite the agreement to end the hostilities, fighting has continued on the ground.

The UN said that the mission had deployed to Minembwe, located in the country’s mineral-rich South Kivu province, where intense fighting has persisted in recent months.

The Swiss government announced on Sunday that the DRC and M23 had agreed on a roadmap for peace talks after closed-door negotiations, and that a mission would be deployed to verify violations of the ceasefire agreement signed in Doha, Qatar in July 2025.

The mission is composed of members of the Congolese government and M23, as well as observers from member countries of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR).

Local journalists reported that the UN Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo (MONUSCO) provided logistical support for the deployment.

The mission will visit Uvira, from where the M23 withdrew in January, as well as Kalehe, where fighting has been reported in recent weeks.

Multiple armed groups have fought over the DRC’s mineral-abundant eastern provinces, including the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC) and M23, which seized swathes of territory and advanced on Goma, the capital of the North Kivu province, last year.

Peace efforts led by Qatar and the United States have sought to end the crisis, leading to the signing of two separate accords.

DRC President Felix Tshisekedi and Rwandan President Paul Kagame – whose country has been accused of backing the M23 rebels – signed a “historic” peace and economic agreement in December aimed at ending fighting, five months after the two agreed to a ceasefire. However, fighting has continued on the ground.

Both sides have accused the other of alleged abuses and ceasefire violations.

In a statement on Monday, the DRC condemned alleged M23 “crimes and serious rights violations” in territory under its control, accusing the group of killing “more than 300 people” in June and July.

The M23 has rejected the accusations. A spokesperson for the group said on X that government forces had launched a “deadly attack” with artillery on a village near Minembwe.

articles.title: Australia news live: WA to get Blue Poles in painting’s first interstate trip in two decades; power line repairs cause Sydney trains chaos
articles.excerpt:
Anthony Albanese will announce a loan of the work to the Art Gallery of Western Australia from April to September 2027. Follow today’s news live

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news po...
articles.body_text:
Anthony Albanese will announce a loan of the work to the Art Gallery of Western Australia from April to September 2027. Follow today’s news live

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

One of the crown jewels of the National Gallery of Australia’s collection, Blue Poles by Jackson Pollock, will go on display in Western Australia for the first time next year.

During a campaigning swing through electorally sensitive WA, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, will on Tuesday announce a loan of the massive work to the Art Gallery of Western Australia in Perth from April to September 2027. It is the painting’s first interstate tour since it featured at the NGV’s 20th anniversary exhibition in 2003/4.

The painting will be loaned as part of a program designed to share key items from Australia’s national cultural collection and coincides with badly needed upgrade works at the NGA in Canberra.

The Whitlam government sensationally bought the painting in 1973 for $1.4m, but it is now insured for more than $500m. When sold, it was the highest price paid for an American work of art.

“Blue Poles changed our nation, so it makes sense that the nation gets to see it,” Albanese said:

double quotation markThe national collection belongs to every Australian – no matter where they live.

That’s why we’re sending Blue Poles to Perth, making sure the west can enjoy this masterpiece and important part of our national story.

ARIA bars ‘wholly AI-generated tracks’ from music charts, but will allow those who use tech in ‘supporting role’

The Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) has barred “wholly AI-generated tracks” from eligibility from its music charts, although recordings that use generative AI in a “supporting role” will be eligible.

ARIA updated its codes of practice, which will apply to tracks that chart from Monday, 31 August. A recording using generative AI will only be eligible if it is “substantially human made” and raises “no stream or chart manipulation concerns”. The body’s CEO, Annabelle Herd, said:

double quotation markThese changes reflect our intent to remain dynamic and promote the human nature of artistry in what is – to say the least – a rapidly developing space.

Artists already use AI tools in their work, the Charts can and should evolve to keep room for that, but music generated wholesale by services built on artists’ recordings is a different matter. … This gives everyone who releases music in Australia a clear rule to work to.

Second wave of bee-killing parasite leads to ‘really scary time for beekeepers’

A second incursion of a bee-killing parasite has brought a more chemically-resistant wave of the pests, raising concerns over their impact on Australia’s food security, AAP reports.

Bees play a crucial role in food production, with an estimated $12.9bn of crops in Australia at least partially reliant on them for pollination.

Varroa mite has devastated countless hives across Australia after first being detected in NSW in June 2022 and quickly spread across most states and territories.

A second incursion of the mites which are resistant to synthetic chemical treatments, confirmed in April 2026, has renewed concerns there won’t be enough bees to pollinate crops if the invaders aren’t properly managed.

“It’s definitely a really scary time for beekeepers,” Apiarist and Australian National University PhD candidate Sara Bryant said.

double quotation markBut if you keep that story going, it’s a scary time for pollination and a scary time for food security.

One of the crown jewels of the National Gallery of Australia’s collection, Blue Poles by Jackson Pollock, will go on display in Western Australia for the first time next year.

During a campaigning swing through electorally sensitive WA, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, will on Tuesday announce a loan of the massive work to the Art Gallery of Western Australia in Perth from April to September 2027. It is the painting’s first interstate tour since it featured at the NGV’s 20th anniversary exhibition in 2003/4.

The painting will be loaned as part of a program designed to share key items from Australia’s national cultural collection and coincides with badly needed upgrade works at the NGA in Canberra.

The Whitlam government sensationally bought the painting in 1973 for $1.4m, but it is now insured for more than $500m. When sold, it was the highest price paid for an American work of art.

“Blue Poles changed our nation, so it makes sense that the nation gets to see it,” Albanese said:

double quotation markThe national collection belongs to every Australian – no matter where they live.

That’s why we’re sending Blue Poles to Perth, making sure the west can enjoy this masterpiece and important part of our national story.

Resources minister defends Albanese’s pledge there will be ’no change’ to WA’s GST share

Madeleine King, the federal resources minister, said she believes the Productivity Commission’s interim report into the GST deal with Western Australia was not a “methodical as it might have been”.

King is on Radio National breakfast this morning, defending Anthony Albanese’s announcement yesterday that there will be “no change” to WA’s share of the GST while he is prime minister.

King said she was troubled the report did not take Western Australia’s concerns or suggestions on the matter with “prominence”:

double quotation markWhen you look through the report, you’ll notice there’s zero reference to suggestions made by the WA government. … the report also doesn’t acknowledge that no state has suffered from the current arrangements. No state has had any money taken from them or any less of it. …

It’s my understanding that all states have actually been better off since the 2018 reforms. … But what’s important to know is that states have all benefited because the iron ore royalties that Western Australia has earned for the country have been distributed for the most part, like 90%, all around the country.

Man charged after alleged attempt to smuggle drugs into Queensland prison

A man has been charged after an alleged attempt to smuggle a million-dollar payload of drugs and associated paraphernalia into prison was intercepted, Australian Associated Press reports.

A drone carrying a package allegedly containing methylamphetamine and GBL (gamma-butyrolactone), a variety of prescription drugs, syringes, a glass pipe, a mobile phone and sim cards was intercepted on 17 May inside Townsville Correctional Complex.

Joint investigations conducted by officers from the Corrective Services investigations unit, the Townsville and Bundaberg CIB and Queensland Corrective Service, resulted in the arrest of a 47-year-old man.

He has been charged with five counts of supplying dangerous drugs into a correctional facility.

He has also been charged with one count each of trafficking dangerous drugs, dealing with a prohibited item in a corrective services facility, supplying a medication and drone-related offences.

Good morning, Nick Visser here. Let’s get to it.

It the latest update, just minutes ago, Sydney Trains reckons it will be some hours before things are back to normal:

double quotation markRepair crews are on site and working to restore train services as soon as possible. The repairs are expected to be completed by 10:00am.

The problem is apparently a lack of tension.

The Sydney Trains chief executive, Matt Longland, told the ABC:

double quotation markWe have very heavy weights that hang off to the side that keep the tension, keep the wires held up.

One of those counterweights failed last night.

So crews have been on track through the night. They’re still working through the repairs at the moment, but it’s likely to be later this morning until that work’s completed and they test the wiring system and turn that power back on.

‘Limited’ buses replace trains on Sydney’s north shore

Transport for NSW has put on “limited” buses replacing trains for Sydney’s north shore this morning, with major cancellations and delays across multiple lines.

The problem, we’re told, is “urgent overhead wiring repairs at Chatswood”.

Commuters are warned their morning journey may take 45 minutes longer than usual, and it’s suggested they use the Metro instead if they can. TFNSW says:

double quotation markLimited buses are replacing trains from Gordon, all stations to Chatswood only due to urgent overhead wiring repairs at Chatswood. An unscheduled rail shuttle service will run between Hornsby and Gordon in both directions.

Trains that normally terminate at North Sydney and Berowra continue as tabled while Train services that normally end/start from Lindfield and Gordan will now end/start from North Sydney. Please note that some services will be cancelled to reduce congestion and avoid longer delays.

The ABC reports crews have been working through the night to fix the problem, but a Sydney Trains spokesperson told local radio:

double quotation markThose travelling from the north, ie through Hornsby, options are to come by Strathfield as well and also connect with the Metro at Epping.

The north, as you know, for the T1 north shore, is also connected to the western line, so we are going to be running a reduced frequency from the west as well, unfortunately, this morning.

There are also impacts to the T1 western line, intercity services and the central coast line.

Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Nick Visser with the main action.

We begin with a classic “commuter chaos” update: there are widespread train cancellations in Sydney this morning due to problems with overhead wiring at a major hub.

articles.title: NFL Sunday Ticket is no longer worth the price | Bobby Burack
articles.excerpt: Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, addresses a congressional hearing probing the NFL's streaming practices and rising costs for fans. Jordan discusses the 1961 Sports Broadcasting Act and antitrust concerns, as...
articles.body_text:
Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, addresses a congressional hearing probing the NFL's streaming practices and rising costs for fans. Jordan discusses the 1961 Sports Broadcasting Act and antitrust concerns, as fans face exorbitant prices to access all games across multiple platforms. He emphasizes the need for affordable access to NFL content for all constituents, not just those who can afford expensive packages.

You may have received an email over the past week about renewing or adding NFL Sunday Ticket, YouTube's exclusive package for out-of-market NFL games.

You may also have noticed the price. It is expensive. And each year, the NFL further reduces the package's value by expanding its national windows.

Sunday Ticket does not include nationally televised games or games available in your local market. Subscribers do not receive Thursday Night Football, Sunday Night Football, or Monday Night Football. Nor does the package include the three or four games available locally across Fox and CBS during the 1 p.m. and 4:25 p.m. ET windows.

For example, viewers in Michigan cannot watch Lions games on Sunday Ticket because those games air locally on Fox or CBS.

We agree. The NFL's television schedule is unnecessarily complicated. And it's getting worse.

Streaming service EverPass Media announced it would become the exclusive commercial option for NFL Sunday Ticket starting with the 2026 season. (Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images)

RESTAURANT ASSOCIATIONS URGE CONGRESS TO ACT AS NFL SUNDAY TICKET STREAMING SWITCH THREATENS BAR REVENUES

Netflix will carry five games this season: 49ers-Rams from Australia in Week 1 on Thursday night, the first Thanksgiving Eve matchup between the Packers and Rams, two Christmas Day games, and an unannounced Saturday game later in the season.

Yes, Thanksgiving Eve means the NFL will play on a Wednesday. And because Netflix will air a Thursday night game in Week 1, NBC will move its Patriots-Seahawks season opener also to a Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026.

The NFL will then play four Friday games: Packers-Bears and Bills-Broncos on Netflix, Rams-Seahawks on Fox on Christmas Day, and Broncos-Steelers on Amazon Prime on Black Friday.

In total, the NFL will play six games on Wednesdays and Fridays this season, two days it long avoided (in part because of legal restrictions).

Further, nine of the league's 18 weeks will include an international game, most of which will air on NFL Network at 9:30 a.m. ET.

An ad for NFL Sunday Ticket on YouTube TV is displayed as bar patrons watch the telecast of the game between the Kansas City Chiefs and the Los Angeles Chargers on Sept. 5, 2025, in Buffalo, N.Y. (Getty Images)

WATCHING THE NFL WILL COST MORE, REQUIRE MORE STREAMING SERVICES THAN EVER THIS SEASON

What does this have to do with Sunday Ticket?

Each time the NFL sells a new national window to a broadcaster, it removes a game that otherwise would have been part of the Sunday early or late-afternoon slate.

The result is fewer games on Sunday Ticket, but for a higher price.

YouTube lists the standard price for 2026-27 Sunday Ticket at $480. Subscribers can divide the cost into eight $60 monthly payments, but they must eventually pay in full. You cannot subscribe and unsubscribe by the month.

Most users can purchase it for less. The $480 price is misleading. It largely exists so the NFL can market lower prices as discounts.

New users can currently sign up for $240 a year. Most returning subscribers can renew for $336. YouTube TV subscribers can purchase the package for $234, though they must maintain their YouTube TV subscription throughout the NFL season.

Teachers, military members, veterans, first responders and medical workers can purchase Sunday Ticket for $198 per year through ID.me. Eligible students can get it for $119, though they can stream on only one device.

The price varies by subscriber. Still, Sunday Ticket lasts just four months. At any of those prices, it remains one of the most expensive streaming subscriptions available.

And because of the scheduling changes cited above, the number of games no longer justifies the cost. Again, most of the week's best matchups will air elsewhere.

NFL fans who want to access every game need YouTube TV for "NFL Sunday Ticket," along with costly subscriptions to Amazon Prime, Peacock and Netflix. (Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images)

'NFL REDZONE' HOST SCOTT HANSON SAYS HE UNDERSTANDS FAN FRUSTRATION OVER COSTLY STREAMING SUBSCRIPTIONS

At this point, Sunday Ticket might be most appealing for fans who live outside the market of their favorite team.

Then again, it may still depend on the team for which you root.

The following teams have have no traditional primetime games scheduled this season (this could change with late-season flexing): Arizona Cardinals, Tennessee Titans, Miami Dolphins, and Las Vegas Raiders have no traditional primetime games scheduled this season.

Sunday Ticket is the only way for fans of those teams to watch them weekly from a a different state.

By contrast, the Los Angeles Rams, Kansas City Chiefs, Buffalo Bills, Seattle Seahawks, Dallas Cowboys and Green Bay Packers each have at least six primetime games. In addition, Fox and CBS will likely feature them heavily in the 1 p.m. and 4:25 p.m. windows available to most of the country (so long as the local team is not airing at the same time on the same channel).

In sum, a Chiefs fan in North Carolina likely won't need Sunday Ticket to watch their team most weeks, a Titans fan in Arizona will.

The NFL got greedy. Sunday Ticket's diminished value is a consequence. And as the league continues to expand its national windows, demand for the package will decline.

Unless, of course, the NFL lowers the price.

articles.title: North Carolina doctor accused of shooting 2 sisters in alleged interstate road rage attack
articles.excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A North Carolina doctor was arrested Aug. 22 after he allegedly fired into a Jeep during an interstate road rage incid...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A North Carolina doctor was arrested Aug. 22 after he allegedly fired into a Jeep during an interstate road rage incident, wounding two sisters, ages 12 and 20, according to Virginia State Police.

Dr. Richard Thomas Arriviello, 61, of Charlotte, North Carolina, was driving north on Interstate 77 in his Mercedes-Benz around 8:50 a.m. when gunfire erupted about three miles north of the North Carolina-Virginia state line.

State police said in a press release that Arriviello fired into the moving Jeep, striking both sisters in the legs.

Both victims were airlifted to a hospital with injuries that were not considered life-threatening, according to police.

'TESLA ROAD RAGE DRIVER' SENTENCED TO SEVEN YEARS IN PRISON AFTER ATTACKING MOTHER AND DAUGHTER IN HAWAII

Dr. Richard Thomas Arriviello is accused of shooting two sisters during an alleged road rage incident. (New River Valley Regional Jail)

Arriviello then fled in his Mercedes-Benz, police said.

Troopers spotted and stopped the Mercedes-Benz about 15 miles away and took Arriviello into custody.

Arriviello faces several felony charges, including malicious shooting into an occupied vehicle, maliciously causing bodily harm to another with intent to maim and use of a firearm while committing a felony.

An aerial view of the skyline of downtown Charlotte, North Carolina. (Omar Vega/Getty Images)

Arriviello remains jailed without bond at the New River Valley Regional Jail, officials told Fox News Digital. He is scheduled to appear in court Sept. 29.

State police have not said what led to the alleged road rage encounter or whether investigators recovered a firearm from Arriviello’s Mercedes-Benz.

The Jeep’s driver was also cited for reckless driving, but authorities did not identify the driver.

SEE IT: DASHCAM SHOWS FLORIDA TROOPER CHASING ALLEGED STREET TAKEOVER SUSPECT AT 140 MPH

Dr. Richard Thomas Arriviello of Charlotte, North Carolina, was driving north on Interstate 77 in his Mercedes-Benz when gunfire erupted, police said. (Stock Photos/New River Valley Regional Jail)

North Carolina Medical Board records show Arriviello has been licensed as an emergency medicine physician in the state since 2010 and has no public disciplinary actions listed against him.

The records list Arriviello as the owner of Family Urgent Care in Monroe.

Fox News Digital reached out to Family Urgent Care in Monroe and Virginia State Police for additional comment.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: ‘Moderate’ Dem gubernatorial candidate embraced DEI budget tool, Green New Deal-style policies
articles.excerpt:
Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate David Crowley,a moderate who upset socialist Francesca Hong in the primary this week, said he would not campaign with far-left streamer Hasan Piker.

Democratic socia...
articles.body_text:
Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate David Crowley,a moderate who upset socialist Francesca Hong in the primary this week, said he would not campaign with far-left streamer Hasan Piker.

Democratic socialist Francesca Hong lost Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary earlier this month, but some of the progressive policies that define the party’s far-left flank may not have disappeared with her campaign entirely.

David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive who defeated Hong after being cast as the more moderate choice, has overseen racial-equity budgeting, expanded the county’s equity bureaucracy and urged the Wisconsin attorney general to sue fossil fuel companies for environmental-related damages. Meanwhile, Crowley has also shared ground with Hong on taxing millionaires and ambitious carbon-neutrality goals.

"Milwaukee County is known for it's beer and brats, but unfortunately it's also the epicenter of David Crowley's budgetary boondoggles. Under Crowley's failed leadership, residents received their largest property tax hike in 15 years, paid higher sales taxes for everyday purchases, and saw millions of their hard-earned tax dollars set up to finance Crowley's Green New Deal 'Net Zero' scam for the county," Wisconsin native and Republican consultant Mark Bednar told Fox News Digital.

"In an era where voters are increasingly focused on the economy and their pocketbooks, Wisconsinites should ask themselves, do they really want to expand Crowley's gross mismanagement and liberal priorities to the whole state?" He continued. "I'm guessing a big Wisconsin 'heck no.'"

WISCONSIN DEMOCRATIC VOTERS CHALK SOCIALIST FRANCESCA HONG'S STUNNING LOSS UP TO ELECTABILITY CONCERNS

Democratic Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate David Crowley greets supporters at a campaign rally on August 10, 2026 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Crowley is polling second behind front-runner Francesca Hong in the Democratic primary, which takes place tomorrow. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

In a recent campaign ad, Crowley touted a record of "getting things done" and "practical bipartisan solutions," while Wisconsin Public Radio described him during the primary as a "mainstream Democratic alternative" to Hong.

CBS News called him a "moderate Democrat" after his primary victory, while Axios framed Crowley's upset as a potential revival for the Democratic Party’s center-left.

But, despite being cast as the more moderate alternative, Crowley has shared several significant policy positions with Hong. Crowley himself acknowledged the policy overlap during the primary, telling supporters that "there’s many things that everybody agrees on, right?" when discussing his differences with Hong, according to WISN 12’s "UpFront," while adding that there were also areas where the two "absolutely disagree."

Both have backed higher taxes on millionaires, a $20 minimum wage, expanded union rights and universal child care. Their climate agendas also contain a notable parallel – Hong campaigned on making Wisconsin carbon-neutral by 2050, while Crowley signed Milwaukee County’s plan to bring county operations to net-zero emissions by the same year.

AOC BLASTED AS TOO MODERATE BY MAOIST DSA FACTION AS 2028 BUZZ GROWS

Progressive firebrand Francesca Hong looks to topple the Democratic establishment in a closely watched Wisconsin showdown. (Talia Sprague/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

Crowley’s record on DEI complicates his "moderate" image as well. It includes embedding a Racial Equity Budget Tool (REBT) into the state budgeting process. Milwaukee County describes the tool as a "structured racial equity lens" for departments to assess how budget decisions affect communities of color.

In his 2022 budget address, Crowley said all the Milwaukee County departments had "once again" used the tool and were asked what they would do with additional funding "to specifically address racial equity."

"Racism is a public health crisis in Milwaukee County," the county's 2024 budget stated. "The REBT is a structured racial equity lens for Milwaukee County departments to use to critically assess the impact of budget decisions on communities of color."

Crowley’s tenure as Milwaukee County executive also transformed the county’s Office on African American Affairs into a broader "Office of Equity," which grew the original office’s reach to "other communities of color, LGBTQ+ and people with varying abilities," while increasing accountability for the county’s existing racial-equity goals.

Climate policy has been another focus of Crowley’s tenure in Milwaukee. In April 2025, he signed Milwaukee County’s Climate Action 2050 plan, developed by his administration after the County Board adopted a carbon-neutrality goal in 2021. The plan seeks to bring county government operations to net-zero carbon emissions by 2050 — the same year Hong’s statewide climate agenda called for Wisconsin to become carbon-neutral.

David Crowley, left, Democratic candidate for Wisconsin governor, points to a group of supporters while campaigning with Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers Friday, Aug. 7, 2026, in Sheboygan, Wis. (Kayla Wolf/AP Photo)

Crowley also signed a 2022 resolution calling on Wisconsin’s attorney general to sue fossil-fuel companies and seek damages for environmental and climate harm in Wisconsin communities. And, in April, he signed legislation reaffirming Milwaukee County’s commitment to the principles and goals of the Paris Agreement amid federal climate-policy rollbacks.

Crowley’s campaign and Milwaukee County’s press office did not respond to Fox News Digital’s requests for comment on his record.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

articles.title: Rare signed Picasso print stolen from gallery turns up in vacant apartment years later
articles.excerpt: A massive Sicily art heist leaves investigators searching for answers after thieves steal four priceless Renaissance masterpieces from a historic local museum. The stolen Italian artwork is valued at ...
articles.body_text:
A massive Sicily art heist leaves investigators searching for answers after thieves steal four priceless Renaissance masterpieces from a historic local museum. The stolen Italian artwork is valued at more than $90 million.

A signed Pablo Picasso etching stolen from a Wisconsin art gallery nearly a decade ago has been recovered after a Milwaukee landlord turned the artwork in to police, authorities said.

The original 1949 Picasso etching, titled "Torero," was brought into Milwaukee Police Department (MPD) District Four on Aug. 5, after the person who found it suspected it had been stolen, the MPD said.

An authenticator confirmed the next day that it was the same print reported stolen from a Milwaukee art gallery in the 700 block of North Jefferson Street on Feb. 16, 2018, police said.

FBI TRACKS DOWN CENTURIES-OLD CHRISTIAN ARTIFACT IN UNEXPECTED PLACE: 'INCREDIBLY EXCITING'

Printouts of a photo of the Pablo Picasso etching, "Torero" are displayed on a table in DeLind Fine Art Appraisals in Milwaukee. (AP Photo/Laura Bargfeld)

"The Milwaukee Police Department is grateful that this community member recognized the etching print and did the right thing and returned it," the MPD said.

Milwaukee landlord Tim Dertz found the rare print by the renowned Spanish sculptor and painter while cleaning out a Bay View apartment after an eviction, WISN-TV reported.

"It was kind of in a weird spot hanging on a wall," Dertz told the news station. He said the artwork appeared to have been there for a long time because it had collected "tons of dust" across the top.

WILT CHAMBERLAIN WARM-UP JACKET BOUGHT FOR $3 AT THRIFT STORE SELLS FOR TENS OF THOUSANDS

Bill DeLind points to artwork inside his Milwaukee gallery after a signed Picasso print stolen in 2018 was recovered. (AP Photo/Laura Bargfeld)

Dertz showed the print to an antique dealer friend, who recognized it as a Picasso and said he believed it could be the artwork stolen from Bill DeLind’s Milwaukee gallery years earlier, The Associated Press reported.

Dertz then turned the print over to police, who contacted DeLind to examine it.

HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS IN STOLEN GOODS RECOVERED AT A USED CAR LOT AFTER ADULT TOY COMPANY PURCHASE

DeLind told the AP he immediately recognized the stolen "Torero," which is one of 30 known copies signed by Picasso. His DeLind Fine Art Appraisals sticker was still attached to the back of the framed artwork.

"I was overwhelmed," DeLind said. "It was indeed mine. It came back full circle."

TITANIC SURVIVOR'S LIFE JACKET SELLS FOR OVER $900K AT AUCTION, FAR EXCEEDING PRICE EXPECTATIONS

Famous sculptor and painter Pablo Picasso in his Paris studio. The co-founder of the Cubist movement died in 1973 at age 91.

The print was appraised at between $35,000 and $50,000 when it was stolen, DeLind told the AP. He said its value may now be closer to $50,000 given the story behind its recovery.

The artwork remains in Milwaukee police custody while the client who commissioned it for sale through DeLind’s gallery works through insurance matters, according to the AP.

Milwaukee police told WISN the statute of limitations for theft and property crimes is generally six years, though the investigation remains open.

DeLind said his former business partner, who died in February, was devastated by the 2018 theft and called police every year on the anniversary of the crime to urge renewed publicity in hopes of finding the piece.

"He would have been over the moon about this," DeLind told the AP.

Milwaukee police told Fox News Digital that no additional information is available beyond what the department has already released.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: US supreme court rules Trump can proceed with crackdown on mail-in voting
articles.excerpt:
Justices’ ruling comes after lower courts had blocked president’s election order ahead of November midterms

The US supreme court has sided with Donald Trump in his effort to crack down on mail-in vot...
articles.body_text:
Justices’ ruling comes after lower courts had blocked president’s election order ahead of November midterms

The US supreme court has sided with Donald Trump in his effort to crack down on mail-in voting, though it remains unclear if his administration can take action ahead of the midterm elections in November.

Justices on the court voted 6-3 along ideological lines to lift an injunction from June that a judge in Massachusetts placed on an executive order issued by the president. But a second injunction remains in place and the ruling leaves room for legal challenges.

Trump has repeatedly likened voting by mail to cheating, despite his own use of it and overwhelming evidence that the system is secure.

In March he ordered the government to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters, requiring that mail-in ballots only be delivered to people on that list. He also directed the justice department to prioritise investigations and prosecutions of state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote in federal elections.

Democratic officials in 23 states and the District of Columbia sued over Trump’s March order, saying the US constitution gives states and Congress the authority to set election rules, not the president. They argued that imposing sweeping changes so close to the election risked disenfranchising voters and disrupting preparations already under way.

A judge in Massachusetts, Indira Talwani, sided with the plaintiff states – nearly half the country – and ruled that Trump lacked authority to dictate how states administer federal elections. She also questioned whether federal agencies could compile accurate citizenship lists.

An appeals court upheld her decision. Talwani later issued a second injunction with nationwide effect.

The justice department had argued that the states’ lawsuit was premature because the administration had not yet taken concrete actions that harmed them and they therefore lacked legal standing to sue. The administration said the Massachusetts injunction prevented it from finalising and implementing policies intended to promote “election integrity” before November.

Republican-led states backed the administration before the supreme court, arguing that states would have an opportunity to provide input on the final lists of eligible voters.

The supreme court, in a 6-3 decision, has now lifted the first injunction, allowing the administration to move forward while litigation continues. The three liberal justices dissented. The ruling does not finally resolve the underlying legal questions and leaves the door open to further challenges as the midterms approach.

The wrangling over how US voters can cast their ballots comes less than 100 days until November’s midterm elections, which will decide the balance of power in the US Senate and House of Representatives.

Democratic voters are deemed more likely to cast their ballots by mail than Republicans: about one in four registered Democrats did so in 2024, according to the States United Democracy Center, alongside one in five registered Republicans.

About 30% of all ballots were cast by mail in the 2024 presidential election, according to federal data. A 2025 Brookings Institution study found roughly four cases of fraud for every 10m mail ballots cast.

Trump’s executive order forms part of a wider effort to reshape the electoral system. He has repeatedly made false claims of widespread fraud in American elections, including his defeat by Joe Biden in 2020, and has pressed the Republican-controlled Congress to pass the Save America Act, a contentious package of voting restrictions.

articles.title: Five best hikes in Tallahassee to try ahead of Florida State and New Mexico State's Week Zero showdown
articles.excerpt: Fox News senior national correspondent William La Jeunesse discusses the shocking video of a grandfather being thrown 8 feet into the air by a wild bison at Yellowstone National Park on 'The Faulkner ...
articles.body_text:
Fox News senior national correspondent William La Jeunesse discusses the shocking video of a grandfather being thrown 8 feet into the air by a wild bison at Yellowstone National Park on 'The Faulkner Focus.'

College football is officially here, and that means traveling to different parts of the country to see the games this season.

The beauty of college football is that most of the games don't take place in some overcrowded metropolitan area, so you'll be able to take in all the natural wonders of a particular venue.

Here at OutKick OutDoors, we wanted to provide you lovers of nature with some of the best hiking spots to hit each week you decide to make the trek to a different college town, and first up on the docket is Tallahassee for the Week Zero showdown between New Mexico State and Florida State.

FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL FANS, "NO FALL WEDDINGS" ISN'T A BIT OR A GIMMICK, IT'S A LIFESTYLE

A general view from above of the Florida State Seminoles with fireworks going off as they run on to the field before the game against the Boston College Eagles at Doak Campbell Stadium on Bobby Bowden Field on Sept. 24, 2022, in Tallahassee, Florida. (Don Juan Moore/Getty Images)

Before we begin, a quick reminder that although college football normally means fall weather and mild temperatures, this is still the Florida panhandle in August, so most hikes will happen under some extreme heat conditions.

Dress and pack accordingly and make sure you are staying hydrated.

Believe me, there's no humidity like Florida humidity, and if you aren't careful, you'll end up in the ER on game day surrounded by college kids who went hard in a different direction.

With that out of the way, here are some of the best hikes Tally has to offer.

Alfred B. Maclay Gardens State Park entrance sign. (Universal Images Group via Getty)

If you want the best overall hike in the Tallahassee area, this is the move.

Lake Overstreet has about five miles of multi-use trails through live oaks (a northern Florida staple), hills and ravines surrounding a secluded 144-acre lake.

The whole area looks a lot like southern Georgia with its hilly terrain, which can be a nice departure from the typically flat walks that the Sunshine State offers.

THE BEST OUTDOOR WEEKEND IN NORTHWEST GEORGIA DOESN’T REQUIRE 'ROUGHING IT' OR SLEEPING ON THE GROUND

Situated a few miles from downtown Tallahassee, Lake Overstreet offers a serene experience to take your mind off the stresses of a game week, and if you're so inclined, the nearby Lake Hall has kayak rentals available to add a little water action to your hike.

Anyone traveling to Tallahassee from out-of-state needs to make the Miccosukee Canopy Road Greenway a must-see on their itinerary.

The scenery is so quintessential North Florida, with the giant oaks forming the canopy overhead that gives the trail its namesake and the rolling countryside is very evocative of the Deep South.

This is also a nice, relaxing walk for anyone not looking to overdo it while they are in town, as it's less strenuous than some of the more advanced surrounding trails.

If you're looking for something that screams rural Tally, give this one a try.

For those hikers feeling more adventurous, Lafayette Heritage Trail Park offers a bit more trail time than the previous two on the list.

The woods and trail network make this a natural choice for both hikers and mountain bikers, though that phraseology feels a little silly in a flat state like Florida.

Nevertheless, bikers will find plenty to like about Lafayette Heritage Trail Park, and the views of the lake at sunrise and sunset are picturesque.

A special mention needs to be made for the wooden pedestrian bridge to the north of the lake that goes over the railroad tracks.

It looks like something straight out of Adventureland at Disney World and makes for a great photo op.

Perhaps the most "wild" of all the trails listed here, the Munson Hills Off-Road Bike Trailhead offers a more rugged approach to Tallahassee for those seeking more of a challenge.

A pine-forest landscape nestled against the Apalachicola National Forest region, this trail will give a stiff test to all but the most seasoned flatland hikers.

Munson Hills represents the less-manicured option for those who are looking for a trail that's more in tune with nature, but be sure to pack plenty of snacks and water, because this one is a doozy.

It's a little off the beaten path, sitting just south of the Tallahassee city limits, but that's just what we want from our nature hikes!

An Indian mound at Lake Jackson Mounds Archaeological State Park. (Universal Images Group via Getty)

Call it burying the lead if you want, but I saved the best trail for last.

Lake Jackson Mounds State Park is an absolute treasure, featuring the preserves of ancient Indigenous ceremonial mounds as well as a 0.75-mile interpretive trail past the site of an early-1800s grist mill plus a 2.2-mile nature trail.

It's basically a hike through hundreds of years of Tallahassee history.

A fair warning, though: according to the park's website, the boardwalk to the large mound remains closed.

Everything else here is fair game, and it's all set to the backdrop of North Florida foliage, giving hikers the perfect taste of Tallahassee for their game week trip.

articles.title: Democrat rips Hasan Piker as 'hack who thrives on hate' over his warning to American Jews about Israel
articles.excerpt:
Controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker said that if American Jews continue to support Israel, "eventually someone will come around and take action" against them.

Controversial far-left Twitch stre...
articles.body_text:
Controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker said that if American Jews continue to support Israel, "eventually someone will come around and take action" against them.

Controversial far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who has become increasingly prominent in Democratic politics, is facing backlash from Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., over his remarks about American Jews' support for Israel that she characterized as "talk of violence" targeting Jewish Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss.

In a statement published Monday, Scholten said Piker was "a hack who thrives on hate, shock and awe because he lacks substance."

"Hasan Piker's talk of violence against American Jews, and directly naming a Michigan elected official, and future member of Congress, Jeremy Moss, is unacceptable. Full stop," Scholten's statement read. "We should all be calling out this disgusting rhetoric so it loses its grip on our politics once and for all. It has no place in Michigan, and no place in our country."

HASAN PIKER IS BECOMING THE 'FACE OF THE PROGRESSIVE MOVEMENT,' FORMER DEMOCRATIC OPERATIVE WARNS

Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., slammed Hasan Piker over his recent remarks about American Jews' support for Israel.

In his response to Scholten's statement, Piker called Scholten an "Israel 1st congresswoman."

"if i was an israel 1st congresswoman with a possible cheating scandal with a republican in the state, i wouldn’t spend so much time vying for the spotlight by actively defaming a prominent antizionist voice to harm the dem senate majority chances over a 90/10 issue," Piker wrote on X.

Piker, who holds a large social media following, has been particularly visible in Michigan this election cycle. He backed Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in a primary earlier this month. El-Sayed was criticized for appearing with Piker during his campaign, with some saying that the streamer's rhetoric was too extreme.

Scholten backed Stevens last month, calling her a "smart, capable, and common-sense leader." She later praised Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer for endorsing Stevens.

El-Sayed also responded to Piker's comments, and while he did not condemn the streamer outright, he denounced antisemitism and rhetoric that puts the Jewish community in danger.

"I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past," El-Sayed wrote.

"My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters," he added. "Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk."

EL-SAYED DISAVOWS HASAN PIKER'S 9/11 COMMENTS BUT DECRIES 'CANCEL CULTURE'

Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., accused Hasan Piker of targeting state Sen. Jeremy Moss in a recent stream. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

In his statement, El-Sayed stressed that Piker did not speak for his campaign, writing that, "nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople."

In addition to politicians, Piker was also criticized by Jewish organizations.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, the Jewish Federation of Detroit said that "Hasan Piker’s talk of violence against Jewish Americans while displaying a picture of a Michigan lawmaker who is Jewish is repugnant and antisemitic."

"We call on all responsible leaders to condemn this extremist, attention-seeking conduct which divides Americans, foments hate, and makes our Jewish community less safe," the Jewish Federation of Detroit's statement read.

The American Jewish Committee (AJC) also said on Monday that by using an image of Moss, "Piker put a target on the backs of Sen. Moss, Jewish candidates and officeholders, and American Jews alike."

"Blaming Jews for the antisemitism directed at them is itself antisemitism," AJC wrote on X. "Every public official who has shared his platform now has a choice: denounce this and walk away, or be complicit. There is no third option."

During his Aug. 20 stream, Piker seemed to warn American Jews against supporting Israel, saying that doing so could lead to violence against them.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., slammed Twitch streamer Hasan Piker as "a hack who thrives on hate, shock and awe." (Julia Demaree/AP Photo)

"People don't f--- with Israel any longer. And if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they're singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone will come around and take action not against Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker said.

When he made the comment, Piker had an image of Moss, who is running to fill Stevens' seat, in his background.

Piker's remarks came amid a controversy over an audio clip circulating online in which Moss purportedly said that the "entire purpose" of his congressional campaign was to ensure America's continued support for Israel.

However, the Michigan Democrat said that the clip was fabricated, calling it "a manipulated and unsourced audio, with things I never did and never would say."

"We are in a dangerous era of disinformation. Circulating a lie because it affirms your bias or belief is equally bad whether it comes from the left or the right. We all have a choice not to spread fabricated images, videos, and audio about candidates and campaigns. We all have a role in stopping the erosion of our democracy," Moss said about the controversy over the audio clip.

Fox News Digital reached out to Piker and Moss for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Rachel Wolf is a media and culture reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: US strikes a vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing 2 people in first attack in months
articles.excerpt:
US Southern Command has struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing two accused of trafficking drugs

The US military has launched a deadly strike on a vessel in the Pacific Ocean, killing t...
articles.body_text:
US Southern Command has struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing two accused of trafficking drugs

The US military has launched a deadly strike on a vessel in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of drug trafficking.

On Monday, US Southern Command (SouthCom) announced it “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific”.

“Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed two narco-terrorists,” SouthCom added.

Southern Command did not provide evidence for the vessel’s alleged involvement in drug trafficking.

In a statement on the strikes, Francis L Donovan, SouthCom’s commander general, said: “We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists – disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership and eliminating cartel terror across the region.”

“This operation is a powerful demonstration of our lethal precision, overwhelming capability, and absolute resolve to protect the US homeland,” Donovan added.

A pixelated black-and-white video posted to SouthCom’s X account on Monday showed a vessel moving through the water before it was struck by an explosion that produced a large flash of light.

Monday’s strike marks the latest in a series of US military strikes since the Donald Trump administration launched what it described as a campaign targeting “narco-terrorists” smuggling drugs into the US, despite numerous reports indicating that the strikes have done little to stem the flow of drugs into the country.

It brings the overall death toll to 223 people killed in 67 strikes during the nearly year-long US campaign of bombing alleged drug boats off Latin America’s Caribbean coast and in the eastern Pacific Ocean. US Southern Command says the campaign has resulted in the destruction of 64 speedboats, three “low-profile” ships and a semisubmersible craft.

The latest strike comes as the Trump administration pursues deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the US to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal.

Ecuador launched similar missions with the US in March.

The Trump administration’s boat bombing campaign began in early September and has left numerous survivors, but most of them have never been recovered.

US Southern Command said in a separate statement on Monday that there have been more than 20 search and rescue efforts overall, almost all of which were unsuccessful.

According to data compiled from the command’s social media posts, the strikes have generated 28 survivors with only three people ever being rescued – one person during a strike in March who was transferred to the Costa Rican Coast Guard, and two wounded people who were later repatriated to their home countries of Ecuador and Colombia.

The very first strike in September 2025 left two survivors who were killed in a second, follow-up strike. When that became public, it drew concern from some lawmakers and those who study military law. The White House insisted it was done “in self-defense” to ensure the boat was destroyed and in accordance with armed conflict laws.

Despite the defense department framing the strikes as attacks against “narco-terrorism”, it has provided little evidence on whether the vessels were actually transporting drugs. The attacks have been condemned as extrajudicial killings by the United Nations and other humanitarian organizations.

According to a 2020 report by the US Drug Enforcement Administration, 74% of the cocaine reaching the US arrived through the Pacific while only 8% came from fast boats from the Caribbean.

Critics have questioned the overall legality of the boat strikes as well as their effectiveness, in part because the fentanyl behind many fatal overdoses is typically trafficked to the US over land from Mexico, where it is produced with chemicals imported from China and India.

The Pentagon’s watchdog said in May that it plans to look into whether the US military followed an established targeting framework when carrying out the strikes. However, the evaluation is focused specifically on what’s known as the six-phase Joint Targeting Cycle and not on the legality of the strikes, the inspector general’s office said.

Meanwhile, an investigation by the Latin American Center for Investigative Journalism (Clip) this year identified 13 previously unidentified victims of US vessel attacks. All came from impoverished communities across Latin America and the Caribbean and several were fishers with no indication of involvement in the drug trade, it found.

“There are communities where they stopped fishing for several weeks – and if they do that, people go hungry – because they were terrified of being bombed,” María Teresa Ronderos, Clip director, said at the time of the report’s release.

Other families continue to grieve as they seek answers about their relatives killed in US airstrikes.

“If the boat was carrying so much cocaine and then exploded and caught fire, where is the evidence? Where is the cocaine? That is what I want to know. I know Ricky. He was a fisherman. That was his life,” Titus, the brother of Ricky Joseph, one of the 13 people identified in the CLIP investigation, said in June from the Carribean island of St Lucia.

articles.title: US public support for Iran war falls as Trump approval at record low: Poll
articles.excerpt:
Support in the United States for the war on Iran has fallen as President Donald Trump’s approval remains at a record low, a Reuters/Ipsos poll suggests.

Public backing for the war has dropped to its ...
articles.body_text:
Support in the United States for the war on Iran has fallen as President Donald Trump’s approval remains at a record low, a Reuters/Ipsos poll suggests.

Public backing for the war has dropped to its lowest level since the early stages of the conflict, with declining Republican support contributing to the shift, according to the poll released on Monday.

Just 31 percent of Americans surveyed said they support US military action against Iran, down from 37 percent in March and 34 percent earlier this month. Support among Republican respondents fell to 69 percent, compared with 77 percent in March.

The war is also continuing to weigh on Trump’s standing with the public, the poll suggests. For the second consecutive Reuters/Ipsos survey, 33 percent of respondents said they approved of Trump’s performance as president, matching the lowest approval rating recorded in the polling series across his first and second terms.

Trump has defended the military campaign as necessary to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. The conflict began on February 28 with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.

But the economic effects of the war remain a concern for Americans. Iran has maintained a de facto blockade of oil exports from the region, contributing to a rise in US petrol prices to near record highs.

The Trump administration has also announced recent pledges to increase economic pressure on Iran. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said on Monday that the US would target all of Iran’s sources of revenue, including oil, with the aim of preventing other countries and companies from doing business with Tehran. The campaign is dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast”.

A growing majority of Americans expect the war to continue for some time, the poll suggests. Eighty-three percent of respondents said they believe the conflict will last for an extended period, up from 80 percent earlier this month.

The prospect of a lengthy war presents a challenge for Trump, who campaigned for the presidency in 2024 on promises to bring down inflation and to adopt an “America First” strategy of avoiding foreign military engagements.

Six months into the conflict, petrol prices are more than $1 per gallon (3.8 litres) higher than they were before the war, adding to economic pressure ahead of November’s midterm elections.

The higher fuel costs could also create difficulties for Republicans defending narrow congressional majorities.

The poll suggests that independent voters favour Democrats over Republicans when asked which party they would support in a congressional election held today. Among independents, 33 percent said they would vote for a Democrat, compared with 19 percent who said they would choose a Republican.

The Reuters/Ipsos survey questioned 1,215 adults across the United States over four days and has a margin of error of 3 percentage points in either direction.

articles.title: Burnham backtracks on spending housing fund only on building social homes
articles.excerpt:
About 40% of £10bn from Affordable Homes Programme will now go on types of housing such as sheltered and shared ownership

Andy Burnham has backtracked on his proposal to rip up the government’s housi...
articles.body_text:
About 40% of £10bn from Affordable Homes Programme will now go on types of housing such as sheltered and shared ownership

Andy Burnham has backtracked on his proposal to rip up the government’s housing plans and boost social home building.

Ministers laid out plans on Monday to spend an initial £10bn from the 10-year Affordable Homes Programme on a mix of subsidised housing types in England, in line with the Starmer government’s policy.

Burnham previously called for the programme to be spent entirely on social homes, which are more heavily subsidised and therefore more affordable than other types of government-funded housing.

He said when launching his campaign to become MP for Makerfield: “There’s £39bn allocated over a 10-year period … I’m saying that should be dedicated to council homes. Let’s not be coy any more … I’m saying council homes because control matters.”

Under the plans announced on Monday, however, £10bn will be spent helping to build 70,000 homes outside London, about 60% of which will be social rented houses. The rest will be other types of accommodation such as shared ownership schemes and sheltered housing.

London will get another £6bn, which will be allocated at a later date.

Ministers said the investment would help bring the government closer to its promise of building 300,000 affordable homes over the next 10 years. It will be spent by 33 “strategic partners”, who will be guaranteed funding for the next decade to help deliver their plans.

The Guardian has learned that for the first time in the history of the scheme, three of those partners will be local councils, as the government looks to deliver what Burnham has promised will be “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period”.

Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said: “Growing up on a council estate and raising children as a young working mum, I know firsthand that access to a secure, affordable home can be a lifeline for families up and down the country.

“Guardian readers will know just how important council housing is too. You will know it’s so much more than just a roof over your head – it gives working parents a safe place to raise their family, offers kids the stability needed to thrive in school and wraps a community around those who need it most.”

She added: “This once-in-a-generation investment will help rewrite these stories, delivering the genuinely affordable homes our country needs, getting people off waiting lists and helping families put down roots so they can get on in life.”

Officials say that another £16bn is yet to be allocated, and that social rent homes and council houses will be prioritised in future funding rounds.

Sarah Elliott, the chief executive of the charity Shelter, said: “Today’s announcement puts councils back on the pitch in the fight to end homelessness. By giving local authorities some of the funding and support they need to start delivering social homes at scale again and ramping up the percentage of funds allocated to social homes, the government has laid the foundations for its council housing revolution.

“But there are still underlying obstacles which hold councils back from building. The government must use the autumn budget to finally remove these barriers, like unsustainable housing debt that councils are saddled with, to make the prime minister’s vision of a new generation of social homes a reality.”

The plans contrast with those announced by Reform UK on Monday, which is promising to boost the supply of social homes by evicting foreign tenants and allowing housing associations to borrow more.

articles.title: Target apologizes for ‘offensive’ Halloween costume after backlash
articles.excerpt:
Retailer removes kid’s clown costume after people said it resembled a racist caricature used in minstrel shows

Target, the US retail corporation, said it pulled a controversial Halloween costume off ...
articles.body_text:
Retailer removes kid’s clown costume after people said it resembled a racist caricature used in minstrel shows

Target, the US retail corporation, said it pulled a controversial Halloween costume off its shelves after criticism across social media that it resembled a racist caricature.

The ad image for the costume, sold as the “Kids’ Glows Under Blacklight Circus Clown Halloween Costume,” depicted a Black child in a bright orange and black top with solid black gloves and a mask with a wide, toothy smile. Both the child’s pose and the costume’s gloves and mask were likened to caricatures of Black people used in minstrel shows.

“As a company, we know we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry,” Target said in its apology statement. “The costume is offensive and should never have been part of our assortment. It is no longer available for sale. We know this is especially hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners. Removing the costume is an important first step, and the company is looking closely at how this happened and what needs to change to ensure this won’t happen again.”

The costume controversy is just the latest in a series for the Minneapolis-based retailer.

Last year, activists called for a boycott of the company, after its decision to walk-back DEI initiatives. And last week, the American Federation of Teachers, a teachers’ union, called on Target’s CEO, Michael Fiddelke, to call for an end to Operation Metro Surge, Trump’s National Guard push in Minneapolis earlier this year.

Target’s stock price decreased from $137.40 on 24 January, the day the company cut its DEI programs, to $104.70 on 15 March. The company is starting to experience a financial comeback after the initial boycott, but could face other challenges.
