articles.title: Trump wants cheaper beef. Republicans in key races warn his plan goes too far
articles.excerpt: Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson joins 'Sunday Morning Futures' to discuss her U.S. Senate bid. Hinson discusses the high-stakes race against Democratic opponent Josh Turek and details her opposition to propos...
articles.body_text:
Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson joins 'Sunday Morning Futures' to discuss her U.S. Senate bid. Hinson discusses the high-stakes race against Democratic opponent Josh Turek and details her opposition to proposed beef import tariffs. She outlines how Republicans plan to address inflation, lower consumer costs and shape their legislative platform ahead of the crucial November midterm elections.

Senate Republicans racing to keep their grip on power have beef with President Donald Trump’s latest affordability push.

A handful of Republicans in the upper chamber aren’t happy with Trump’s directive to allow hundreds of thousands of tons of foreign beef into the U.S. in a bid to lower grocery bills. It comes as Americans’ struggles with everyday affordability have erupted as a key issue for voters across the country.

Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., who is up for re-election this cycle and is one of Trump’s top allies in the Senate, argued that beef prices are high "for a simple reason: Our cattle herd is too small."

TRUMP URGED TO STOP TARGETING FELLOW REPUBLICANS AS GOP FIGHTS TO KEEP MAJORITY

President Donald Trump wants to flood the market with hundreds of thousands of metric tons of foreign ground beef to lower grocery costs, but Republicans running in key races warn that the move hurts American ranchers. (Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images)

"Imported beef below market prices will only put more pressure on our cattlemen," Cotton said on X. "I have advised the President against this ill-advised action in the past and I now urge him to reconsider. We need to support our cattlemen, grow the herd, and let the market work."

Trump last week announced on Truth Social his intent to flood the market with 300,000 metric tons of imported ground beef with a commitment that the product would be sold at 25% below current market prices over a 90-day span.

It comes as ground beef prices have soared to roughly $7 per pound, while the nation’s cattle herd earlier this year hit historic lows not seen since the 1950s, according to data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).

TOP GOP GROUP PUMPS $37M INTO FIGHT ON KEY ISSUE DOMINATING MIDTERM RACES: 'MUCH MORE TO COME'

Trump defended his import plan as he headed to South Carolina to stump for Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., arguing "that’s what the people want."

"That’s what the voters want, and that’s what I want. The ranchers are great. They’re my people. I love the ranchers," Trump said. "They’ve done a fantastic job, but they admit that we need a little help in order to get the prices down, so that’s what we’re doing."

Neither Trump, nor the administration, has so far said which countries the ground beef would come from. But earlier this year, he signed an executive order similarly aimed at lowering beef prices by allowing an influx of 80,000 metric tons of beef trimmings from Argentina.

Republicans at the time privately fumed over the directive in a closed-door meeting in the Senate with Vice President JD Vance.

And now, Republicans running for office in America’s heartland again disagree.

"I want to lower prices, but this is a bad idea," Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, said on X.

SENATE MAP TIGHTENS AS TOP FORECASTER MOVES 3 RACES TOWARD DEMOCRATS

Republican candidate for the Senate Ashley Hinson speaks during a campaign event on June 1, 2026, in Dubuque, Iowa. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

Hinson is running in one of the tightest races in the country to replace retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa. Cook Political Report rated the race a toss-up last week.

Other in-cycle incumbents aren’t thrilled with Trump’s push, either. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., charged, "This Hurts!," while Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., contended that he appreciated the work to "lower grocery prices," but warned that "short-term policy shifts do not equal long-term solutions."

"Flooding the market with lower quality beef compromises Nebraska farmers and ranchers," Ricketts said.

Trump’s other key Senate allies aren’t thrilled with the plan either.

Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., said he’s advised Trump not to do this for the last year because it would harm American ranchers, "most of whom are MAGA Republicans."

"The president’s heart is in the right place on wanting lower prices for the American people, and beef prices have been impacted by the Mexican screwworm," Sheehy said.The White House and the USDA did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

articles.title: Problems brewing for the proper pint as Camra membership falls
articles.excerpt:
Cost of living has hit campaign group while multinationals are threatening to squeeze out independent  breweries

For centuries, the wooden real ale pump has been the hallmark of a good British boozer...
articles.body_text:
Cost of living has hit campaign group while multinationals are threatening to squeeze out independent  breweries

For centuries, the wooden real ale pump has been the hallmark of a good British boozer. But now problems are brewing for the proper pint, as the Campaign for Real Ale has seen its membership sink to an eight-year low and its accounts show it is firmly in the red, making an £800,000 loss last year.

Real ale is a traditional draught cask beer, a “living” product that is produced and stored in its cask. It differs from a cold, fizzy lager, in which the yeast is killed and carbon dioxide is added. Real ale contains live yeast so it continues fermenting until it is served.

Outside the Devonshire pub in Soho, central London, there is an ever-present horde of drinkers downing pints of Guinness, a stout made by the multinational company Diageo. But the landlord and co-owner Oisín Rogers says: “Real ale is all I drink.”

He says: “It is a properly handmade British product produced in exactly the same way it has been for centuries. It has never been industrialised like some of the other drinks that are for sale in bars in London.” His favourite tipple, is, appropriately, a pint of Landlord, made by the family-owned Timothy Taylor brewery in Keighley, West Yorkshire.

Tom Stainer, Camra’s chief executive, says independent breweries are facing unfair competition from multinationals. If you walk into a pub on the high street, you are often confronted with the same few beers, most of which are made by the same large companies, Stainer says.

“Our recent beer report highlighted that the beers people want aren’t available in bars because of the ways the huge international brewers operate – they have a stranglehold on the industry,” he says. “We call it an illusion of choice – a lot of people walk into bars and don’t realise everything in front of them is owned by the same big company.”

He says these “big global brewers who have deep pockets and huge influence” make it “hard for small brewers to get to market”. The incentives offered to large pub companies include cheap packages for beers, wine and soft drinks, with a multi-year tie-in, and minimum purchase orders where “pubs are forced to sell a certain amount of this product”.

Stainer adds: “We have heard of pubs taking off independent beers because they are too popular and stop people buying that product they have a minimum purchase order for.”

Camra is calling for the Competition and Markets Authority to investigate the big beer companies’ stranglehold on the market.

There are no such problems at the King Charles I pub in King’s Cross. As an independent, community-owned venue, the team can choose what’s on tap. They have a healthy range of cask beers, swapped out every five weeks.

Matt Roberts, the manager, says: “I like to choose local beers – today we have one from Southwark, some from Kent and one from the West Midlands. Cask ale is still very popular, it makes up around 30% of our sales. We are lucky we don’t have a big pub company telling us what to sell.”

Despite the delicious range of cask ale on offer, including the very drinkable Bankside Blonde by Southwark Brewing Company, Guinness still appears to be the order of the day among the customers.

Camra is facing a nadir: last September it announced it had been forced to cancel its pivotal Great British Beer festival, formerly the largest of its kind in the UK, for the foreseeable future due to financial pressures. Writing in the accounts, the chair, Ash Corbett-Collins, said it had been “one of the most challenging years Camra has faced”, pointing to a restructuring in which “a number of roles were sadly made redundant”.

The cost of living crisis is making it more difficult to run a membership organisation, Stainer says. “When you look at your bank balance each month, membership might be something you might economise to offset your huge energy bill or the rise in food prices.” A Camra membership is £35 a year.

articles.title: ‘Fix that little spot’: Danish PM receives beauty tips even when in a war zone
articles.excerpt:
Mette Frederiksen, who was attending meeting in Kyiv, advises high-profile women to embrace self-acceptance

Sick of getting unsolicited beauty tips on social media, even while she’s in a war zone, Da...
articles.body_text:
Mette Frederiksen, who was attending meeting in Kyiv, advises high-profile women to embrace self-acceptance

Sick of getting unsolicited beauty tips on social media, even while she’s in a war zone, Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen rebuffed a male cosmetic surgeon’s offer to “fix” her and advised women in similar situations to embrace self-acceptance.

Frederiksen, a Social Democrat and Denmark’s second female prime minister, posted on Instagram that she had just returned from a trip to Ukraine where she was subjected to air raid sirens when she found a message proposing some help with her appearance.

She included a screenshot of the exchange in which the doctor, who was not identified, said he could “fix that little spot on your nose”.

Her retort was swift and pointed: “Oh no. I’m happy with my body – I really don’t need a male plastic surgeon to have an opinion about it!”

Frederiksen, who has led the EU and Nato member country since 2019 and is one Europe’s longest-serving heads of government, said being a woman in the public eye meant regular exposure to such unwanted and superficial scrutiny.

“I’ve lost count of how many messages I’ve received over the years about my appearance,” the 48-year-old wrote. “Especially that I have ugly teeth and thin hair. That I have an ugly ‘wart’ on my nose and well-meaning advice to get some Botox.”

Frederiksen’s global profile has grown this year as she stood up to US president Donald Trump’s repeated claims on Greenland, a semi-autonomous Danish territory. She is also a staunch supporter of Ukraine against the Russian onslaught.

In a moment of striking candour, Frederiksen admitted annoyance with pushy beauty advice while offering her own guidance how to deal with it.

She said she did not volunteer opinions about other people’s looks and said that “I’m perfectly fine with my body – as it is when you’re a woman approaching 50.”

Frederiksen said she was fine to stay in conversation with the public on a range of topics but encouraged Danes to set the bar higher with their chosen subject matter.

“If you’re going to write to me (and you’re more than welcome to), I hope you’ll use your time to talk about something more meaningful,” she said. “Not my nose.”

Although the mean-spirited suggestions made her feel “indignant”, she said, “today, I’m sending an extra loving thought to all of you who have to put up with the ‘perfect imperfections’ we all walk around with every day.”

The Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title: Russia to seize poorly protected infrastructure as Ukraine barrage persists
articles.excerpt:
President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree opening the way for the Russian state to take temporary control of critical infrastructure found to be inadequately protected from attack.

The decree, pub...
articles.body_text:
President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree opening the way for the Russian state to take temporary control of critical infrastructure found to be inadequately protected from attack.

The decree, published on Monday, would allow Moscow to strip owners of physical and financial control over facilities should it be determined that they are failing to secure them or repair damage quickly. The move comes as Ukraine maintains an intense drone campaign against Russian infrastructure.

Under the decree, ownership powers would transfer to Russia’s Federal Agency for State Property Management or another designated body, which would take responsibility for the site’s safety and could conduct an inventory of its assets.

Fuel and energy facilities, including nuclear power, are included under the legislation as well as industry, communications, transport and logistics, public utilities and other facilities deemed essential to state security and economic stability.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but with the front line in eastern Ukraine bogged down, the conflict has become increasingly focused on drone and missile strikes.

Kyiv has found significant success in long-range drone attacks. Its targeting of Russia’s energy infrastructure in particular has produced results, sparking fuel shortages across the country and impacting public opinion and an economy that has been enduring increased international sanctions for close to five years.

Kyiv has also struck at least two dozen warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, destroying a significant share of its storage capacity and causing billions of dollars of damage to companies across the nation.

Ozon, Russia’s second largest online retailer, said on Monday that four of its logistics hubs in southern Russia had been hit.

The same day, Russia was also forced to halt operations at the Perm oil refinery, industry sources told the Reuters news agency. The facility, a major processing  plant, has been hit numerous times by Ukrainian drones in recent months.

An attack last week damaged key processing units. Repairs are expected to take up to two weeks, adding to fuel shortages reported in several regions.

articles.title: Survivors of violent crime criticise MoJ for not explaining offender restriction zones
articles.excerpt:
Campaigners accuse ministers of trying to grab headlines with announcement before a working system is ready

Survivors of violent crime and families of victims have criticised the UK government for an...
articles.body_text:
Campaigners accuse ministers of trying to grab headlines with announcement before a working system is ready

Survivors of violent crime and families of victims have criticised the UK government for announcing “world first” plans to introduce restriction zones for serious offenders freed from prison within a few weeks without spelling out how they would work.

Key campaigners who have championed the idea of the zones, designed to “lock” offenders into specific areas, accused the government of seeking to grab headlines rather than providing the detail that would reassure survivors and families.

Rhianon Bragg, who has become a leading campaigner on domestic violence after she was stalked and held hostage at gunpoint by her ex-partner, said she was concerned that the announcement had come before a working system was ready.

She said: “Victims can’t rely on headlines. I can’t imagine how anxious victims whose offenders may be being released are feeling right now. The announcement leaves critical questions unanswered.”

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said at the weekend that restriction zones would be introduced in October in England and Wales and would mean serious sexual and violent offenders could be confined to areas of a few miles.

Offenders would be tagged to keep tabs on their movement and victims would have a say in setting boundaries.

The MoJ said it was the first measure of its kind in the world and was a “more rigorous” version of “exclusion zones”, which ban offenders from specific locations such as a victim’s home or place of work.

Bragg said she and fellow campaigners wanted more detail on which offenders would be included, how zones would be implemented, what would happen if an offender left their zone and whether agencies such as the Probation Service and the police had the capacity to manage the system.

Announcing the scheme, the justice secretary, Alex Norris, said no victim should “fear the shadow of an abuser”.

Bragg said: “Speaking from my own lived experience, if that is to be achieved then restriction zones need to be the other side of the country from the area the victim is in.”

Bragg and fellow campaigners wrote to the government before the parliamentary recess asking for a meeting so that specifics could be discussed, but it has not taken place. She said: “We need more transparency. If the system’s not ready, victims will be put at risk.”

The campaigner Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, whose best friend, Joanna Simpson, was killed by Simpson’s estranged husband, said: “A headline doesn’t help victims one jot. The lack of detail is a huge issue.

“We have been asking them for two months to meet with us to discuss how they are going to implement it and which offenders are going to be eligible.

“You’ve got thousands of victims out there today who are utterly terrified at a visceral level of their offenders coming out of prison and they don’t know if their offender is going to be subject to restriction zones or not.

“It creates more uncertainty for them, more trauma for them. The MoJ needs to hurry up and engage properly with victims.”

Barkworth-Nanton, who co-founded the Joanna Simpson Foundation, which campaigns on domestic abuse and homicide, agreed the size of the restriction zone was not relevant. “I don’t care whether it’s 2 miles, 5 miles, 10 miles, 15 miles. The important thing is twofold.

“One is whatever that restriction zone is, probation needs to be confident that they can monitor them. And the second thing is it needs to be far away from the victim. So a 2-mile restriction zone, 5 miles away from the victim’s home is hopeless.”

Joanna Simpson’s mother, Diana Parkes, a leading campaigner for restriction zones, said: “On the whole I’m happy but we want to hear what the total plan is.”

Natalie Queiroz, who was repeatedly stabbed by her partner while she was eight months pregnant and is now a victims’ advocate in the West Midlands, said: “Restriction zones are a really positive solution and all credit goes to all those who campaigned hard for them.

“However, I’m yet to be convinced of the breadth of their impact in reality. The MoJ have stated that they will be enforced for the most serious violent offenders as well as for serious sexual offenders. Many domestic abuse offenders who still pose a significant risk to their victim will not fall under this definition and hence will not have a restriction zone applied to them.”

The MoJ said further details would be announced in due course. It said the government would work closely with victims’ groups and other stakeholders as the scheme was rolled out to ensure it was operating as intended.

Queiroz added: “The effectiveness of restriction zones will rely heavily on them being properly monitored and any breaches being addressed without delay. There needs to be clear commitment to investment into the active monitoring of them.”

articles.title: No 10 says glorification of dangerous driving ‘for clips and entertainment is utterly disgraceful’ – UK politics live

articles.body_text:
Downing Street repeats calls for social media platforms to review content and policies following a fatal crash near Middlesbrough on Saturday

In other news, No 10 has described the glorification of dangerous driving “for clips and entertainment” as “utterly disgraceful” after a viral trend showing young people going the wrong way down roads renewed scrutiny of social media regulation following a fatal crash near Middlesbrough on Saturday.

TikTok is among the social media firms that have been urged to remove wrong-way driving videos from its platforms after two police officers and five others were killed in a crash on the A66, as we mentioned in the opening post.

A Downing Street spokesperson said this afternoon:

double quotation markThe glorification of dangerous driving for clips and entertainment is utterly disgraceful and that is why we have raised the issue of this appalling content with social media companies since the tragedy, and the secretary of state for culture, media and sport (Lisa Nandy) is clear that it should be removed in line with their legal obligations.

She added that Ofcom has the government’s “full backing to take tough action” against platforms which fail in their legal duties. TikTok is already under investigation by the regulatory body due to worries about the effectiveness of its age-checking software.

TikTok has denied that its content puts children at risk, claiming its policies strictly prohibit content that could cause significant physical harm, including dangerous driving, and said that it is removing any videos and accounts that break its rules.

People trying to cross the Channel to the UK have reported an increase in French police use of violence on beaches to prevent them from getting into dinghies, according to a French NGO.

Utopia 56, which works on beaches from where migrants attempt Channel crossings, says so far this year 2,720 people have reported being victims of French police violence, compared with 1,954 over the same period last year, when crossings overall were much higher.

The organisation says that due to increased enforcement activity on French beaches, for which the UK provides funding, crossings have become more dangerous and disorganised, putting more lives at risk. So far this year at least 21 people have died trying to cross the Channel to reach the UK.

The NGO’s report alleges that the UK and French governments are “the architects of this chaos”. It calls for an overhaul of the European asylum system and the opening of safe routes, which it says would stop the boats and neutralise the smugglers.

Twelve people have been arrested on offences including being involved with organised crime by detectives investigating the lead up to the A66 crash which killed two police officers.

Cleveland police said nine men and three women, aged between 19 and 61 have been arrested on suspicion of offences ranging from possession of a firearm to participating in the activities of an organised crime group.

The force said its officers had responded to reports two cars were being driven dangerously on Saturday 22 August.

The Volkswagen Passat, which collided with the vehicle of Pc Matthew Blades and Pc Tom Clough, had earlier been sought in connection with a Volvo XC60 that was seen ramming properties in the Middlesbrough area.

Four of the five people in the Passat, including three teenagers, had previous convictions.

The force statement continued: “At the current time, there is no evidence to indicate that filming of the activities that took place on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for the purposes of TikTok.”

Back to that Reform UK press conference about social housing for a moment, during it MP Lee Anderson said that people living in social housing could face eviction if they don’t keep their gardens tidy and the property decorated.

Anderson claimed “If you go back in time and look what actually happened … the people that rented council homes had to be married under a Labour, socialist government. They had to look after their property. They had to keep it well maintained. The gardens done and decorated, and they were inspected on a regular basis by officers from the council.”

He continued, using the well-worn phrase “alarm clock people”, to outline Reform’s plan to evict people who don’t look after properties, saying:

double quotation markWe see all sorts of people moving into these brand new houses and creating mayhem and disturbances on these brand new housing estates. And the hardworking British taxpayer, the alarm clock people who get up at 5am or 6am, go to work and see the house next door with 4ft of weeds, dustbin not been emptied for three weeks and a waft of weed coming out the window, is not acceptable.

As far as I can tell, since it was introduced, social housing in England has never been legally restricted to only married couples as Anderson claimed, however there was a strong social stigma against unmarried people and single parents being allocated places in the 1950s and 1960s when the priority was rehousing people from slum areas and places damaged by second world war bombing.

Scottish Labour party leadership candidate Michael Marra has said he would be open to deals with other parties in the Scottish local elections next year.

Speaking to PA Media in Glasgow on Monday, he said Scottish Labour would want to work with other parties at the elections to “make sure that we lock out Reform from the halls of power in Scotland”.

He said: “All they bring is division, distrust and a brand, I think, of right wing populism that is actually a challenge to the soul of our country. That’s not something the Scottish Labour party will accept. It’s what we’ve always fought against, and we’re going to be on the frontlines fighting against them this time round, too.”

He added “I think we have to recognise that Scottish politics has changed; that we have a very fractured polity, lots of different parties competing for space and a voice. The days of two-party politics are long in the past in Scotland so we have to make sure that we are able to speak to parties.”

While Andy Burnham is in Kyiv – which my colleagues Vivian Ho and Jakub Krupa have been covering on Europe live – Andrii Madzianovsky, Ukraine’s consul general in Edinburgh has been among those paying respects at the Stone of Remembrance in the city on Ukraine’s independence day.

Simita Kumar, the SNP’s minister for equalities and international development, laid a wreath at the Stone of Remembrance on behalf of the Scottish government.

Graduate job vacancies in the UK have sunk to their lowest level since they started being tracked a decade ago, according to a recruiting website.

Just 8,383 jobs for people leaving university were advertised in July, Adzuna reported on Monday, down 45% compared with the same point last year and the lowest since the company started gathering the data in 2016.

The number comes as 262,820 people prepare to go to university in September, a record high that underlines the tough conditions facing graduates entering the job market as entry-level roles are threatened by AI.

About 1 million young people in the UK were not in education, employment or training, otherwise known as Neets, in the first quarter of this year, according to the Office for National Statistics.

Adzuna said sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies, adding that the figures suggested that a recovery reported during the spring had gone into reverse.

Andrew Hunter, a co-founder of Adzuna, said: “July’s numbers are a step backwards, not a blip. The annual vacancy decline got worse for the first time since January, and (the number of) jobseekers per vacancy are now higher than they were a year ago. You can read more here:

In other news, No 10 has described the glorification of dangerous driving “for clips and entertainment” as “utterly disgraceful” after a viral trend showing young people going the wrong way down roads renewed scrutiny of social media regulation following a fatal crash near Middlesbrough on Saturday.

TikTok is among the social media firms that have been urged to remove wrong-way driving videos from its platforms after two police officers and five others were killed in a crash on the A66, as we mentioned in the opening post.

A Downing Street spokesperson said this afternoon:

double quotation markThe glorification of dangerous driving for clips and entertainment is utterly disgraceful and that is why we have raised the issue of this appalling content with social media companies since the tragedy, and the secretary of state for culture, media and sport (Lisa Nandy) is clear that it should be removed in line with their legal obligations.

She added that Ofcom has the government’s “full backing to take tough action” against platforms which fail in their legal duties. TikTok is already under investigation by the regulatory body due to worries about the effectiveness of its age-checking software.

TikTok has denied that its content puts children at risk, claiming its policies strictly prohibit content that could cause significant physical harm, including dangerous driving, and said that it is removing any videos and accounts that break its rules.

Back at the press conference, the Reform UK MP for Ashfield and party chair, Lee Anderson, described the low fertility rate among British couples as a “scandal”.

“If we can get young British workers into housing they are more likely to start a family and end this scandal,” Anderson said.

“I see it in my own village, where my own school now has got school places spare and they are really struggling through the pupil premium to keep that school properly funded. We need more babies in this country. We need more children.”

In 2025, the fertility rate for England and Wales fell for the third year in a row to reach a record low, as my colleagues note in this story, with a lack of affordable housing and childcare support thought to be among the main reasons behind the decline.

The total fertility rate across both countries, meaning the average number of live children women can expect to have across their child-bearing life, stood at 1.41 in 2024, down from 1.42 in 2023, the lowest since comparable data was first collected in 1938, according to the ONS.

Richard Tice was also asked on Times Radio this morning if Reform’s housing plans would mean a married British couple would get priority over a single British person, he said:

double quotation markYes, that is the preference… Well, because actually families are a good thing. Having British children, British-born children is a good thing. We need to encourage that.

And it’s a very natural, normal thing - has been over centuries for people to get together, to get married, have children and contribute to their communities. And everything that we’re doing is focused solely on that.

When pushed by Times Radio presenter Calum Macdonald on the fact that single people may also have children, Tice added: “They might. But in an ideal world, it is well known that married couples – children in married couples, for example – will do really well at school. And we want to encourage that.”

“Of course, sometimes life doesn’t work out, we understand that. But as an objective that is surely preferable,” he added.

This article includes content hosted on platform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

In a Q&A with journalists after the press conference, Sky News’ political reporter Ben Bloch asked about Reform designating marriage as a core allocation factor for social housing. Q: What is your message to single parents? Are they less worthy of help than a married couple with children, for example.

Richard Tice takes the question. He said he doesn’t think it is “wrong” to “promote marriage”. “That’s the right thing to do in our judgment,” he said.

Experts have said that prioritising people based on nationality, age and family status, as Reform has suggested, could punish some of society’s most vulnerable people.

Sarah Elliott, the chief executive of the charity Shelter, said: “Designed to stoke division, these plans will only serve to disrupt the lives of thousands of families, tear communities apart, and put even more people at risk of homelessness.

“Putting nationality and employment ahead of housing need, and moving away from a system designed to prioritise people who are homeless or at urgent risk of homelessness, could leave even more families trapped in awful temporary accommodation for years on end. Not to mention putting those escaping domestic abuse and violence at serious risk of harm.”

A Labour spokesperson said: “Illegal migrants, asylum seekers and migrants on student or work visas are not eligible for social housing. This policy would go after long-term UK residents that have contributed to our country but are not British citizens, including NHS staff.”

Tice says young British workers, married couples and veterans under 35 should be prioritised for affordable housing.

“It is not fair that young British working families, couples, individuals, veterans can’t get on the housing ladder when overseas nationals have come to the UK and in a sense because of the current rules, based on need rather than suitability, they have jumped ahead of the queue and we just don’t think that is right,” he said.

Under the terms of a previous announcement by Reform UK’s leader, Nigel Farage, foreign nationals would be barred from social housing, with those already in homes given three months to find private accommodation or face deportation.

Tice failed to mention that UK or Irish nationals made up 88.5% of main social home householders - the person in whose name the social home is rented - in 2024/25, according to the English Housing Survey, and 11.5% were non-UK/Irish nationals.

There are also already strict rules around the allocation of social housing based on who has the greatest need, making it relatively difficult for non-UK nationals to access it. There are an estimated 470,000 non-UK and non-Irish citizens living in social housing.

Tice explains how Reform will pay for all of the affordable social homes he promises will be built. He says a Reform government will “reactivate an attractive right to buy housing programme” for existing tenants.

Tice says if someone has lived in a council house or housing association for five years they’d receive a 30% discount, and a 40% discount if they lived there for ten years, as examples. He said the failure of the Conservatives in the 1980s laid in the fact that the party didn’t “reinvest the proceeds” back into building affordable homes.

Local authority tenants have been able to buy their homes since 1936, but changes made under the first Thatcher government in 1980 triggered a boom in sales at steep discounts to market value. Although welcomed by many, the policy fuelled vast shortages in the social housing stock and turbocharged inequality.

“That’s the key difference. Here we know it (the money) will go back into building affordable homes by a factor of two to one. So that will be about a third of the total money involved,” Tice told journalists.

Reform’s deputy leader went on to claim that the rest of the funding will come via housing authorities and through the “British sovereign wealth fund” that the party argues would boost economic growth by investing in British businesses.

Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, says we have a “desperate shortage” of affordable housing and council housing. In order to address the shortage, he says a Reform government would build an extra £50,000 extra “affordable social homes” every year for a decade, a significant uplift on the 18,000 the government has promised to build on average each year for a decade.

Labour’s plans are being financed by a £39bn affordable housing scheme, 60% of which is due to be allocated to social homes, which are the most heavily subsidised, as my colleagues note in this story. Reform said its plans would be funded, with no extra borrowing or taxation required to pay for the additional homes. It is yet to give details about where exactly the money will come from (this may come shortly).

articles.title: Sam Burns is one of America's best golfers, but faith, family and the USA matter more to him than golf
articles.excerpt:
Sam Burns joins OutKick's own Dan Zaksheske to discuss golf bringing people together, family & faith, the LSU Tigers, and much more!

Sam Burns is headed back to represent the United States.

Burns of...
articles.body_text:
Sam Burns joins OutKick's own Dan Zaksheske to discuss golf bringing people together, family & faith, the LSU Tigers, and much more!

Sam Burns is headed back to represent the United States.

Burns officially clinched an automatic spot on the U.S. Presidents Cup team Sunday, giving the 30-year-old his third Presidents Cup appearance and fifth consecutive Team USA appearance across the Presidents Cup and Ryder Cup.

EXCLUSIVE: SAM BURNS WANTS LIV GOLF STARS JON RAHM, BRYSON DECHAMBEAU BACK ON THE PGA TOUR

If you're a diehard golf fan, none of that is particularly surprising.

Team USA's Sam Burns walks on the 17th green during the 2025 Ryder Cup at Bethpage Black. (PGA of America via Getty Images)

Burns first represented the United States at the Junior Ryder Cup when he was 18 years old. More than a decade later, he's a five-time PGA Tour winner, one of the best American golfers in the world and a fixture on U.S. teams.

His son is going to experience it with him.

"Bear this year, he'll be around the team and get to hang out and really enjoy it," Burns told OutKick in an exclusive interview on Aug. 18.

Burns and his wife, Caroline, welcomed Bear in April 2024. Their daughter, Belle, arrived on July 3.

Bear is only 2, so he’s still too young to understand what his dad is doing when he represents the United States. Burns knows his children won't fully comprehend what their dad has accomplished for quite some time.

LSU ALUM SAM BURNS MAKES IT CLEAR HIS SON WAS NOT NAMED AFTER BEAR BRYANT

But they're going to grow up watching him wear USA on his chest, and that clearly means something to Burns.

"It is such an honor for me to be able to represent your country and also play for ultimately something a lot bigger than yourself," Burns said. "And you have teammates that week that you're playing for and their families."

Sam Burns with his wife, Caroline, and son, Bear, at the Par 3 Contest prior to the 2026 Masters Tournament at Augusta National Golf Club. (PGA TOUR via Getty Images)

Golf is about as individual as sports get.

Most weeks, Burns is trying to beat everyone else in the field.

For a few weeks throughout his career, he's been playing for something else.

"It's such a special week," Burns said. "And it's a week that I think most guys, when they look back on their career, when it's over, those will be the weeks that they remember."

Casual sports fans might not immediately put his name alongside the biggest stars in golf, but his résumé is getting increasingly difficult to overlook.

Burns has won five times on the PGA Tour, though he hasn't won since 2023. This summer, he came painfully close to winning his first major championship, finishing second at the U.S. Open and third at The Open.

Burns held the 54-hole lead at Royal Birkdale last month before ultimately finishing two shots behind winner Ryan Fox.

He played in the final pairing at the FedEx St. Jude Championship alongside world No. 1 and close friend Scottie Scheffler last weekend. Scheffler ultimately hoisted the trophy, but Burns locked up another top-five finish, his fourth of the 2026 season.

All of that makes him one of the best American golfers casual sports fans might not know, and golf isn't even the most important thing in his life.

Sam Burns clinched an automatic spot on the U.S. Presidents Cup team, earning his fifth consecutive Team USA appearance across the Presidents Cup and Ryder Cup. (Getty Images)

Burns spoke with OutKick at The Highlands Golf & Tennis in St. Louis, where he partnered with Raising Cane's to work with local kids ahead of the BMW Championship.

The 30-year-old is now a father of two, and OutKick asked him what becoming a dad has taught him about himself.

"I think you don't realize how impatient you are until you have kids," Burns said.

He talked about trying to reason with a toddler or newborn who doesn't understand what Dad is trying to explain. But then Burns got to the part of fatherhood that seems to have changed his perspective the most.

"You feel like they may be an inconvenience at times and then you just realize they want your attention and they want your love," Burns said. "So it's really special to be a dad for sure."

GOLF STAR BRYSON DECHAMBEAU OPENS UP ABOUT WANTING FOUR KIDS AND HOW HE THINKS FAMILIES SHOULD WORK

Burns has already had to put those priorities into practice this year.

Earlier this summer, he was prepared to miss The Open because Caroline was due to give birth around the same time.

Belle arrived early, 13 days before the first round of The Open, and Caroline ultimately encouraged her husband to make the trip to Royal Birkdale.

This isn't someone using "golf isn't everything" as an excuse for being indifferent about golf.

Sam Burns competed for Team USA at the 2014 Junior Ryder Cup at Blairgowrie Golf Club in Scotland as an 18-year-old amateur. (Getty Images)

He's an elite professional athlete who wants to win. He puts an enormous amount of time into trying to become better and has spent this season coming extremely close to one of the few accomplishments still missing from his résumé: a major championship.

But Burns has also spoken openly about his Christian faith and his belief that golf is what he does, not who he is.

Saying that is one thing. Maintaining that perspective while trying to beat the best golfers in the world is another.

OutKick asked Burns if he could remember a moment when golf truly tested his faith.

Anyone who has ever picked up a club knows golf has a way of doing that.

"You put so many hours and so much effort into something, and a lot of the times you don't really see the results right away," Burns said. "You can hit really good shots and end up in bad places, or bad shots end up in good places. Sometimes it seems silly, but ultimately it's a game that teaches you a lot about life and definitely can make you realize what's most important."

For Burns, the perspective comes back to three things: faith, family and country.

Burns didn't become a five-time PGA Tour winner, contend for major championships and earn five consecutive Team USA spots without pouring himself into the game.

But Burns also seems to understand the distinction between caring deeply about something and allowing it to define you.

When Burns heads to Medinah next month, not only will he be there representing the United States, but his son Bear will be there to start watching him do it.

Burns has plenty of golf left, and plenty of time to add to an already impressive résumé. A major championship remains out there. So do more PGA Tour wins and, presumably, more opportunities to wear the red, white and blue.

But when Burns eventually looks back on all of it, he already has a pretty good idea which weeks will stand out.

The ones when he was playing for something bigger than himself.

articles.title: Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon price rises in western Europe ‘highest in world’
articles.excerpt:
World’s largest streaming services have also increased subscription costs repeatedly in US, research finds

Subscribers to Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon Prime Video in western Europe have faced higher p...
articles.body_text:
World’s largest streaming services have also increased subscription costs repeatedly in US, research finds

Subscribers to Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon Prime Video in western Europe have faced higher price increases than in any other market in recent years, according to research.

Over the past four years the world’s largest subscription video streaming services have dramatically changed their business models introducing lower-priced, basic advertising tiers to attract new subscribers, while also increasingly monetising users willing to pay more for a premium experience.

Research by Ampere showed that a series of price rises over the past three years, to fund the production of content and drive profits, have led to western European subscribers being hit by the largest average price increases.

Over this period the average increase in the cost of a monthly subscription has risen by $1.86 (£1.36) – more than the US, the world’s biggest streaming market, at $1.70 – and all other world regions.

Pricing in different markets is influenced by a number of factors, including domestic competition and household income, with subscribers in sub-Saharan Africa facing the smallest average price increase of less than $1 over the past three years.

In March, Netflix increased prices in the US for the second time in a little over a year. UK subscribers last faced price increases, ranging from £1 to £2 a month, in February 2025, the first increase since October 2023.

The most recent price increases pushed the cost up £1 to £5.99 a month for the basic package with ads, and up £2 to £12.99 a month for Netflix’s standard ad-free package.

Netflix UK’s recently published financial figures for last year show that the streaming company passed £2bn in annual revenues for the first time. The record £2.06bn marked an 11% increase on the £1.85bn reported in 2024.

The company, which also reported a healthy increase in pre-tax profits from £63m to £72.5m, said the revenue boost was “driven primarily by a 7% growth in the average number of paid memberships and by higher average monthly revenue per paying membership”.

Disney+ last moved to raise prices in the UK and US in September and October last year, with the cost of a UK subscription to its package with advertising £5.99 a month and standard ad-free tier £9.99 a month, or £99.90 annually.

Amazon introduced a £2.99 monthly fee on top of its Prime Video membership for users wanting to pay to avoid seeing ads in February 2024.

While semi-regular prices rises have become a facet of the streaming sector, Ampere’s research also showed that the scale of each bump up in subscription charges has dropped significantly “as consumers reach limits on willingness to pay”.

Average price rises across the three streaming companies have fallen from 24% of the previous subscription price in 2023-24 to 14% in 2025-26.

In dollar terms the streamers’ ad-free subscription packages have received larger price increases than their tiers that include ads, which are targeted at much more cost-conscious consumers.

Jaanika Juntson, a senior research manager at Ampere Analysis, said: “The decline in price increases comes as streamers diversify how they monetise their audiences.

“As streaming businesses mature, revenue growth is becoming less reliant on price increases, while intense competition is also making streamers increasingly mindful of how they are positioned against rivals.”

Last week it was reported that the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to make her acting comeback in Guy Ritchie’s Netfix series The Gentlemen, shortly after reports that the Duchess and the Duke of Sussex were poised to return to live in the UK six years after moving to the US.

However, multiple subsequent reports suggest that Markle, who made her name in the legal drama Suits, is not in fact in the running for a role in the third season of The Gentlemen, which is yet to receive an official green light from Netflix. In 2020, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex signed a multi-year Netflix deal, reportedly worth $100m.

articles.title: Indiana mayor calls it ‘unacceptable’ for thousands to have no power two weeks after storm
articles.excerpt:
Gary mayor says 12 days is ‘too long’ for residents to go without power after storm downed trees on to power lines

The mayor of Gary, Indiana, has said it is “unacceptable” that thousands of resident...
articles.body_text:
Gary mayor says 12 days is ‘too long’ for residents to go without power after storm downed trees on to power lines

The mayor of Gary, Indiana, has said it is “unacceptable” that thousands of residents in the city are still without power nearly two weeks after an 11 August storm known as a derecho brought 90 mph, straight-line winds, downing trees on to power lines.

“We’re at day 12, and 12 days is too long for families to be without power,” Eddie Melton, Gary’s mayor,  said in a video address on Sunday, adding that he is continuing to pressure the Northern Indiana Public Service Company (Nipsco) to restore the city’s power before the end of Tuesday.

“Twelve days is too long for parents to worry about their children, and for businesses to lose revenue, and for families to wonder when the relief is finally going to come. Today, I want the people of Gary to know this. I want you to know that I share their frustration.”

On Sunday, there were still more than 14,500 power outages in Gary. That number had been reduced to 10,187 by Monday morning, according to the company.

At the peak of the outages, 374,500 were without power.

Most school students in Gary were able to return to classes on Monday, officials said.

“That’s progress, but Nipsco has so much more work to do,” Melton said. “We’ve pushed them to do more and do it faster.” Gary currently has 700 lineworkers and 300 vegetation crews working to restore power, the mayor added.

Thousands of residents of north-west Indiana have been without electric power since storms swept through the state, leading to food lines, closed businesses, dead phones, no schools, spoiled food, dirty clothes and dry gas pumps.

Nipsco has said Gary may not see full service restored until Tuesday. ComEd, the largest electric company in Illinois, has also sent crews over to help expedite repairs.

Residents have filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against Nipsco that accuses it of failing to trim trees that brought down the power lines.

“This situation was predictable. It was obvious and it was preventable,” attorney Otto Shragal of the Allen Law Group said.

Nipsco denied the allegations, arguing that it maintains a vegetation management program.

“We strongly disagree with the characterization of NIPSCO’s vegetation management practices,” the company said. “NIPSCO’s vegetation management spend has more than doubled since 2016, demonstrating our commitment and focus on maintaining a safe and reliable electric system.”

Melton’s pressure on Nipsco to restore services comes after Mike Braun, Indiana’s governor, said in an interview with Inside INdiana Business that the company “needs to pick up the pace, because we’ve given them national guard help [and] all of our agencies”.

Braun also said nearly two weeks without power “is a long time in the middle of summer”.

Gary has contracted three organizations to help with the recovery, including Egis Group, an insurance agency, to execute damage assessments; Thompson Consulting Services, a Florida-based company, to oversee debris collection; and AshBritt, a disaster response services company, to execute debris removal.

Melton has asked residents to organize storm debris in separate piles for a smoother collection operation.

Meanwhile, on Monday, food critic and social media personality Keith Lee, Indiana Pacers basketball team star Tyrese Haliburton, the Salvation Army, Ace Hardware and Gary city officials planned to co-host a relief supplies event for locals outside the community’s Roosevelt Pavilion, according to organizers.

Organizers said Lee committed $15,000 in supplies for the event, which Haliburton matched to bring the total contribution to $30,000. The other entities provided additional support.

“Gary has always been a resilient city,” Melton said. “We’ve always overcome challenges before, and we’ll overcome this one as well. The lights are coming back on, neighborhood by neighborhood.

“Resources continue to arrive to our city. Neighbors continue to help neighbors until every family is taken care of. We will not stop pushing, and we will not stop fighting for the people of the city of Gary.”

articles.title: Iran faces 'greatest financial offensive ever', says US treasury secretary
articles.excerpt:
The US treasury secretary has threated Iran with "the single greatest financial offensive ever", claiming the US-Israel war with Iran was "entering its endgame".

Scott Bessent said the US would sever...
articles.body_text:
The US treasury secretary has threated Iran with "the single greatest financial offensive ever", claiming the US-Israel war with Iran was "entering its endgame".

Scott Bessent said the US would sever all economic ties with the country in "an economic D-Day" and that any nation partnering with Iran financially would also be isolated.

Bessent's threat to the Iranian regime follows several U-turns and extended deadlines from US President Donald Trump's administration on previous threats.

Iran dismissed Bessent's comments and said it would shut down all oil exports from the region "if the war continues", according to news agency Reuters.

The Iranian regime has also issued a new warning to shipping not to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its permission, the agency reported.

One fifth of the world's oil and gas usually passes through strait, a waterway south of Iran, but the flow has been effectively blocked by the country since the conflict began at the end of February.

Bessent made the comments in an opinion piece for the Financial Times, external. He did not detail what the economic pressure on Iran would involve, but he is expected to do so in a press conference in the US at 13:00 local time (18:00 BST) on Monday.

"The world should understand that our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," he wrote in the piece.

The US has made several threats to Iran over the course of its war with the country, including Trump saying in April that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" unless Iran agreed a deal to end the war and unblock the Strait of Hormuz.

The US eventually climbed down from that position after mediator Pakistan intervened and called for more diplomacy.

The economic impact of the Iran war is being felt in the US and across the world. Higher oil prices have fuelled concerns over the cost of living, with petrol and diesel  prices much higher than they were a year ago.

In the US, gasoline prices have surpassed $4 a gallon and affordability is among the top concerns of American voters ahead of the mid-term elections in November.

Last week, Bessent announced the US government would intervene in the bond markets and buy back more government debt in a bid to boost demand for bonds and lower borrowing rates.

But the impact of the annoucenment was short-lived, with long-term borrowing costs bouncing back up a day later.

How much could Trump's 'economic D-Day' hurt Iran?

The Iranian regime already faces tough economic sanctions from the US.

Former US president Barrack Obama and several US allies had agreed a deal with the country in 2015 which lifted many sanctions in return for Iran agreeing to limit its nuclear programme.

However, Trump pulled out of that deal in 2018, calling it "defective at its core, and reimposed all US sanctions on Iran.

During Joe Biden's term as US president, he made some attempts to reinstate the Obama-era deal, but this did not happen.

In April this year, the Trump administration launched a wave of sanctions on foreign banks and firms doing business with Tehran after it became clear its military operations had not caused Iran's regime to surrender.

articles.title: Birth tourism scams draw sweeping crackdown as visa revocations climb
articles.excerpt:
State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Fox News Digital that the Trump administration is ramping up efforts to curb birth tourism.

The State Department is cracking down on a popular form of ...
articles.body_text:
State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Fox News Digital that the Trump administration is ramping up efforts to curb birth tourism.

The State Department is cracking down on a popular form of visa fraud through a sophisticated worldwide operation that has already revoked hundreds of visas.

The department's spokesman, Tommy Pigott, told Fox News Digital that under the direction of President Donald Trump, the American government is partnering with agencies across the globe to halt the practice of birth tourism.

Birth tourism refers to travel to the United States for the primary purpose of giving birth so a child can obtain U.S. citizenship. The practice has been linked to visa-fraud schemes in which applicants conceal or misrepresent the purpose of their travel, often while seeking entry on visitor visas. A U.S.-citizen child may also create future immigration options for family members, including the ability to petition for a parent after turning 21.

TRUMP SIGNS EXECUTIVE ORDERS TARGETING BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP, BIRTH TOURISM AFTER SUPREME COURT SETBACK

Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David on July 31, 2026, in Maryland. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

It has also become a for-profit industry, where facilitators of the fraud market their services for helping women break America's laws through "birth in the U.S." services, including arranging visa scams to get women into the country.

"The first step in that is identifying them," Pigott said. "We have consular officers around the world that work with international partners, that work for law enforcement officials to identify patterns that indicate a birth tourism network, and then when that is identified, we take actions such as revoking their visas, which was the recent announcement that we made, to make sure that we're dismantling those networks."

ABBOTT ORDERS PROBE AFTER TEXAS HOSPITAL ADVERTISES 'BIRTH PACKAGES' IN MEXICO: 'CITIZENSHIP IS NOT FOR SALE'

Earlier this month, the State Department announced that it was launching a Birth Tourism and Prevention Task Force.

"We're making adjustments because it's very unfair," Trump said. "They're building businesses around birthright citizenship. That's not the way it was supposed to work. It's a disgrace. They're buying their way in, and we're not going to let it happen."

Through the task force, government officials are now analyzing in real time travel trends by visa holders around the world that are indicative of the practice.

TEXAS GOV ABBOTT SIGNS EXECUTIVE ORDER CRACKING DOWN ON 'BIRTH TOURISM,’ SAYS US CITIZENSHIP NOT FOR SALE

In one recent case, a woman who came to the United States on a tourist visa under the impetus of a weeks-long vacation, continuously received visits from her partner, who lived outside the country. That pattern raised officials' suspicions, who understood the partner's movements as visits to the United States to support the woman in the latter stages of her pregnancy and possibly present in the country during the child's birth.

"That was an indication that this was actually a birth tourism effort here, and we were able to take action to revoke those visas," said Pigott. "So we're able to analyze those travel patterns, analyze those instances that indicate fraud, look into those, and the task force we have allows us to take that action.

More than 100 mothers traveled to the U.S. to give birth so their children could obtain citizenship and benefits, authorities said. (iStock)

Pigott provided some examples of the blatant fraud.

BIRTH TOURISM COULD SOON CARRY A SEVERE NEW CONSEQUENCE FEW WOULD RISK: 'EXISTENTIAL CRISIS'

"There were some advertisements that were being published talking about a world without borders or automatic guaranteed citizenship in their advertisements while they were pretending to offer health care services," he said. "In reality, that is fraud, and the fraud actually doesn't just end when it has to do with the birth tourism example of lying to the consular officer."

"These networks are set up in the United States and then further coach these individuals on how to not pay their medical bills," he continued. "So you have fraud when you enter the United States and then the American taxpayer is left footing the bill. It comes down to the fundamental principle: we're gonna protect the sacred privilege of American citizenship and not allow this fraud to happen."

President Donald Trump gives a thumbs up before boarding Air Force One en route back to Washington, D.C., at Cleveland Hopkins International Airport in Ohio on Aug. 11, 2026. (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images)

TRUMP DOJ UNLEASHES LARGEST DENATURALIZATION EFFORT IN DEPARTMENT HISTORY — AND SAYS IT’S ‘ONLY THE BEGINNING’

The task force, officially launched on Aug. 12, has already revoked more than 750 visas tied to suspected birth-tourism activity. The State Department expects that number to increase dramatically in a very short period of time.

Pigott added that under the Trump administration, visa security is an important part of a much broader overall effort to secure the border, adding that the Biden administration, "did everything they could to allow for the abuse of our legal immigration system and allowed for the unprecedented border crisis that we saw."

Under President Joe Biden, an estimated 10 million people crossed the border into the United States illegally.

Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

Twelve people have been arrested on suspicion of offences including being invol...
articles.body_text:
Nine men and three women aged between 19 and 61 arrested as part of investigation of events leading to deadly collision

Twelve people have been arrested on suspicion of offences including being involved with organised crime as part of the investigation into events leading to a crash on the A66 which killed two police officers and five others.

Cleveland police said nine men and three women, aged between 19 and 61, had been arrested on suspicion of offences ranging from possession of a firearm to participating in the activities of an organised crime group.

The force said its officers had responded to reports of two cars were being driven dangerously on Saturday 22 August.

The Volkswagen Passat which collided with the vehicle of PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough had earlier been sought in connection with a Volvo XC60 that was seen ramming properties in the Middlesbrough area.

Both vehicles had cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology, the force said, and the Volvo XC60 had been traced and recovered in Middlesbrough.

Four of the five people in the Passat, including three teenagers, had previous convictions.

The force said in a statement: “At the current time, there is no evidence to indicate that filming of the activities that took place on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for the purposes of TikTok.”

articles.body_text:
It’s a common refrain from the president, but perhaps takes on a new meaning ahead of the fresh sanctions that we’re expecting later today

Meanwhile, ahead of the treasury secretary’s annoucement, Donald Trump has taken to Truth Social to insist that “IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!”

It’s a common refrain from the president, but perhaps takes on a new meaning ahead of the fresh sanctions that we’re expecting later today. My colleagues are covering the latest reactions to the Iranian economy ahead of Bessent’s press conference. This includes the news that Iran’s currency has weakened to an all-time low.

The rial was trading at 1.992m per dollar on the unregulated market on Monday, according to Bloomberg News, which cited data from tracking website Bonbast – down 4.5% since last week.

New Mexico will continue funding gender-affirming care for minors after a federal rule ending Medicaid support for such care goes into effect.

On 13 August, the Trump administration finalized a rule – set to go into effect on 13 October – that will end funding for gender-affirming care through Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program (Chip).

New Mexico’s “Health Care Authority is planning to continue covering these services using state funds”, Timothy Fowler, a state health care authority spokesperson, wrote in an email to the Santa Fe New Mexican.

Earlier this year, New Mexico also announced that it would cover the cost of expiring Affordable Care Act tax credits for residents who purchase health insurance on the state marketplace. In July, a news analysis showed that New Mexico was the only state in the country where Affordable Care Act enrollment increased after federal subsidies expired at the end of 2025.

In recent years, New Mexico has become a haven for gender-affirming healthcare in the south-west. In 2023 the state legislature passed a Reproductive and Gender-Affirming Health Care Freedom Act, and a growing number of families have relocated to the state as protections for transgender youth disappeared in neighboring states. The Williams Institute at the University of California, Los Angeles, estimates that 4,800 transgender teens between the ages of 13 and 17 live in New Mexico today.

Meanwhile, ahead of the treasury secretary’s annoucement, Donald Trump has taken to Truth Social to insist that “IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!”

It’s a common refrain from the president, but perhaps takes on a new meaning ahead of the fresh sanctions that we’re expecting later today. My colleagues are covering the latest reactions to the Iranian economy ahead of Bessent’s press conference. This includes the news that Iran’s currency has weakened to an all-time low.

The rial was trading at 1.992m per dollar on the unregulated market on Monday, according to Bloomberg News, which cited data from tracking website Bonbast – down 4.5% since last week.

Today we can expect a new round of sweeping sanctions on Iran from treasury secretary Scott Bessent.

The US also said it would impose steep penalties on any country trading with Tehran.

Bessent called the plan, which he prefaced in an op-ed in the Financial Times, as “the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary”.

We’ll bring you the latest from the treasury secretary’s press conference at 2pm ET.

He warned of an “economic D-Day” for Iran, as the war –now in its sixth month – shows no signs of easing.

As my colleague Patrick Wintour reports, in advance of the US announcement, the United Arab Emirates, Iran’s single biggest trading partner in the Middle East, announced it was ending all trade with Iran. It’s a move Tehran believes was coordinated between Washington and the UAE.

The new sanctions will also be a test for China and Russia to see if the US follows through on its vow to punish the countries for their continued trading with Iran.

Donald Trump is in Washington today. He’ll spend most of the day in meetings that are closed to the press, but we’ll hear from the president at 2.30pm ET when he hosts a Rose Garden event at the White House.

We’ll bring you the latest lines here as that gets under way.

Election deniers are back on the ballot. In most swing states, at least one major Republican candidate has questioned or outright denied the results of the 2020 US presidential election, which Donald Trump lost to Joe Biden.

While voters in swing states have previously largely rejected candidates who denied election results, Republicans running for statewide offices across much of the country are trying again.

In Arizona, gubernatorial candidate and US representative Andy Biggs voted against certifying his own state’s election results. In Wisconsin, Republican gubernatorial hopeful Tom Tiffany similarly voted against certifying the 2020 results as a US representative for his state.

Candidates for governor in Pennsylvania and Michigan have cast doubt on the validity of the 2020 results. And some swing state Republican candidates for secretary of state have questioned or denied election results.

Governors sign off on state election results, issuing certificates to the presidential electors of whichever candidate wins. They can call for investigations or special sessions, and use their bully pulpit to cast doubt on election results. Secretaries of state are meanwhile the chief election officials in most US states, overseeing voting systems and advising the local jurisdictions that run elections. They usually play a role in certifying election results, too.

In 2020, Trump pressured governors and secretaries of state, alongside a host of state and local officials in several swing states, to withhold their signatures in a broad campaign to overturn his loss. Swing state governors and secretaries of state refused to stall or impede their states’ results.

But if election deniers or skeptics are elected to these key statewide roles, they would be in office in 2028, raising apprehension that they may refuse to sign off on results, or succumb to pressure from Trump and his allies, should Republicans lose.

Over a dozen US companies that signed a 2021 letter urging Congress to strengthen the Voting Rights Act continue to contribute to state political groups that are actively working to undermine the legislation, according to a campaign finance watchdog.

Researchers at the Center for Political Accountability (CPA), a nonpartisan organization that tracks financial disclosures, found that companies – including Airbnb, DoorDash, Target and Zillow – that signed the letter are contributing to groups known as 527 organizations that prop up key state races, according to data provided exclusively to the Guardian.

Four longtime donors to these groups, Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft, had either stopped contributing entirely or lowered their contributions to Republican and Democratic groups for the 2022 midterms, but have resumed contributions for the current election cycle.

The January 6 insurrection created a brief reckoning among corporate leaders, many of whom criticized Donald Trump’s role in inciting the violence. The Republican Attorneys General Association (Raga), a 527 organization, was under scrutiny after reports revealed the group sent out robocalls to people encouraging them to attend a “Stop the Steal” rally in front of Congress on January 6 2021 – which preceded the insurrection. Raga leaders later said they had no knowledge of the robocalls.

But the companies have resumed their donations to Raga and, in some cases, have become new contributors to the group. Google’s contribution went from $100,400 in the 2018 election down to $50,000 in 2022. So far this election, the company has donated $325,000 to Raga.

Dan Sullivan supports Dan Sullivan against Dan Sullivan in Alaska’s US Senate election, says a former Alaskan mayor who recently backed the race’s Republican incumbent over a challenger sharing their name.

That development provided another of multiple absurd elements to Dan S Sullivan’s campaign for a third term in the US Senate, which – beside Mary Peltola, a former Alaska Democratic congresswoman – has drawn opposition from Dan J Sullivan.

Dan J Sullivan emerged from an 18 August primary to join a four-candidate field rounded out by Dan S Sullivan, Peltola and one other contender. His presence in the field for the general election during the 3 November midterms has prompted accusations that he is a Democratic plant aiming to draw enough votes away from Dan J Sullivan – whose name was positioned consecutively to him on the primary ballot – so that Peltola can win.

Donald Trump’s Republican party is projected to lose congressional seats during the midterms, and the president wrote on social media on the day of the primary: “ALASKA: Be careful. VOTE FOR THE REAL DAN SULLIVAN TODAY.

“The Dumocrats know how good he is and have put up an imposter of the same name.”

Trump was not the only Republican politico to come out swinging for Dan S Sullivan’s re-election bid on the day of the primary, in which Peltola finished first. Another who came out in favor of the incumbent was Dan A Sullivan, the mayor of Anchorage, Alaska, for six years beginning in 2009.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries’ meeting with Jared Kushner, the president’s influential son-in-law, has sparked backlash from his own party and other Donald Trump critics.

The reported meeting comes months ahead of the November midterm elections in which Democrats are favored to retake the US House, a development that would make Jeffries speaker.

If they are in the majority, Democrats are expected to use their oversight power to aggressively investigate the Trump administration, including self-enrichment by the president and his family.

There are longstanding conflict-of-interest concerns about the way Kushner has continued to make money from foreign nations as he works on foreign affairs, including conflicts in Ukraine, Iran and Gaza.

Asked about the reported meeting, Jeffries said in a statement:

double quotation markThroughout this Congress, Republicans have adopted a my-way-or-the-highway approach to governing that has failed the American people. To stop the madness, we have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition.

The American people want bold change and that’s what House Democrats will deliver. In every conversation that we have with the Trump administration, we will continue to make it explicitly clear that the affordability crisis is not a hoax and nothing short of transformational policy change is acceptable. We are fighting for an affordable America. The question is whether Republicans will join us.

Nonetheless, among some who lamented the reported gathering was Tommy Vietor, previously an aide to former president Barack Obama and now a co-host of the left-leaning podcast Pod Save America.

“Jared Kushner has no actual government job he just uses his family connections to get money from gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals. The only way [Jeffries] should work with him is with demands for documents and subpoenas,” Vietor posted.

Asked whether he supported the meeting during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, Senator Chris van Hollen – a Maryland Democrat – said: “I’m in favor of people meeting with whoever they want to discuss ideas. But it’s one thing to have a meeting. It’s another thing to see something real come out of that.”

Adam Kinzinger, a former Republican congressman from Illinois who is an outspoken Trump critic and served on a House committee that investigated the Capitol attack, posted in reference to the meeting, “Make this make sense,” while tagging Jeffries.

Tim Scott defended fellow US South Carolina Republican senator Darline Graham’s knowledge of national security issues ahead of their state’s runoff election on Tuesday. Graham, who was appointed to fill the Senate seat held by her brother Lindsey Graham after his sudden death in July, is in a Republican primary runoff against South Carolina congressman Ralph Norman.

That development provided another of multiple absurd elements to Dan S Sullivan’s campaign for a third term in the US Senate, which – beside Mary Peltola, a former Alaska Democratic congresswoman – has drawn opposition from Dan J Sullivan.

The Donald Trump aide Natalie Harp flooded a since-disabled social media account with pro-Trump posts on the day that the president’s supporters attacked the US Capitol in early 2021, years before she went to work for him and developed an extraordinary close relationship with him, a new report has revealed.

A series of moves by Donald Trump’s administration to sow doubt in the integrity of US elections has intensified concern among voting experts – and sparked hope among election deniers – that it could declare a national emergency. The White House and US federal agencies have released a string of documents this summer – including disputed analyses of alleged voting by noncitzens and historical intelligence memos – stoking expectations that the US president could move to exert greater control over November’s US midterm elections.

Iran’s foreign minister has dismissed the threat of a fresh round of US economic sanctions as a “desperate” ploy, even as its president acknowledged that the Iranian people are facing “many problems” amid Washington’s efforts to isolate and debilitate the country’s economy.

Tens of thousands of people in Nevada were urged to evacuate as a fast-moving, wind-driv...
articles.body_text:
Fast-moving, ‘human-caused’ fire in Reno leaves thousands of homes and businesses without power, officials say

Tens of thousands of people in Nevada were urged to evacuate as a fast-moving, wind-driven wildfire bore down on the city of Reno.

The Hawk fire began on Saturday to the north-west of the city, and quickly grew, showing “extreme fire behavior”.

No deaths have been reported, but at least six people have been injured – including three first responders – with several mountaintop houses destroyed, according to local media.

Officials said the fire was “human-caused”, but did not say how it started.

About 42,000 people have been forced to evacuate and an additional 45,000 have been told to get ready to leave, Reno’s mayor, Hillary Schieve, told CNN.

All but one school in Washoe county, where Reno is located, will remain closed on Monday, authorities said. Nearly 10,000 homes and businesses in Washoe county were without power. Portions of US Route 395, a major north-south highway, were closed.

The rapidly expanding fire was surrounded by neighborhoods. Richard Edwards, the local fire chief, urged people to be ready to evacuate immediately when told to do so.

“The Hawk Fire is a very dynamic incident for us as it’s being driven by the winds. The wind-driven fires move very rapidly into our residential areas,” he said.

“If you have been told to evacuate, please don’t wait!” Schieve, the Reno mayor, said in a statement on social media.

“It was extremely confusing,” said Darin Balaam, the Washoe county sheriff, describing how changing winds sent the flames in different directions.

The fire had already proved to be a challenge on Saturday night, moving exceptionally fast, jumping over fire trucks and making it difficult for responders to get to hotspots while residents were trying to get out, Balaam said.

Joe Lombardo, Nevada’s governor, has declared a state of emergency in Washoe county.

A local fire rescue service said about 800 people were supporting firefighting efforts, including crews from Australia and New Zealand.

articles.title: Sonya Massey's killer Sean Grayson dies in US prison
articles.excerpt:
