articles.title: New daily diabetes pill that helps with weight loss launches in UK pharmacies
articles.excerpt:
Foundayo will be available on private prescription, with pharmacists warning of counterfeit GLP-1 problem

A new daily pill that treats diabetes and helps with weight loss will be available in UK phar...
articles.body_text:
Foundayo will be available on private prescription, with pharmacists warning of counterfeit GLP-1 problem

A new daily pill that treats diabetes and helps with weight loss will be available in UK pharmacies from Monday.

Pharmacists said the move would be welcome for people who cannot use weight-loss jabs, but also issued a warning over the growing problem of fake, unlicensed or counterfeit versions of GLP-1 tablets.

Orforglipron, known as Foundayo and made by the US pharmaceutical firm Eli Lilly, was authorised by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) earlier this month. The UK is the first country in Europe to approve it, after approving another weight-loss pill in June.

“The UK is the first country in Europe where Foundayo is now available,” said Khalil Asmar, the vice-president of cardiometabolic health at Lilly Northern Europe. “We’re pleased that this means there is another oral treatment option for eligible UK patients alongside licensed injectable treatments.”

The drug will initially be available through private prescription, with Eli Lilly saying it is working with the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) on its assessment of Foundayo for a potential rollout on the health service in England.

Th drug is licensed for people with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or above, or those with a BMI of between 27 and 30 and at least one weight-related condition. It can also be used to improve blood sugar levels in patients with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. The pill is taken once a day, at any time, with no food or water restrictions.

Henry Gregg, the chief executive of the National Pharmacy Association, said: “This is another significant day with a second weight loss pill available from today in certain pharmacies. This is particularly significant for patients who cannot or do not want to take an injectable medicine and could make weight-loss treatment available to a wider range of patients.”

However, there are concerns about the marketing of fake, unlicensed or counterfeit drugs, which can be easier to produce in pill form than injectables. Last year, the MHRA seized £250,000-worth of unlicensed weight-loss pens and ingredients from a factory in Northampton, and Eli Lilly is suing various suppliers it accuses of participating in an illegal hidden market for its drugs.

Patients are being urged to ensure that they access weight-loss treatments only through safe and regulated pharmacies.

Gregg said: “There must now be a redoubling of efforts within government and the NHS to use pharmacies to make sure more eligible patients in clinical need can get weight loss treatments on the NHS, rather than the current postcode lottery that exists for weight management services via GPs.”

The MHRA approved the first GLP-1 pill for weight loss, a tablet form of Wegovy, in June.

articles.title: Air conditioning push favoured over emissions cuts in five European nations, survey finds
articles.excerpt:
Poll also finds sizeable majorities who believe it should be easier to install air con in homes

Given the choice, more people across five major European nations including the UK favour encouraging th...
articles.body_text:
Poll also finds sizeable majorities who believe it should be easier to install air con in homes

Given the choice, more people across five major European nations including the UK favour encouraging the adoption of air conditioning over keeping carbon emissions down, a survey has found.

After four extreme heatwaves that have caused thousands of excess deaths across the continent, the survey showed between 30% and 52% of people in six countries had feared for their household’s health in temperatures close to or above 40C (104F).

Large numbers of people, ranging from 27% in Spain to 41% in France and 53% in Germany, said they felt they could not keep their homes cool enough, and many wanted governments to explore a variety of ways to help make them more comfortable.

The YouGov polling, carried out in mid-July in France, Germany, Italy, Poland and Spain and in early August in the UK, found that between 61% and 73% of respondents favoured air conditioning being installed as standard in all new homes.

A further 65% to 75% backed making it easier for people to install air conditioning without needing permission from local councils or landlords, and between 52% and 66% said they would support government subsidies for homeowners to have it installed.

In every country except Italy, significantly more people – between 41% and 48% – said allowing and encouraging more air conditioning to reduce harms from heatwaves should be prioritised over lowering CO2 emissions, with 20% to 33% believing the reverse.

In all countries, more people thought more air conditioning would have a very or fairly large impact on reducing harms from heatwaves (29% to 61%) than that it would have a very or fairly large impact on their country’s climate figures (19% to 40%).

Air conditioning is much less common in Europe than in the US, where 93% of people have a central or portable system. The poll put take-up at 63% in Italy and 58% in Spain, but only 30% in France, 23% in Poland, 16% in Germany and 11% in the UK.

Those figures do not reflect broad opposition to air conditioning, however, with attitudes mainly positive (46% to 60%) or neutral (31% to 39%). France was an outlier, with 20% hostile, and left-leaning voters notably more negative than elsewhere.

Air conditioning has become a new front in Europe’s culture wars, with mainstream parties accused of blocking its large-scale use on “ideological” green grounds, and far-right parties, which are broadly opposed to combating the climate crisis, pushing it as vital.

Rightwing US commentators say low take-up shows Europe is badly governed and overregulated. European experts back air conditioning for people at risk, but many favour longer-term solutions – such as more shade, better insulation – over mechanical cooling.

Scientists have long said human-made global heating is making extreme weather events more frequent and more intense, turbocharging severe heatwaves, prolonged droughts and violent storms, which are breaking more and more records.

Few Europeans – between 12% and 24% – thought more air conditioning would make people less dedicated to combating the climate crisis, and those with air conditioning were generally no less likely to be concerned about the climate than those without.

Asked why they did not have air conditioning, 51% to 75% of people in each country said cost was the main obstacle. Climate impact was notably less important, at between 6% and 17%, except in France (27%).

But while most people would support making it easier to get air conditioning, between 35% and 46% in each country thought most problems associated with people being unable to keep cool during heatwaves could also be solved without it.

Asked what their government’s priority should be, more people (27% to 42%) said other methods of keeping homes cool – including external shutters, insulation and reflective roofs – should be prioritised over air conditioning (12% to 20%).

The survey showed that for people who had air conditioning, the impact was clear: 79% to 85% of those with it said they were able to keep internal temperatures comfortable during the recent heatwaves, compared with only 35% to 47% among those without it.

It found that 14% to 17% of air conditioning owners in Italy, France and Spain had felt unable to use it as much as they needed because of the cost, while 28% to 38% said they had used it often but as a result would need to cut spending elsewhere.

articles.title: ‘An amazing relief’: implant offers hope for those with refractory angina
articles.excerpt:
Study finds device brings significant fall in chest pain in 75% of patients, but further trials and NHS approval are needed

“It’s an amazing relief, both physically and emotionally, to be able to liv...
articles.body_text:
Study finds device brings significant fall in chest pain in 75% of patients, but further trials and NHS approval are needed

“It’s an amazing relief, both physically and emotionally, to be able to live my life again normally, without feeling that I’m limited all the time in what I can do.”

Cristian Jensen is describing the difference that an implant inserted in his chest – to reduce the symptoms of his debilitating angina – has had on his life.

The 64-year-old used to have five angina attacks a week, each involving a sharp, acute pain that reminded him of the heart attack he once had. Now he has an attack every week or two.

He used to have to limit the amount of exercise he did, in case strenuous activity induced an attack. Now he’s walking further and faster and no longer worries about climbing stairs.

“It’s made a huge difference to my confidence,” the packaging designer adds. “Angina is a reminder that something isn’t right with your body. It’s like a sharp pain in the middle of your chest that stops you doing what you are doing.

“The fear that the pain of an episode of angina could be a heart attack. Suddenly not having that anxiety at the back of your mind changes your life.”

Angina, a common form of heart disease, involves pain in the chest, neck, shoulders, jaw or arm.

Jensen had a long and troubled history of heart problems before consultant cardiologist Dr Ranil de Silva fitted him with the implant – a coronary sinus reducer (CSR) – at the Royal Brompton hospital, a renowned centre of specialist NHS heart and lung care in London, in 2021.

In 1990, he was diagnosed with angina at an unusually young age – at just 28 – after an angiogram showed he had blocked arteries.

Open heart surgery helped. “That fixed me, for a while at least,” he says. “I was angina-free for 17 years until I had a heart attack in 2007.” That led to him having the first of what became eight stents put in, to help his arteries stay open and his heart to keep pumping blood around his body.

But in 2015 he began taking drugs to lower the high level of bad cholesterol in his bloodstream – fatty deposits that narrow the arteries. He also started using another drug, a spray called gylceryl trinitrate (GTN), to banish the pain each of his angina attacks brought.

Jensen is one of an estimated 300,000 people in England with refractory angina. That is angina that remains problematic despite the patient having drugs, stents and heart bypass surgery.

When Jensen’s symptoms persisted, de Silva suggested he have the implant fitted. Despite the large number of people with the condition, only a handful have had what is still an experimental treatment.

The small, hourglass-shaped device is implanted near the heart using keyhole surgery through the patient’s neck. It works by narrowing a vein at the back of the heart. That helps to redirect the person’s blood flow to the parts of the heart muscle that are getting too little oxygen. Each device costs the NHS £11,400.

A new study – the largest of its kind worldwide to date – has found that the device brings about a significant fall in chest pain in 75% of people with refractory angina within six months of its implantation.

“In this respect it is potentially a gamechanger,” says de Silva, who co-led the study with his colleague Dr Kevin Cheng. It was based on observation of 491 people with refractory angina between 2014 and 2024, 474 of whom had the implant fitted at 19 hospitals in England and Scotland.

Most patients went home the day of the procedure or the day after and serious complications were rare, the study also found.

According to de Silva, it shows that the device can greatly reduce the debilitating symptoms of refractory angina that significantly compromise quality of life and the ability to undertake normal day to day activities, and can help people avoid being admitted to hospital and boost their mental wellbeing.

“Many patients report their lives being transformed and that it helps them to achieve the quality of life they wish for, that they were unable to enjoy prior to the reducer implant – they get their life back,” says de Silva.

Despite the apparent success of the implant, and that only “a tiny fraction” of the 300,000 people with refractory angina have had one fitted, it is too early to yet see CSR as a standard treatment for people with this very painful form of coronary artery disease, he says.

More trials are needed and the NHS needs to approve the funding needed to expand access, he adds.

Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, a consultant cardiologist and the British Heart Foundation’s clinical director, said: “The findings are reassuring as they show that in routine clinical practice the device is being delivered safely and is resulting in fewer symptoms for patients.”

The device “offers hope for people living with this challenging condition”, she said.

articles.title: New Fed chair faces critical test at Jackson Hole as inflation fears mount
articles.excerpt:
Investors will hope Kevin Warsh offers ‘comfort blanket’ at annual meeting of central banks amid bond market anxiety

The new US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, faces a critical test this week ami...
articles.body_text:
Investors will hope Kevin Warsh offers ‘comfort blanket’ at annual meeting of central banks amid bond market anxiety

The new US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, faces a critical test this week amid anxiety in government bond markets over inflation and Donald Trump’s tax and spending plans.

As the world’s most powerful central bank prepares for its annual Jackson Hole conference, analysts said bond traders would be looking for signals from Warsh over its commitment to fighting inflation.

The Trump-appointed head of the US central bank has previously signalled reluctance to “spoon-feed” financial markets over how it plans to set interest rates to keep fast-rising prices in check.

However, anxiety over Trump’s handling of the economy and investor fears that his war with Iran is stoking inflation have rocked global financial markets amid a dramatic sell-off in US government bonds.

Dan Coatsworth, the head of markets at the stockbroker AJ Bell, said: “Investors will be looking for a comfort blanket when Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh addresses the Jackson Hole meeting.”

James Smith, an economist at ING Bank, said: “By offering less commentary on where rates are headed … [Warsh] risks injecting yet more volatility into an already febrile bond market.”

Warsh is expected to give a highly anticipated speech on Friday at the Fed’s annual symposium in the Rocky Mountains resort of Jackson Hole, against a volatile backdrop in global financial markets.

The gathering of the world’s most powerful central bankers in the Grand Teton national park is a blue riband event in the financial calendar, as a vital platform for the Fed chair and other top officials to signal their policymaking approach.

However, Warsh has signalled reluctance to use his speech for the “more traditional setup” of dropping hints over how the US central bank may respond to inflationary pressures when its officials next meet to set interest rates in September and December. Instead, he has said his Jackson Hole speech could be “focused on bigger questions”, including concerns over productivity and demographics.

However, the meeting comes as selling pressure intensifies in the $30tn (£22tn) US government debt market despite efforts by the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, to assuage investor worries after he committed to at least double Washington’s purchases of US Treasury bonds.

With investors fretting over the inflationary impact of the Iran war and the US national debt surpassing $40tn for the first time, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on long-term US Treasury debt at first fell, before rising back towards the highest levels since 2007.

Warsh was accused by investors of sending confusing signals in his first press conference as Fed chair in July, after he expressed his commitment to curbing inflation without giving details.

The Fed held rates in July, and trading in financial markets reflects investor expectations for a hold again in September, although a rise is thought possible. Markets anticipate at least one, and possibly two, quarter-point increases by the middle of next year.

Trump, who appointed Warsh, has called on the Fed to cut rates, fuelling investor concerns over interference at the central bank.

Stephen Brown, an economist at the consultancy Capital Economics, said Warsh maintaining a tight-lipped approach could be risky. “He might even stick to the official subject of the symposium, ‘Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy’, in which case his speech could be something of a snoozefest.

“That said, even that approach would risk giving the impression that Warsh is not taking inflation risks seriously, so there could still be volatility in markets.”

articles.title: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
articles.excerpt:
The governor of Jawzjan province, Abdullah Sarhadi, who fought for the Taliban was held in US detention in Guantanamo Bay for several years

Governor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy's brok...
articles.body_text:
The governor of Jawzjan province, Abdullah Sarhadi, who fought for the Taliban was held in US detention in Guantanamo Bay for several years

Governor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy's broken arm and hands out funds for a local mosque - then, in his office in northern Afghanistan, an astonishing exchange unfolds.

A young woman tells the grey-bearded former Taliban commander that she wants to divorce her husband, who she accuses of months of abuse and beatings.

In a country where girls are banned from secondary education, the 18-year-old argues her case calmly and confidently, her face completely hidden behind a full-face veil and sunglasses.

"If there was any chance to live together, I wouldn't be here… I have taken my decision," she says.

After trying to persuade her to avoid divorce, the governor later comments that women are "mindless" and "deficient in intellect", to laughter from the male officials, bodyguards and elders around him.

The moment gives a rare glimpse into the day-to-day realities of the Taliban's rule, five years after they swept aside the US-backed government in 2021.

Watch: Eighteen-year-old woman argues her case for a divorce, saying her "honour and dignity have already been ruined"

In that time, women have been excluded from most workplaces, banned from universities and may not travel alone or visit parks and leisure centres.

In encounters spread over two years, the BBC gained unusual access to influential figures in the extreme Islamist movement, spending time with men who once planned suicide attacks or spent years in underground hideouts, but are now officials and soldiers.

The Taliban came into power saying they had changed, but many of their policies are similar to the hard-line interpretation of Sharia - Islamic religious law - they imposed in the 1990s.

The men we met seemed to want to present themselves as reasonable, yet were not keen to discuss their past violence. And we saw moments of unease between the rulers and those they rule.

Afghan women tell the BBC their lives are unrecognisable after five years of Taliban rule

Five years of the BBC questioning the Taliban over women and girls' education

Governor Sarhadi says Tuba – not her real name – should stay in the marriage.

"Ask yourself: 'Who would marry me after I get my divorce?'" says Sarhadi. "You'll have to compromise a lot or you'll lose your dignity and honour."

"Mr Governor, my honour and dignity have already been ruined," she responds.

Her husband listens, awaiting his turn to speak.

Under Sharia, a woman requesting that her husband agrees to a divorce may have to return some or all of the money given to her by him when they married. A financial settlement is often agreed. But this woman's husband says he wants four times the amount, which her family refuses to pay.

The governor says the woman should be given her own room. He adds that officials will warn him not to beat her - "otherwise he'd be jailed".

Unsatisfied, Tuba's father later tells the BBC the family will pursue divorce through the courts, even though, under the Taliban's court system, it is very difficult for a woman to get a divorce without the husband's consent.

A hole left by the destruction of one of the Buddha statues in Bamiyan -  Sarhadi says he destroyed it

Sarhadi was a military commander during the Taliban's first stint in power in the 1990s. He was among thousands of insurgents who surrendered in late 2001 as a US-led coalition ousted the group.

He was held for several years in US detention in Guantanamo Bay, but eventually released.

When the Taliban regained power, he became a governor - first in the province of Bamiyan, then when we met him in late June, in Sheberghan city in Jawzjan province. He has recently become deputy commander of a military corps in the northern province of Kunduz.

Tapping on an old-style mobile with a tiny screen, he says a recent ban on smartphones for officials has slowed things down. "Before, you could send a quick message… sending documents and getting an answer fast." If he says any more about the ban, "it will cause trouble", he adds.

But in other ways his worldview seems largely unchanged from the Taliban's position 25 years ago. Then, he was a military commander in Bamiyan, where the Taliban blew up ancient giant Buddha statues, triggering international shock and condemnation.

He initially tries to avoid our questions about the archaeological site, but eventually, he says: "I destroyed it with my own hands.

"Whatever we did and we do is in accordance with the guidance and God's law… We smash idols rather than sell them. Why should I regret? It was God's will."

In the capital Kabul, we meet another senior Taliban figure who swapped a violent past for a role with the ruling administration.

Habibullah Badr drives us through the streets in an armoured car.

He says he was previously "responsible for the operations of suicide attackers" in Kabul.

"I know all the roads and streets very well… we had all the information we needed about Kabul and its alleys," he says. "There were areas that needed a long time to plan."

Taliban suicide attacks killed thousands of people in Afghanistan, including many civilians.

Badr is cautious about discussing his past though, fearing it will "make people upset" and could "reopen wounds".

Asked about civilian deaths, he says the Taliban targeted US convoys and that civilians were urged to stay away from foreign bases.

Whenever I try to ask him about specific attacks that took place in civilian areas, he evades the question.

Habibullah Badr says that in the past he was involved in operations involving suicide attacks

He is currently taking time out from official roles for medical treatment, but was previously deputy head of prisons for the whole country – and ran the very jail where he was held on death row under the previous government.

Badr invites us to join him at a tribal gathering, where the head of a charitable foundation is to honour him with a medal. But things take an unexpected turn.

"Mr Badr is a pride for Afghanistan and a great fighter," says Sultan Mohammad Talaee. "But I also have a complaint. If the schools and education were open to all it would be a great work for Afghanistan. I hope this doesn't offend you."

An awkward silence follows, his audience unsure how to react. Talaee's microphone is swiftly removed.

Afterwards, he tells the BBC: "I requested for the girls' schools to reopen… seeking knowledge is an obligation for both men and women in Islam."

He adds: "There were other things I wanted to say but they didn't let me talk more."

Often those who speak out face much more severe consequences.

Women told us of the deep despair they felt over dreams thwarted by restrictions on education, and of friends jailed for protesting.

Most journalists we spoke to said they had been summoned or questioned by the Taliban's intelligence organisation, Estikhbaraat.

The BBC put some of these concerns to the Taliban government's spokesman, known as Zabihullah Mujahid.

Zabihullah Mujahid says women's rights and freedom of speech need to be seen "through the Sharia lens"

He has been a public face for the Taliban government since 2021. He still uses the pseudonym he went by for years during the insurgency, but he told us his real name is Tahir Shah Seddiqi - revealing it publicly for the first time.

In a lavish press centre funded by the Americans for the previous government, we ask him about the first press conference he gave there, two days after the Taliban took control of the country.

Then, he told the world the Taliban government would allow women to work and study "within our frameworks" and they would "be very active" in society. Why did they fail to keep their word?

"We are committed to women's rights, freedom of speech and other things within Sharia," he replies. "We should see everything through the Sharia lens."

Allowing women to work in offices such as his own "would lead to immoralities" and "their dignity would be undermined", he adds.

He says the issue of education for women is "under discussions… we need a Sharia-based solution for it".

When questioned about the Taliban's crackdown on media freedom, he says: "In a society like Afghanistan we have our restrictions. We can't let media do whatever propaganda they want… they can't broadcast against Islamic laws and rites."

The Taliban government sits in Kabul, but Mujahid spends a lot of time in the southern city of Kandahar, the Taliban's heartland, which some now consider the de facto capital.

We ask to meet the Taliban's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, who is based there. He rarely appears in public and has never given a media interview - we are told it will not be possible at the moment.

Restrictions have been tightened in Kandahar since I last visited two years ago. Now men must have beards. Radio stations are not allowed to play music or broadcast women's voices, and we were not allowed to film in the city.

Two hours' drive away, along dusty roads, some of the group's most devoted former fighters showed the BBC the insurgents' old secret cave network.

Abid Lalai, a former fighter who now mans a checkpoint as part of a security force under the interior ministry, shows us the holes he fired from and the places he used to put his Quran and hang AK-47s.

Abid Lalai is one of many Taliban fighters who hid out in caves to evade capture under previous governments

His superior, Abdul Samad, shows us an unmarked graveyard, saying his father is buried here, killed fighting for the Taliban.

The area is one of the most deprived in a country where the UN says three in four people cannot provide for their basic needs. Samad says the local population desperately need water, roads and clinics.

"Emirate [Taliban] officials have not forgotten us," says Samad. He says the leaders may be busy with other priorities. "We are hopeful, they will look after us sometime."

Five years since the Taliban began their second stint in power, poverty, unemployment and economic instability remain pressing concerns.

Taliban figures we spoke to said they were working to tackle them, but we met other people who believe the group itself is the country's main problem.

"I'm speechless about how a group that has no understanding about life is suddenly in power," says Hoda - not her real name - a woman who protested on the streets when the Taliban first returned to power.

"Women can't accept this situation," she tells the BBC. "They might advance restrictions but it won't stay like this forever."

"I think the Taliban are scared of educated women," she adds. "That's why they restrict women. They want uneducated women so they can't raise wise men. Because that would end the Taliban."

Additional reporting by Hafizullah Maroof

Five years after the Taliban swept to power, does the West have any influence?

articles.title: US envoy Tom Barrack retracts comment that Syria’s Golan is occupied
articles.excerpt: United States Ambassador Tom Barrack has reasserted Washington’s position that Syria’s Golan Heights belongs to Israel after saying last week that the territory is occupied against “all of the interna...
articles.body_text:
United States Ambassador Tom Barrack has reasserted Washington’s position that Syria’s Golan Heights belongs to Israel after saying last week that the territory is occupied against “all of the international order”.

US President Donald Trump’s ambassador to Turkiye and envoy for Syria walked back that comment on Sunday, underscoring Trump’s policy of recognising Israel’s claimed sovereignty over the stretch of land in southern Syria.

“United States policy on the Golan was set by President Trump in 2019 and is unchanged,” he told The Associated Press news agency in a statement.

Israel occupied the Golan during the 1967 Six-Day War and annexed the territory in 1981.

Until Trump backed the Israeli claim to the Syrian territory, no country had recognised the Golan as part of Israel.

The recognition sparked an international outcry. Legal experts warned that it could upend a core tenet of the post-World War II global order: the prohibition on acquiring land by force.

Former US President Joe Biden promoted the so-called rules-based order early in his tenure, but he failed to reverse Trump’s policy on the Golan during his four-year term.

Recently, Colombia’s right-wing government joined the US in backing Israel’s claim on the Golan.

In an interview with podcaster Mario Nawfal on Friday, Barrack appeared to acknowledge that the Golan is occupied Syrian land.

Barrack was asked whether Israel has plans to annex parts of southern Lebanon. He said regardless of intent, Israel knows that it would be difficult to claim Lebanese territory as its own.

“Saying that, in the Golan with Syria, they still occupy the Golan against the UN resolutions, against all of the international order, which has said the Golan is Syria’s,” Barrack said.

Israel’s advocates were quick to criticise Barrack’s comment. Far-right commentator Laura Loomer called on the envoy to step down.

“He should resign for his lack of understanding of US foreign policy,” she wrote in a social media post, sharing Trump’s 2019 proclamation saying that the Golan belongs to Israel.

Republican Senator Rick Scott also criticised the ambassador, saying Barrack was confirmed by the Senate to enact Trump’s agenda.

“It seems the Ambassador forgot that or failed to do his research, so here’s a refresher for him,” Scott wrote in a social media post that included Trump’s executive order on the Golan Heights.

“President Trump has been CLEAR about Israel’s sovereignty over the Golan Heights for years!”

Barrack had also been criticised for opposing Israeli air strikes on a Syrian airbase last week.

In his interview with Nawfal, Barrack suggested that the Israeli strikes in Syria were aimed at antagonising Turkiye, which is allied with the Syrian government.

“One theory is they were just baiting Turkiye, and it’s a very aggressive, but maybe well-received pre-election concept,” Barrack said, referring to US midterm elections in November.

articles.title: Popular erectile dysfunction drug linked to eye disease that can cause irreversible vision loss
articles.excerpt:
Dr. Daniel Amen discusses emerging research showing saffron may be as effective as SSRIs in treating depression, and could also improve sexual function.

A drug used to treat erectile dysfunction and ...
articles.body_text:
Dr. Daniel Amen discusses emerging research showing saffron may be as effective as SSRIs in treating depression, and could also improve sexual function.

A drug used to treat erectile dysfunction and enlarged prostate symptoms may raise the risk of glaucoma, a serious eye condition that can cause gradual vision loss, according to new research.

An international team of researchers analyzed health records from nearly 74,000 men ages 40 and older with lower urinary tract symptoms to examine whether long-term tadalafil use was associated with a greater risk of glaucoma.

The study, published in the British Journal of Ophthalmology, compared about 37,000 men prescribed tadalafil with a similar group who did not use phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, the drug class that includes Cialis.

Researchers followed the men for up to five years and looked for new cases of glaucoma and high pressure inside the eye, along with whether patients needed treatment for glaucoma.

VISION PROBLEM LEADS TO MAN'S STAGE 4 LUNG CANCER DIAGNOSIS, NEW DRUG EXTENDS SURVIVAL

New research suggests tadalafil, the drug sold as Cialis for erectile dysfunction and enlarged prostate symptoms, may be linked to a higher risk of glaucoma. (iStock)

Men who used tadalafil were 22% more likely to develop glaucoma than those who did not use the drugs, according to the findings.

They were also 32% more likely to develop high pressure inside the eye and 33% more likely to develop primary open-angle glaucoma, the most common type of the disease.

Dr. Valerie Kattouf, an optometrist at the Illinois Eye Institute who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital that glaucoma can be difficult to notice in its early stages.

"Glaucoma is an eye condition that especially in its early stages often does not present with visual symptoms," Kattouf said.

As glaucoma progresses, people may gradually lose their side, or peripheral, vision, she said.

The study found that men who used tadalafil were 22% more likely to develop glaucoma than men who did not take the drug. (iStock)

"Clinical findings of glaucoma are best detected in a comprehensive vision evaluation," Kattouf added.

Kattouf said people with a family history of glaucoma, high pressure inside the eye or severe nearsightedness may face a higher risk. Those who take Cialis daily over a long period of time may also warrant closer monitoring, she said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

People who regularly use the medication should have a comprehensive eye exam to establish a baseline for their eye health, according to Kattouf. Doctors can check pressure inside the eyes and perform other tests to look for changes that could signal glaucoma.

The researchers noted several limitations to the study.

People who take the medication regularly should get a thorough eye exam to establish a baseline for their eye health. (iStock)

The study was observational, meaning it found a link between tadalafil use and glaucoma but could not prove that the medication caused the condition.

Researchers also could not account for changes in medication use or other health conditions that developed over time.

The researchers stressed that the findings do not mean people should stop taking tadalafil. Instead, they said, patients who use the medication long term, particularly those with existing glaucoma risk factors, may benefit from regular eye monitoring.

Fox News Digital reached out to Eli Lilly, the manufacturer of Cialis, and the study’s researchers for comment.

Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: WATCH: Young bear takes rough tumble from Denver tree after wildlife officers tranquilize it
articles.excerpt:
The 100-pound bear was tranquilized and caught by officers before being relocated to better habitat (Credit: CPW NE Region).

A young black bear took a rough tumble from a tree in Denver on Sunday aft...
articles.body_text:
The 100-pound bear was tranquilized and caught by officers before being relocated to better habitat (Credit: CPW NE Region).

A young black bear took a rough tumble from a tree in Denver on Sunday after wildlife officers tranquilized the animal before relocating it to a more suitable habitat.

Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) said in a thread on X Sunday that officers responded to the bear near Louisiana Avenue and Pennsylvania Street in Denver.

"This morning we responded to a bear in a tree ... in Denver," the post read. "Not a typo. In Denver."

BEAR CAUGHT ON CAMERA PERCHED ATOP NEW MEXICO UTILITY POLE BEFORE REPORTEDLY SUFFERING FATAL ELECTROCUTION

A tranquilized black bear falls from a tree as Colorado Parks and Wildlife and Denver police respond in Denver on Aug. 23, 2026. (Colorado Parks and Wildlife NE Region)

Wildlife officers tranquilized the bear and worked with Denver Police Department officers to catch it as it fell from the tree, according to CPW.

"It didn't have the smoothest landing, but the bear is ok!" authorities said.

Video posted as part of the X thread showed the bear dropping through branches before officers secured the animal on the ground.

GATLINBURG POLICE FREE BLACK BEAR THAT LOCKED ITSELF INSIDE HOTEL BATHROOM IN WILD VIRAL VIDEO

A young black bear sits in a tree in Denver before Colorado Parks and Wildlife officers tranquilized and removed it on Aug. 23, 2026. (Colorado Parks and Wildlife NE Region)

CPW identified the animal as an approximately 1.5-year-old male yearling weighing about 100 pounds. The agency said the bear would be transported to better habitat and released.

The unusual Denver encounter comes as Colorado wildlife officials report an increase in bear activity this year, which they have linked to drought conditions and dwindling natural food sources.

CPW received 6,129 reports of bear sightings and conflicts between Jan. 1 and Aug. 13, compared with 3,115 during the same period last year, according to the agency.

BEAR CRASHES COUPLE'S ANNIVERSARY GETAWAY, RUMMAGES THROUGH TENNESSEE TEA SHOP BEFORE JUMPING ON COUNTER

A Colorado Parks and Wildlife officer prepares the tranquilized bear for transport after it was removed from a tree in Denver on Aug. 23, 2026. (Colorado Parks and Wildlife NE Region)

CPW also said in the X thread that drought conditions are driving more bears into neighborhoods in search of food.

"You're not crazy, we are seeing more bear conflicts this year," CPW wrote. "The drought is forcing bears to seek food in our neighborhoods."

Wildlife officials are urging Coloradans to secure their trash until the morning of pickup, remove bird feeders and keep cars and windows locked to prevent bears from finding food around homes.

The Denver encounter also came just days after a mother bear and cub wandered into the city's Harvey Park neighborhood. CPW tranquilized and relocated those animals after they remained in the populated area for several days.

Colorado Parks and Wildlife warns that bears can become increasingly active as they prepare for winter and search for enough calories to build their fat reserves.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

articles.title: Fast-fashion giant Shein aims for $27bn valuation in Hong Kong market debut
articles.excerpt:
Known for selling cheap clothing, the online retailer has seen its value drop sharply from earlier estimates amid scrutiny over its environmental footprint

Shein will debut on the Hong Kong stock exc...
articles.body_text:
Known for selling cheap clothing, the online retailer has seen its value drop sharply from earlier estimates amid scrutiny over its environmental footprint

Shein will debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange on 1 September, the fast-fashion retailer said on Monday, in a long-awaited listing that would value the group at close to $27bn.

Founded in China and now headquartered in Singapore, the online retailer secured Beijing’s approval last month to make its initial public offering in Hong Kong.

Its valuation has dropped by about 70% from a near $100bn private market peak four years ago, as it aims to raise up to HK$13.86bn ($1.77bn) ⁠in its Hong Kong IPO launched ⁠on Monday.

Shein is selling 280m shares between HK$47.60 and HK$49.50 per share, the filings showed, valuing it at close to $27bn at the top of that range. The company will announce the final price on 31 August and start trading on 1 September. With the funds raised from the market, Shein said it aims to finance its technological capabilities as well as boost its international presence.

Known for selling $5 dresses and $10 jeans to ⁠shoppers in about 160 countries, the ​marked decline in valuation comes after Shein faced questions over slowing ‌growth, rising costs and changing market conditions.

Plans to list in New York and London had been held back in recent years by regulatory hurdles, according to media reports.

The firm moved its headquarters to Singapore between 2021 and 2022, a move analysts say was intended to avoid increasing global scrutiny of Chinese firms.

But it still benefits from China’s unique combination of a huge, low-cost textile manufacturing sector and a highly sophisticated e-commerce logistics network.

By the end of last year, its European customer base rose to 156 million average monthly users, making Shein one of the continent’s biggest e-commerce platforms alongside China’s AliExpress (193 million users) and Amazon (about 180 million users).

In November, the group made waves with its first-ever physical outlet, a dedicated space in the storied BHV department store in Paris.

Hundreds of customers lined up on its opening day, and dozens more people gathered to protest, requiring a heavy police presence to keep the tense situation from getting out of hand.

Demonstrators slammed what they alleged were inhumane working conditions at Shein’s suppliers, the environmental costs of selling clothes not made to last, and unfair competition against brick-and-mortar retailers struggling to stay open.

The company says it holds its suppliers to strict compliance standards and does not tolerate forced labour.

Shein also drew criticism last year in France over the discovery of childlike sex dolls on its platform. The company pledged to cooperate with French authorities and announced it was banning all sex dolls on its platform.

In June, French authorities imposed two fines on Shein totalling more than 22m euros ($25.1m), citing problems with product traceability, environmental labelling and delivery times. At the time Shein said it would contest the “disproportionate” penalties, arguing that no consumer harm had been established.

Overall, Shein has paid over 210m euros in various French fines over the years, and Italy has also imposed fines alleging misleading environmental claims.

Reuters and Agence-France Presse contributed to this report

articles.title: Photo of Disraeli among missing parliamentary works of art, FoI request finds
articles.excerpt:
Press Association given list of 65 items from publicly owned collection that have gone missing since 2024

A photograph of Benjamin Disraeli, an engraved portrait of William Wilberforce and a cartoon ...
articles.body_text:
Press Association given list of 65 items from publicly owned collection that have gone missing since 2024

A photograph of Benjamin Disraeli, an engraved portrait of William Wilberforce and a cartoon of Barbara Castle have all been misplaced by the UK parliamentary authorities, a freedom of information (FoI) request has revealed.

The Press Association has been given a list of more than 65 works of art that have been missing since 2024. They also include a photograph of Margaret Beckett, the UK’s first female foreign secretary and the first woman to lead Labour, and a satirical cartoon by Martin Rowson from the Conservative leadership battle of 1995.

A parliamentary spokesperson said it was a working collection, which meant that objects moved around frequently. None of the works had been permanently written off, they said.

The photograph of Disraeli, Queen Victoria’s favourite prime minister, was taken by John Jabez Edwin Mayall. Mayall was a prolific Victorian portrait photographer who captured the images of many of the era’s best known figures.

Art UK, which catalogues Britain’s publicly owned art, lists 212 Mayall works in UK collections including portraits of Charles Dickens, Karl Marx, Isambard Kingdom Brunel, the soprano Anna Bishop, the scientist Michael Faraday and the explorer David Livingstone.

Mayall also made a fortune photographing Victoria and the wider royal family with his carte de visite portraits feeding the 19th-century “cartomania” collecting craze.

The misplaced Disraeli photograph is likely to be the same as one in other collections, including the Royal Collection, showing a tired, heavy-lidded Disraeli in his 60s.

The missing print of Wilberforce, the most celebrated campaigner against the slave trade, was made by the printmaker William Holl and his brother Francis.

The Rowson cartoon is from the 1995 Tory leadership campaign when John Major resigned as party leader, telling opponents to “put up or shut up”. It shows Major seeking to lance the literal “boil” of the contest, as his deputy Michael Heseltine and challenger-apparent Michael Portillo look on.

Rowson said the issue of cartoons going missing was not uncommon. He said a cartoon of the Foreign Office Christmas party in 2004, sent to the then junior minister Denis MacShane at his department, “never got beyond reception”.

Rowson said: “It’s a shame but it’s hardly the crown jewels – and the point about cartoon originals is that they’ve been published already: the artefact is probably the impression in the newspaper, as that’s its ticket to posterity.

“The original is the modern equivalent to one of Hogarth or Gillray’s copper plates used to create the – reproduced – satirical print. That’s why we belong more properly to journalism than art.”

He said the misplaced work was “small beer compared to one of my cartoons which was part of a touring exhibition of work by members of the British Cartoonists’ Association, all of which were destroyed by a Nato airstrike in the Serbian public library it had reached on its British Council sponsored tour in 1998.”

The missing satirical cartoon of Barbara Castle depicts her as Florence Nightingale.

The number of works involved is much fewer than the 224 reported missing after a similar FoI request in 2018. At the time it included portraits of William Pitt the Younger, and a wartime oil painting by William John MacLeod of the scene after parliament was bombed.

A parliamentary spokesperson said: “There is little evidence of works of art going permanently missing from the Parliamentary Art Collection. As a working collection, artworks are frequently moved between their recorded locations and are often subsequently found, meaning none of the items currently recorded as missing have been written off or are considered a financial loss.

“Parliament continues to reduce the number of artworks recorded as missing through ongoing audits.”

They said five of the “missing” works had been found this year. The art collection is one of four parliamentary heritage collections, which contain 26,000 objects including furniture and decorative arts.

articles.title: Scrapping of Berlin swimming day for Black children becomes latest in long list of race-linked pool rows
articles.excerpt:
Rightwing voices seize on plans to offer Black children an exclusive afternoon at an outdoor pool in the German capital

It was meant to be an outing for Black children in Berlin and their families, o...
articles.body_text:
Rightwing voices seize on plans to offer Black children an exclusive afternoon at an outdoor pool in the German capital

It was meant to be an outing for Black children in Berlin and their families, offering them an exclusive afternoon at an outdoor pool set up by a local theatre.

But the plans, slated for earlier this month, had to be scrapped after they were seized on by rightwing and conservative voices to whip up outrage, leaving organisers fending off racist emails and threats.

Berlin’s Volksbühne theatre said it had extended the invitation in hopes of dismantling some of the barriers that would normally keep these children away from the pool. While other groups had similarly been invited to use pool exclusively without incident, the idea of Black children enjoying a private afternoon at a public pool proved to be controversial among some.

“Berlin is a livable, diverse, colourful and free city. So why do we need safe spaces?” a local Christian Democrat politician, Aileen Weibeler, said on social media, while the far-right Alternative für Deutschland co-leader Alice Weidel described it as “an apartheid” in which “white people are temporarily denied access”.

It was the latest in a long list of incidents linking swimming pools to racism. Across North America and Europe swimming pools have often acted as a flashpoint for wider racial tensions and exclusions.

Earlier this summer, an open-air swimming lake in the eastern German city of Halle made headlines after it refused entry to bathers who did not speak German. In the Netherlands, the Institute for Human Rights recently ruled against a pool after it was found to have singled out a Black child for an identity check.

The list of incidents spans decades. In 2013, the Swiss town of Bremgarten moved to restrict asylum seekers’ access to swimming pools. In Bulgaria, Roma have sounded the alarm about being discriminated against at public pools, while in 2022, a swimming pool in Romania was fined just over €2,000 (£1,716) for barring entry to Romani children.

Some of the association between racism and pools most likely comes down to the intimacy of these spaces, said Jeff Wiltse, the author of Contested Waters: A Social History of Swimming Pools in America. “They’re visually, physically, and socially intimate spaces, and I think that continues to pique people’s social anxieties,” he said.

Wiltse has long studied pools in the US, recasting them as sites that reflect the wider tensions in society at any given time, from James Brock in 1964 pouring hydrochloric acid into a whites-only pool where Black men were swimming, to the Texas police officer who in 2015 pinned an unarmed Black teenager to the ground and drew his gun as he sought to break up a pool party.

In the US, “throughout much of the 20th century, swimming pools were homogenous spaces”, he said. “There was explicit racial segregation of public pools.”

In the late 1940s, as public swimming pools in the US began to be racially desegregated, private pools began to spring up, particularly in suburbs that were almost exclusively white. Many people came to see swimming pools as “a certain type of social space in which the people there are all socially similar”, said Wiltse, who advocates tackling the issue by increasing public investment in community pools that could bring together people from different ethnic and racial backgrounds.

The racialised history of pools – and its continued legacy today – has helped to give rise to a stark racial divide when it comes to swimming ability, one that has had deadly consequences. In the US, the fatal-drowning rate of Black and African American children is three times higher than that of white children.

The statistics are even worse in England, where recent data found that children from Black, Asian and minority ethnic communities are 3.5 times more likely to drown than their white counterparts. Recent figures from Sport England suggest that 95% of Black adults and 80% of Black children do not swim at all.

In 2022, Katrice Rodrigues set out to change this with the launch of Unity Swimming, a community organisation that runs weekly classes aimed at Black and Asian communities.

“People get angry at that, saying: ‘How can it be inclusive if it’s just for Black and Asian communities?’” said Rodrigues, who is also a keynote speaker on diversity in aquatics. “My thing is that we’re making the whole of swimming more inclusive by creating these safe little spaces, which lead to more people swimming, and that makes swimming, as a whole, more inclusive.”

The success of the programme has relied on Rodrigues and her team confronting the wide range of cultural barriers that keep minorities out of the pool, from having parents who are terrified of water to concerns over feeling out of place, dressing modestly or protecting Black hair.

Other barriers have proven more enduring. “There’s a myth and a stereotype that Black people can’t float and can’t swim,” she said. “It’s not true, but I’ve had to correct two experienced swim teachers who thought that was a thing.”

As summers become hotter across the globe, sending more people into rivers, lakes and pools in search of respite, the imperative has grown to ensure that as many people as possible know how to swim, said Rodrigues.

“It’s the only sport that’s going to save lives,” she said. “If you’ve got water safety knowledge, you could help save someone else’s life as well as your own and your whole family. So this has a knock-off effect on families, on communities and for generations.”

articles.title: Most English secondary schools are breaking healthy food rules, finds report
articles.excerpt:
‘Shocking’ breaches such as sweets and crisps at breakfast uncovered just before expansion of free school meals

Three-quarters of secondary schools in England are breaking the rules on food offered t...
articles.body_text:
‘Shocking’ breaches such as sweets and crisps at breakfast uncovered just before expansion of free school meals

Three-quarters of secondary schools in England are breaking the rules on food offered to pupils by serving chips, burgers and hash browns too often – and sweets and crisps at breakfast time, according to a report.

“Shocking” breaches of school food standards have been exposed on Monday, in a new analysis of the food provided at almost 400 state secondaries undertaken by Bite Back, a food charity set up by the chef Jamie Oliver.

D’Arcy Williams, Bite Back’s chief executive, said the picture of schools’ widespread noncompliance with the government-set standards that emerged from its analysis was alarming.

Three out of four menus it analysed at 391 state secondary schools in England contained at least one breach of the standards. Most involved schools offering unhealthy foods more often than is allowed.

At 206 schools (53%), products high in fat, sugar or salt that are meant to be banned altogether – such as crisps, Oreos, Mini Cheddars, chocolate bars and pastries – were being offered to pupils to buy as snacks, including at breakfast time and at lunchtime. Schools are allowed to sell only nuts, seeds, plain vegetables and plain fruit as snacks.

There were 224 schools (57%) providing meat products such as burgers, nuggets, sausages and goujons more often than the twice a week permitted by the standards.

Hash browns, which as a fried starchy food should be a menu option only twice a week, were being offered more often than that at 144 schools (37%).

There were 123 schools (31%) using chocolate in solid form, such as chocolate chips or chocolate coating, as an ingredient in dessert or bakes, despite it being banned.

“These findings are very alarming and expose a system that is fundamentally failing our children,” said Williams.

“It is shocking to find crisps and chocolate being pushed at breakfast time or processed meats like sausage rolls and bacon baps being served far more frequently than the rules allow.

“Young people have been telling us for years that their school food is ‘beige, bland and boring’ and now we have more evidence that they are being surrounded by unhealthy food throughout the school day.

“Schools should be a sanctuary for health and learning, yet the current postcode lottery of food quality is undermining that mission.”

But in other findings that parents may find reassuring, only eight schools (2%) were flouting the ban on selling confectionery such as KitKats, Haribo sweets and Maltesers as standalone items. And even fewer – just three schools (1%) – were selling banned sugary drinks such as Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Fanta and Sprite.

Campaigners for healthier food voiced concern at the findings. Katharine Jenner, the executive director of the Obesity Health Alliance, said: “Schools should be one of the places where we can be confident children are being given nutritious food. Yet this research suggests too many are still being routinely exposed to processed meat, fried foods, pastries and confectionery beyond what the standards allow.

“Children are already growing up surrounded by unhealthy food across the wider food system, from what is marketed to them to what is promoted in shops. If we can’t even get the food environment right in schools, where children spend such a large part of their lives, then we have a serious problem.”

Ministers are preparing to unveil an overhaul of the school food standards, which child health and anti-obesity organisations have been seeking for years.

At the start of the new academic year in England next month, there will be a major expansion of access to free school meals instigated by the Labour government. From now on, all pupils from a household where someone is receiving universal credit will qualify in England.

The Department for Education acknowledged that schools did flout the standards. A spokesperson said: “We want every child to be healthy, happy and ready to learn, and nutritious food plays a vital role in helping them achieve that.

“That’s why we are delivering the most ambitious overhaul of school food in a generation, making sure children have access to healthy, balanced meals, get more of their five a day and are protected from the harms of eating too much ultra-processed food.

“We know not every school is following these standards, which is exactly why we will introduce a strengthened enforcement regime, alongside requiring every school to publish their food policy and menus online to improve transparency for parents.”

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's three child victims forgotten amid crowds of support: mother of six
articles.excerpt: Writer Bethany Mandel, a mother of six, says Cora, Dawson and Callan have been cast aside as crowds rally behind Lindsay Clancy. "We all know her name. Very few people know the names of her children,"...
articles.body_text:
Writer Bethany Mandel, a mother of six, says Cora, Dawson and Callan have been cast aside as crowds rally behind Lindsay Clancy. "We all know her name. Very few people know the names of her children," she told Fox News Digital.

A mother of six says that Lindsay Clancy's three young victims have been forgotten amid the crowds rallying behind the woman who killed them, and is now on trial for murder.

Lindsay Clancy, 36, has been charged with three counts of first-degree murder in connection with the deaths of her children — Cora, Dawson and Callan, all younger than 6 — who were discovered strangled at the family's home in January 2023. The prosecution wrapped up its case Monday morning, after which her defense attorney began presenting arguments, contending that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis at the time she killed her children.

Bethany Mandel, a conservative columnist and mother of six, said in an interview with Fox News Digital that she believes the three children killed by Lindsay Clancy, Cora, Dawson and Callan, have been cast aside in conversations about the case.

LINDSAY CLANCY MURDER TRIAL BECOMES SOCIAL MEDIA OBSESSION AS TIKTOKERS, SLEUTHS DEBATE CONTROVERSIAL CASE

Lindsay Clancy's three children, Cora, Dawson and Callan, were killed at the family's Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Plymouth Superior Court)

"We all know her name," Mandel said, referring to Lindsay Clancy. "Very few people know the names of her children."

Particularly, Mandel was disturbed by the hundreds of people who stood outside the Plymouth Superior Court on Thursday in support of Lindsay Clancy. Those who have gathered in pink say the show of support is not an endorsement of what happened, but a stand for maternal mental health awareness and for mothers suffering from postpartum conditions.

LINDSAY CLANCY’S PARENTS GET MASSIVE GLOBAL DONOR SUPPORT AS FUNDRAISER SURPASSES $830K

Lindsay Clancy, who is on trial for killing her three children, Cora, Dawson and Callan, in a family photo entered as evidence. (Plymouth Superior Court)

"We don't see any of them standing out there with a button with the three children's faces on them. When you listen to interviews with all of the women who are standing out, they almost never mention the three child victims," Mandel said.

A not-guilty verdict by reason of insanity would not result in Clancy's release; instead, she would be committed to a state psychiatric hospital and subject to periodic reviews.

LINDSAY CLANCY'S EX-HUSBAND HAS QUIETLY REMARRIED AND STARTED OVER AMID HER MURDER TRIAL

Two of the three Clancy children in a family photo shown as evidence at their mother's murder trial. Cora, Dawson and Callan were killed in January 2023. (Plymouth Superior Court)

Just days after Lindsay Clancy killed her kids in January 2023, Patrick wrote on a GoFundMe page, "I want to ask all of you that you find it deep within yourselves to forgive Lindsay, as I have...The real Lindsay was generously loving and caring towards everyone - me, our kids, family, friends, and her patients."

(L) Lindsay and Patrick Clancy with two of their three children in this undated photo and (R) Lindsay Clancy listens to testimony from her former mother in law at her murder trial in Plymouth Mass., Tuesday Aug. 18, 2026 in Plymouth, Mass. (Lindsay Marie Clancy facebook and Pool)

Jonathan Hatami, deputy district attorney in the complex child abuse section in the office of the Los Angeles County District Attorney also agreed that much of the conversation has been surrounding how Lindsay Clancy has conducted herself during the trial, not on her children who were killed.

LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS COME ACROSS AS 'TONE DEAF,' 'UNCARING' AND 'SNARKY,' DEFENSE ATTORNEY SAYS

A photo of one of Lindsay Clancy's three children, shown as evidence at her murder trial in the 2023 deaths of Cora, Dawson and Callan. (Plymouth Superior Court)

"This shouldn't be about the defendant even though it's become that, it's became this entire show about her, really should be about the victims and what the defendant did to those victims. And we try to do that in our trials and in our cases. And it seems like that's gotten lost. In this specific case, and it's really disappointing, and people don't realize these children matter," Hatami told Fox News Digital.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

Expert witnesses called by both the defense and prosecution focused their Friday testimony on Lindsay Clancy's mental state at the time she killed her children, specifically whether she was experiencing psychosis.

LINDSAY CLANCY DESCRIBED A MALE VOICE ORDERING HER TO ‘KILL HER CHILDREN AND KILL HERSELF’: TESTIMONY

Dr. Phillip Resnick, a forensic psychiatrist and authority on filicide, said Lindsay Clancy was functioning for much of the day she killed her kids, even making a snowman with her children, until she suffered the hallucination and what he called a "delusion of influence," feeling her body was taken over and out of her control and was feeling like a "puppet."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Dr. Avram Mack, a child and forensic psychiatrist, a prosecution expert, said Lindsay Clancy's actions on the day her children died were methodical and organized, stating she should be found criminally responsible for their deaths, directly rebutting the defense.

PROSECUTOR CORNERS LINDSAY CLANCY'S CATHOLIC MOTHER-IN-LAW WITH 'MORTAL SIN' QUESTION

"My opinion is that she retained the capacity required for having criminal responsibility for these actions," Mack testified.

Closing arguments could begin as soon as Monday or Tuesday before jurors begin deliberating in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial.

Adam Sabes is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Adam.Sabes@fox.com and on Twitter @asabes10.

articles.title: Ex-cricket captains urge 'proper medical care' for Imran Khan
articles.excerpt:
Imran Khan, shown here in 2022, has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges which he denies

A group of former cricket captains, including Indian batting legend Sunil Gavaskar and one of England...
articles.body_text:
Imran Khan, shown here in 2022, has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges which he denies

A group of former cricket captains, including Indian batting legend Sunil Gavaskar and one of England's longest-serving skippers Sir Alastair Cook, have called on Pakistan to ensure its ex-PM Imran Khan be given proper care while in custody.

The cricketer-turned-politician has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges which he denies.

In a letter to Pakistan's current leader Shehbaz Sharif, the 21 former skippers aired concern that Khan, 73, was allowed "only a few hours" at a hospital last week where he was examined by a state-appointed team.

Khan's party has also filed a contempt petition against the government for not giving him access to his own doctors, as ordered by the top court.

The former cricket captains laid out three demands in their letter, the first of which is that Khan be assessed by a medical board directed by Pakistan's Supreme Court – which would include his personal physicians – particularly on the reported loss of vision in his right eye.

They also urged authorities to allow weekly visits by Khan's family, as ordered by the court, "without interruptions or administrative delays".

Finally, they asked that any treatment recommended by the medical board be "provided without delay".

"Imran Khan is 73 years old and has now spent more than three years in custody," read the letter initiated by former Australian captain Greg Chappell.

"Whatever the legal and political arguments surrounding his case, the basic decency of ensuring a court-ordered medical process is actually completed is not, in our view, a controversial request."

Among the other signatories were England's Michael Atherton, Michael Brearley, Nasser Hussain, Andrew Strauss and David Gower, India's Kapil Dev and Dilip Vengsarkar, and Australia's Belinda Clark, Adam Gilchrist, Steve Waugh and Kim Hughes.

Fourteen of the former skippers had also supported an earlier appeal for "humane treatment and proper medical care" for Khan which was submitted in February.

Khan's lawyer claimed at the time that his client had 15% vision left in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.

The signatories of both letters had described themselves as "former colleagues and rivals who share a bond forged on the cricket field", adding that the bond "transcends the borders and disputes that too often divide countries".

Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.

He was imprisoned in August 2023 and has faced charges in more than 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts, all of which he and his party Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf say are politically motivated.

His jailing sparked large-scale protests by supporters, which were met with a crackdown by authorities.

Pakistan's Supreme Court had on Tuesday directed the government to transfer Khan to a private hospital to be examined by physicians.

He was instead seen by doctors at a government-run hospital in Islamabad, who deemed him "medically fit", before he was moved back to prison.

articles.title: 'Office' star says James Talarico's religious beliefs 'achingly close' to Jesus Christ
articles.excerpt:
"The Office" star Rainn Wilson claimed that Texas U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico's form of religion was "achingly close" to Jesus despite Republican critics.

"The Office" star Rainn Wilson insi...
articles.body_text:
"The Office" star Rainn Wilson claimed that Texas U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico's form of religion was "achingly close" to Jesus despite Republican critics.

"The Office" star Rainn Wilson insisted Thursday that Texas' Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico was "achingly close" to Jesus' "brand of Christianity" compared to his conservative opponents.

On his "Soul Boom" podcast, Wilson and New York Times journalist Ezra Klein called out what they believed was hypocrisy from Texas GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton and his supporters repeatedly attacking Talarico despite their "aggressively professed Christianity."

"Whenever I watch these attacks, I think, ‘You all would have hated Jesus Christ,’" Klein said. "You would have found him to be the most annoying, weepy, worrying about the wrong people — the outsiders, the outcasts…"

BILL MAHER BLASTS DEMOCRATIC PARTY, SAYS IT IS FINE WITH RELIGION 'AS LONG AS THAT FAITH ISN’T JEWISH'

Texas U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico has been criticized for pushing progressive politics under a Christian banner. (Danielle Villasana/Getty Images)

Klein, who is Jewish, and Wilson, who subscribes to the Bahá'í Faith, added that they were not against Christians as a whole, with Wilson describing many of them as the most "caring" and "compassionate" people he's met.

"Well, that's why I frame this around Talarico, because Talarico is Christian. That's the point, that it is his Christianity they hate," Klein said.

"His brand of Christianity, which is so, so achingly close to Jesus' brand of Christianity," Wilson responded.

TALARICO SAYS HE 'HATES CHRISTIANITY' IN UNEARTHED INTERVIEW WITH TRANSGENDER 'LATINX' THEOLOGIAN

Klein and Wilson also criticized "contemporary Christianity" for not focusing enough on "greed" in society while fixating on sexuality.

"The Office" star Rainn Wilson defended James Talarico's faith as "achingly close" to Jesus. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"It is harder for a rich man to get — harder for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to get into heaven. And then you're cutting taxes on the rich and obsessed with who's f---ing whom," Klein said.

"Yeah. Jesus didn't talk about who's f---ing whom. He really didn't. The hypocrisy of contemporary Christianity is astonishing," Wilson said.

JAMES TALARICO ADMITS PAST COMMENTS 'MISSED THE MARK' WHEN CONFRONTED ON CLAIMS LIKE GOD IS 'NON-BINARY'

Fox News Digital reached out to Talarico's campaign and Paxton's campaign for comment.

Talarico has frequently touted his religious background. He has been attacked for pushing progressive views that many see as being at odds with Christianity, such as support for abortion and transgender ideology.

Earlier this month, a 2025 clip of Talarico resurfaced in which he attacked a Texas bill that required schools to teach Bible stories as historical fact. He argued that this amounted to pushing "propaganda" on children and was not just bad for state schools, but for society overall.

Frank Turek pushed back on the idea that James Talarico's faith was close to Jesus Christ. (Getty Images)

"It was a new state curriculum that would teach Christian Bible stories as historical fact, as the only truth to our youngest students, and, I mean, kindergarten, first-graders," he said.

"These are kids who aren’t able to think for themselves yet. They haven’t formed their own worldviews," Talarico continued.

He further warned that the alleged effort to "push propaganda, to push indoctrination on those youngest students is deeply immoral and should trouble all of us."

In a comment to Fox News Digital, Christian author Frank Turek pushed back on the claim, calling it a "war" on the reality of Jesus.

"Calling James Talarico's brand of Christianity ‘achingly close’ to Jesus's reveals a social-justice lens so thick that people no longer care to interpret Jesus on his own terms, but would rather reimagine him on theirs," Turek said. "Talarico defends the murder of the unborn, the sexualization of children at drag queen story hour events, and has described teaching Bible stories in public schools as immoral. To describe such a person's position as being ‘achingly close’ to Jesus is a war on the reality of who Jesus is, what He taught, and what it means to follow Him."

Fox News' Alexander Hall contributed to this report.
